I bought these primarily to use as studio monitors. I have or have had a number of high end cans over the years, Grado, Beyerdynamic, Sennheiser, Etymotic Research, etc.. however for recording purposes I have always preferred my AudioTechnica ATH-M40 due to their sealed design and extremely neutral response compared to most of the aforementioned cans which 'color' the sound in one way or another.

I've had the M40 monitors since they first came out in the early 90's and they were really starting to fall apart so I decided to look for a replacement. I was somewhat surprised by all of the praise for these Denon cans considering that last time I paid attention to the headphone scene Denon wasn't even making headphones. However, after looking at the response curves and reading all the glowing reviews from knowledgeable users on these and the D5000 series I decided to give these a shot as my new studio monitors.

Overall, I would say they live up to the hype. These are definitely the best sealed cans I have heard, the highs are very accurate with an airy presence which feels like you are listening to an open headphone. They do not sound quite as neutral as the M40 to me, primarily due to the punchy low frequency response which can be a bit excessive with certain sources but that may soften up once they are properly broken in. Like any good headphone these will greatly benefit from quality amplification, but I must say they sound quite good unamped compared to some of my other high end cans like the Beyer DT990 which I consider useless without proper amplification.

These are also very comfortable although they could have made them a bit smaller, my head is somewhat small and they just barely fit me on the smallest setting.. all of my other headphones are too tight on the smallest setting so I am not sure what denon was thinking when they came up with the sizing for these.

Sony's Handycam line of video recorders has been a solid choice for years, and with the introduction of the HDR-PJ430V Handycam Sony has brought another excellent recorder to the market. It produces excellent quality video, it takes good still shots and it has some features I have never seen in other camcorders.

This is a very small, compact and lightweight camcorder, roughly the size of a box of butter sticks. Out of curiosity I put the camcorder with the battery installed on the kitchen scale and it weighed in at under 14 oz. The small size and very light weight make this camcorder very easy to hold in one hand without fatigue. This is very good news for people who either do not have a tripod or would rather hold the camera for all of their work.

At first power on, the user gets to select all of the necessary first-time settings - date and time, language and other preferences. This is all done on the touch-screen LCD. My last camcorder did not have a touch screen so I was minorly surprised by this feature. It also revealed the one and only issue I have had with this camera so far - the touch screen is slightly unresponsive compared to other devices I have used that offer the technology, and I find myself having to be very deliberate about accessing the screen's features.

Once the first-time defaults are set, this camcorder is ready to start recording. Without too much thought about what I was doing I pointed the camera at a target and started recording. As I panned the room, the camera made the necessary adjustments for light and dark, making a huge adjustment as I passed the screen of my computer and adjusting back to normal lighting as I passed it. This is a normal camcorder feature and it seems to handle the light differences very easily.

The zoom is above average. From about 40' away the camera can be zoomed in enough to read small lettering on a box. This is great for recording when the subject is at an appreciable distance.

The camcorder also seems to do a very good job of auto-focusing, which it does as light conditions change. Setting the camera close to a wall and shining a light around it, you can actually see it making focal adjustments on the screen and settling on a good balance of light and focus.

Video quality is, in a word, outstanding. Videos I have taken have come out exceedingly clear and bright without a lot of graininess that I have gotten with lesser camcorders. Even zoomed in all the way, image quality remains very good. Sound is also very clear and crisp.

Where this camcorder excels over any other camera I have used, though, is in the image stability (anti-shake or anti-jitter, if you prefer). Sony makes a big deal about their stability component and it works as well as advertised. Turning the camera around so that the lens is facing the user, one can jiggle the camera and actually see the lens being adjusted as the camera moves. It moves very much like an eyeball which honestly is a little creepy but it works very well. If holding the camera instead of using a tripod, video will definitely come out better as a result of this feature.

This is not just a camcorder, though. It also takes still shots. I like that this camera can be used as a still-shot camera, and though the user can make a few adjustments to make the image come out better, most of the settings are automatic. I have had better success with dedicated still-shot cameras, personally, though I have managed to render some good photos with the Handycam as well. The camcorder definitely does a better job than the typical smartphone when it comes to taking photos... It is very convenient to have a single device doing the work of two.

Probably the most interesting feature of this camcorder is the built-in projector. I had low expectations of this feature until I actually tried it. Projecting roughly 30' down a dark hallway, the projector built into the camcorder lit up the wall with bright, clear images that looked great. As I moved farther from the wall image quality diminished as expected and it got better as I got closer, but this feature really does work nicely. It does not work well enough to give a professional presentation, of course, but it is fine for entertaining small groups and for quick playback right after shooting. Be aware, however, that the projector runs through all available images and movies in one sweep without taking a pause between.

The software that installs when the camcorder is plugged into a computer is called PlayMemories Home, and it is actually a decent application for managing the content on the camera. It has more features than one would expect from the software that comes with a device. It allows for importing/exporting media, making basic edits on media (such as quick color adjustments and trimming/cropping), putting together slide shows, creating CD/DVD media, share online with several social media sites and a lot more. Most included software packages (at least, the ones I have seen) provide for much more basic handling of media.

The camcorder is supposedly wifi-capable, but this requires an accessory that I do not have so I cannot really comment on this other than to say the capability is available.

One of the things that Sony's HandyCam series is known for is the infrared/night vision modes that allow for better filming in extremely low light conditions. This particular camcorder does not seem to have that mode. It does recognize low-light conditions, but there is no option to turn on night vision recording. Though not a feature I really need, it is important to realize it's not available on this model. Curiously absent from this camcorder (considering that infrared is not available) is a light. So far this has not been an issue but I am curious to see how it does outside on a moonless night. Now, all of this said, Sony does have an accessory that is available that adds both a light and infrared capability. If you need a light or infrared with this camera, you will need that add-on, but be aware that it's a little pricey ($150 as I write this, which would bring the overall cost of this camcorder with the light to roughly $1000 at this time).

Sony's new HDR-PJ430V HandyCam is a very nice camcorder with some interesting and useful features. It produces very good quality imagery, it is very easy to use and it is very compact and light which makes it a camera that can be used for a long period of time without fatigue. This camcorder is very much worth consideration if you're in the market for a good-quality device - especially if the projection feature is of interest.

As a freelance camera operator, I'm no stranger to these. This is clearly designed for us low budget video shooters using small DSLR style cameras, which is why it uses a Sony camcorder battery plate and designed with a hood for outdoor viewing. It has some pretty great features for the price point, including crop mark overlays, peaking indicators, and individual color channels. That being said, it can be used for all sorts of things, such as a Raspberry Pi monitor, backup camera screen, or even a second monitor for your laptop (that's a fun one!). It even has included sound, something a lot of these monitors do not, more on that later.
This is really designed for video use, and for that it does a pretty great job for the price. It comes with a hotshoe mount adapter to put on top of your camera, and uses standard batteries (most LED lights and other accessories also use these batteries, so you probably have some already if you work in video). The colors are vivid and sharp, more accurate than my Atmost Ninja 2 recorder screen, and nice and big for focus checking.
The hood is a nice touch as well, but it requires the snap on frame to attach, and the frame has a weird problem in which it partially obstructs the HDMI port. Maybe I'm just doing it wrong, but I found I needed to leave that corner off the frame if I wanted to use the HDMI plug.
Speaking of the HDMI plug, it comes with one included which I thought was pretty rad of them, but it isn't the more modern micro HDMI type, but the slightly older MINI one. That's the outdated kind that older devices use (such as 3rd generation Intel laptops or cameras like the GH2), but pretty much everything made in the last few years has been using the newer micro one. So it seems weird that they included this one. Personally, it will come in handy because I DO have a laptop that still uses that plug, but I don't intend to use it with this monitor. All my cameras that use that plug are long gone at this point.
Another couple of things to note: The focus peaking is pretty much useless. It oversharpens the image and thinks high contrast parts of bokeh are "in focus", which is weird. Thankfully my Sony cameras have peaking built in so that isn't much of an issue. Also, the screen is large enough and is HD enough resolution (not full 1080 but more than 720) that you don't really need peaking to tell what's in focus. You can see it with your eyes. Also, if using with a camera that is outputting a 16:9 image, you have to change the screen size setting from the default, which is to maximize the screen. Everything looked a little stretched because the display is a little taller than the output of my camera until I turned that off.
As far as sound, I mentioned earlier that this monitor has a speaker. That's good for when you want to review footage on the monitor, and even better if using with a Raspberry Pi or monitor for other things where it might be your only source of sound. It is also really useful if shooting with a Sony A6000 or similar smaller camera that doesn't have a headphone jack... this offers a headphone jack so you can monitor off the HDMI feed. That's pretty useful right there! But don't forget, when you turn the live view back on, you are going to get major feedback from the mic to the speaker unless you quickly turn the volume all the way DOWN first! Or just leave headphones in if that's how you roll.

It is important to note however that it will not accept a 4k signal. The actual resolution is 1280x800, and it will accept up to 1080p as an input, but more than that fails. At the time I'm reviewing this, it seems that there are similar monitors that can accept a 4k input for around the same price. I'm guessing they are updated versions of the same design, as there are no monitors that actually have that resolution for this price, rather they just accept the feed and down-sample to 1280x800, just like this one. So at the end of the day, it probably won't matter if it accepts 4k or not. Some cameras don't like outputting a different resolution than they are recording, so if you are recording in 4k and outputting 1080p, that might be an issue. Otherwise, this is a solid value.

First off, this was purchased for a 27" iMac for home usage.

I changed my previous configuration where my modem, router, NAS and iMac were all located in or on my office desk. These were all connected to a CyberPower CP1000PFCLCD that's been working perfectly for almost 5 years. After moving the location of the modem, router and NAS to a more central location; I moved the CyberPower UPS along with them. This left me for a need for a small UPS for the iMac only.

I originally looked at the smaller Cyberpower UPSs but then looked at the competition. The two I had narrowed it down to were similar in price, but the Tripp Lite offered a larger battery capacity. I then looked at their listings and found the Origin listed under the Product Information. The Tripp LIte stated that it was Made in USA or Imported while the Cyberpower was listed with a China origin. A little more searching and Tripp Lite is based out of Chicago. This essentially sealed the deal and the INTERNET 550U was ordered from Amazon.

Much to my disappointment, there was a large label on the side of the box clearly stating MADE IN CHINA. -1 Star

From the Manufacturer section of the listing would have you believe that the PowerAlert Software will work on the Mac OSX. After trying to find the PowerAlert Software from the Trip Lite web site would state the following...

"If you are a home or small office user, PowerAlert Local is for you. It allows you to monitor and control a UPS system connected to your computer through a USB or serial cable. It also supports automatic file saves and unattended computer shutdown during power outages."

Looking below this statement and there is no download availability for Mac OSX. The only Mac OSX software availability is called PowerAlert Network Shutdown Agent and it states the following...

"If you need to automate computer shutdown during an outage without a USB or serial connection to a UPS system, or if you can’t use Java, PowerAlert Network Shutdown Agent is for you. When it detects a user-selected event (such as low battery) broadcast by a network-connected UPS system, it initiates shutdown or hibernation after a user-defined delay."

Not quite what I was looking for but I did find that the native software within Mac OSX seems to do what I need it to do without the need of installing additional software. -0 Stars

This UPS is considerably light compared to the larger CyberPower. For whatever reason, I was expecting something heavier. It gives the impression that it's cheap in feel. Not necessarily of any fault of the device but some perceived notion that I had. But when coupled with the horrible, plastic smell; it comes off as another characteristic of a cheap, Chinese product. -1 Star

In summary, we had a long power outage last weekend while I was at the computer. The UPS worked as it should, allowing me to shut down the computer.

This GE 40529 ULTRAPRO SIGNAL FINDER HD TV ANTENNA (LED Signal Meter Technology; Built in Amplifier; Indoor 60 Mile Range; VHF | UHF | HDTV; 10ft. Coaxial Cable) isn’t cheap, but it’s an excellent antenna. On my older 40” Samsung Smart TV, the antenna recognizes 48 free HDTV broadcast stations (many are local advertising channels, of course) when set up in my downstairs living room. Most of the broadcast channels display clear, non-pixelated pictures.

This is better performance than my previous favorite antenna (not amplified) which brought in about 43 stations with many pixelated displays, when set up in an upstairs bedroom with an old 26” digital/analog TV. Because I live in a hilly area, upstairs is a far, far better location for any indoor antenna in my condo. I was surprised that this antenna gets the San Jose NBC channel that is 51 miles away across many hills--the other antenna didn’t pick up that channel at all.

The signal meter, which shows 1-3 (top-row) LED lights to indicate weak, good, or strong signals for each channel, is very useful for finding the best position and orientation of the antenna in a room. I love the fact that this antenna can be mounted on a wall, can sit upright on a table (using the included stand), or can lie flat on a table.

The coaxial cable has a good, threaded connector that attaches the plug firmly to the TV antenna connector.

I bought these on impulse because 1) they were Klipsch, 2) they were "noise isolating" and 3) they were on sale. $30. Sorry to say they aren't worth half that.

They are NOT noise canceling. They are noise "isolating" because they are the ear bud design that seals into the ear canal, like millions of other ear buds. Nothing special. Any descent set of silicon earbuds will do the same noise isolation.

I knew in 30 seconds these earbuds lacked any low end. No bass at all. The specs say they go down to 12 Hz. Hah. No way. The music is simply not full and rich. The highs are excellent, but with no bass, the music is really thin.

I'm amazed how many reviews say how nice the music is. My throwaway Creative earbuds are much fuller and more sensitive.

With the S3's I have to turn the volume up more and there's still no bass. I would consider this somewhat dangerous. You crank up the volume to get more bass and you burn your ears out with the excessive treble.

I tried all three sizes of earbuds, too, just to see if it was a sealing problem. But no matter which size earbud I tried, the music sucked.

I tried all the EQ settings on my iPhone 4. None added any noticeable bass. Maybe it's an impedance mismatch

This concerns me about other things Klipsch.

I did like the way you can turn them upside down and drape the wires over you ears to hold them in place for running, but I didn't actually try them before putting them away. Might work. Might not. My initial feeling with any of the bud sizes is that they tended to fall out of my ears.

Strangely, the buds that came with an old Creative MP3 player are far superior.

If I had paid the full $49 for these things I would be really upset.

The sound is fine. It's what I would expect from quality tweeters and a reasonable size woofer with a decent driver. It does not compare to a decent set of bookshelf type monitors like the JBL LSR series but the price is far lower so I guess they're ok for PC speakers.

But the excellence ends at the sound. The speakers do not have an analog signal input from the computer (there is one at the puck for a MP3 player or whatever). Instead, the signal comes via USB. The problem is the speakers do not come with any drivers. Bose assumes you have the drivers already on your Windows installation. That's a very bad assumption as many people do not have the drivers (just do a google search on Bose Companion 5 drivers to see). There's no help from Bose here. The drivers cannot be downloaded from their web site. I called Bose's tech support and after half and hour they were not able to solve the problem. I eventually solved the problem myself on my Windows 7 Pro 64-bit install but I think it's terribly lame that Bose cannot provide the driver for their product. If I wasn't using the pre-load install of Windows they assume everyone uses, then I would be screwed.

So exactly what do I get for this odd USB input in lieu of a standard audio input? Nothing except incompatibility and the inability to use the speakers apart from a full blown PC. The audio quality and features are not improved by USB audio input. Period.

Room mode correction should be a straightforward feaure on speakers like these. It is not. Although my sound card supports it, the Bose speakers do not have the DSP to do it independently. The lack of sound-card independent RMC doesn't justify the high cost of these speakers. If it were included, the price would look a little better.

I installed the Companion 5 system on an Ergotron cart. The two speakers fit perfectly under the monitor the way I wanted (I removed the stands). The acoustimass is bulkier than I would have liked but I think it's fair to say a smaller module would not perform as well and for most under-desk installs it would be fine. What I do think it's fair to complain about is the poor design of the acoustimass module case. Despite being very heavy, it features a plastic rear end-cap that is fragile. Come-on. For the price, give me painted steel not brittle plastic. The case is also oddly shaped with curves that prevent anything but a bottom-down mount position. The case is not designed to be mounted in a down-firing position, up-firing or on it's side or upside down. The case is also not equipped or rated to be flown or ceiling mounted (it could fall apart and drop parts on people below). Bose should know these are all viable positions. Not everyone can have this thing on the floor with like six wires running out for people to trip over -- seriously, that is totally not acceptable in a public space.

Bose has a habit of not publishing Watts RMS specifications for their amplifiers or speaker handling abilities. I sort of understand not wanting to confuse consumers who don't understand driver efficiencies, but at least give us some max. 1 meter SPL's so we have some clue how loud these things are. As it is, the Companion 5 is loud enough for a PC system in a fairly live medium-sized residential room. It's much louder than my Wave system which proved way more anemic than it was made out to be. The Wave is useless except in the smallest bedroom. I use the Companion 5 primarily in my kitchen (on the Ergotron cart). The kitchen is fairly live but has some acoustic paneling to tame some of the reverberations. If I were putting this system in a small classroom, I would think twice. As a PC system for someone who sits right in front of it, it's obviously perfectly good. I probably wouldn't even use it at half-volume sitting that close.

To mention right off the bat, I am not even an amateur radio operator, just someone who enjoys radio. I find radio to be far more romantic and compelling than modern methods of broadcasting. Staying up late in the night and turning the dial with the soft glow of the tuner, the sound of static and mystery that can sometimes accompany radio broadcasts offers something truly genuine that you can't get anywhere else today. That feeling is priceless and not duplicable (If that was even a word).

Anyway, this radio is good quality and contains the capability needed to reach further than most others. If you enjoy radio as I do, a clock radio, ghetto blaster or home stereo won't cut it. If you know what I am talking about, then this radio is for you. I've stayed up many nights listening to Coast to Coast AM on the internet, but it lacked the feeling something like this radio will bring you. I was unable to pick up a station on my home stereo to listen to CTC and was forced to use the internet. The internet provided a clear, stereo sounding broadcast and was very clear.

The CC Radio has been spoken about on the program for many years. I finally picked one up and am very pleased with it's performance. I can now pick up the radio broadcast of Coast to Coast AM and with all the nuances I expect of a a late night radio broadcast. When interesting speakers talk about compelling topics, a crystal clear internet broadcast does not move you inside. However, using the CC Radio, the slight static, the slight fading in and out and all other fantastic experiences you can only receive using a real radio, it has the ability to make you feel and even send chills up your spine. There is just something a good solid radio can do for you that nothing else can and the CC Radio delivers on that 100%.

You will not be disappointed and I really need to get my license.

An air mouse is not something you would normally use with a PC-based system unless you are trying to save space or are giving a presentation in which case it is a convenient accessory. Such a mouse is a lot more useful for things like Smart TVs, though it is also useful for embedded systems like a Raspberry Pi. I have used several air mice and I was curious to see how well this one would compare to others I have used. So far it has worked well, under both Linux as well as Windows. I will state up front that I have not used it with a Smart TV.

At a glance, this little device looks like a TV remote and little more, but it is quite a bit more than that. It does work as a remote, of course, but it also works as a mouse with a full-up keyboard. On one side of this device there are all of the controls you would expect to find on a remote for a Smart TV remote – volume control, channel settings, mode buttons, play, search and more. Flip the unit over and there is a keyboard, with 38 keys and most regular keyboard functions accessible through function key settings.

The unit requires two AAA batteries, not included.

I decided to try it with my Linux workstation, running CentOS 7 with a 64-bit 3.10.0-series kernel. I did not have to load special drivers and I did not need to do any special configuration at all, it was just plug and play. I was able to move the mouse just by waving the device in front of the screen and several of the buttons on the remote side worked as I would have hoped – Home took me to the browser home page, volume controls worked, Search worked, the menu button brought up the menu for the current application with focus and more. The keyboard portion worked as it should and I was able to type, though I found it a little awkward after being used to a full-sized keyboard for so long.

I also tried it with my Windows 10 system and I got nearly identical results. It required no drivers, no special configuration, no extra set-up – it just works as expected. The buttons works the same under Windows as they did under Linux for me and I was able to navigate as desired.

This is a good air mouse that works well under Linux and Windows. It should work fine with smaller systems like the Raspberry Pi (which uses a derivative of the Linux kernel). As an added bonus, it is relatively inexpensive. If you need an air mouse, this one is worth some consideration.

This is a tablet running a real operating system (Windows 10) hooked up to a small keyboard with a trackpad. And it's all right.

It's thicker and heavier but smaller than my 11 inch MacBook Air, which makes it more convenient in some respects and less convenient in others. The MacBook Air is a used 2012 model with a Core i5 and 4gb ram. It's snappy, but it didn't come with an SD slot, and used it cost about a hundred more than this. The quad core atom processor on the transformer book is pretty fast for a tablet, but it is definitely a lightweight compared to a core i5. Or even an i3.

My iPad Air runs iOS. Way less versatile than Windows 10 in terms of doing work-a-day things, having a browser respond the way you're used to having it respond, etc., but it's still pretty good. However, the keyboard experience is something of a pain, especially since there's no trackpad and you have to touch the tablet face to do the mouse-like things. And using the mail program is harder on the iPad than it is on a mac laptop or on the transformer book.

The transformer book is noticeably slower than either of the other devices, but I was able to do everything I set out to do on it. The Office apps are good and integrate seamlessly with the other Office installations on my other stuff. The screen is as nice as or nicer than my iPad Air. I had a MeMo for a year, and I loved the screen on that. This is very similar - excellent resolution, nice and bright, a bit wider aspect than what the iPad Air has.

The sound is about as good as one would expect. Which is to say, meh. But that's what headphones are for.

Cortano makes it easy to get set up. I asked it to find the apps I wanted. When I want something from the control panel, I ask for that. Since this is my first time with Windows 10, having the assistant helps a lot.

There do seem to be some battery issues. Charging takes a long time. There was an issue with the MeMos, as well, that I sort of resolved by fully cycling the battery a couple of times.

All things considered, I like this tablet/transformer book quite a bit. My only significant issue with it is weight. For my purposes, the ultralight notebook or the regular tablet will meet my needs on any given day. However, if you like your PC desktop and need, essentially, a shuttle craft, though. this is a pretty good compromise machine. It's a decent enough tablet. You can do business stuff, check email, surf the web, and watch movies. You won't be transcoding video or playing resource intense games, but this ultimately is a nice tablet with a keyboard. Not a desktop substitute. Maybe not even a laptop substitute, depending on your needs. But definitely a nice tablet.

I was getting really annoyed with battery life/charging issues. My iPad Air will stand by for a couple of weeks, no problem, whereas this thing dies if I leave it off the charger a couple of days. I was able to solve some of this by running task manager and disabling some of the high impact background apps (Microsoft OneDrive is a big offender). I wore out Sgt Pepper on that thing, and then, a friend happened to have it playing on his parents' high end Marantz receiver and impressive speakers when I stopped by one day. Notebook computers can overheat. It isn't a worry when you use your computer sparingly, but it can become a problem with extended usage. This cooling pad was designed to solve the problem by circulating air via two small fans with the power supplied by your notebook's USB. The movement of air is, supposedly, enough to keep your notebook from overheating or at least lessen the chances.

A product like this certainly sounds like a good idea and a practical solution to a problem, but does it really work as promised? Well, it does cause some extra flow of air, as expected, but the cooling effects are minimal. The main reason is because the flow of air is so light. Turn on the fans and place your hand next to them. You will barely feel anything and this is reason enough to suspect that it makes little difference.

Another thing to keep in mind with this cooling pad is that it will not work if you do not set it up properly. It has to be standing on a flat surface so that the air can flow underneath. If you're the type who holds your notebook on your lap, then a product like this will not work for you. There has to be space underneath so that the fans can operate and get the air moving.

The Mac Cooling Pad does fit securely on Mac's of different sizes and can be used for non- Mac pc's as well. I suppose it could make some difference in temperature, but it seems like a novelty product to me. Unless you are already experiencing an overheated notebook, a product like this is a waste of money.

This little monocular/camera has an unique design. Canon made lots of compromises to build it for this size and price. As with any gadget that is full of compromises, it is not for everyone.

As the product description states, this camera has 2 optical lenses (nominally 100mm and 400mm equivalents) and one digital crop to 800mm. These are paired with a very small image sensor (1/3 inch) to get the camera down to this size. Because of the small sensor, the camera is really only usable in bright sunlight; image quality is mediocre to poor indoors or at night or even early or late in the day or on cloudy days when the sun is not strong. The 100mm and 400mm are fixed lenses, you cannot zoom to levels in between those 2 values.

The viewfinder has pretty good brightness and resolution, but is somewhat small, so looking at it for long periods of time was uncomfortable to me, especially in lower-light situations when the image quality was not so great.

The minimum focusing distance is 3 feet with the 100mm lens and a huge 15 feet with the 400mm lens. That makes this camera impractical for most closeup photography.

Battery life is a mediocre 1 hour of screen-on time or about 150 photos. You have to beware of the time limit if you are using this device as a monocular. While you can recharge the device in the field via the USB-C port, that is awkward at best since you have to hold the fragile battery door open while recharging it.

Those are the main limitations to this camera, so who is it really for? The 100mm and 400mm lenses are equivalent to about 4x and 16x zoom levels on a smartphone or point-and-shoot camera. The Canon camera has no wide angle lens, but if you are carrying a smartphone with you, you can use that for your wide angle camera. I believe today's top-of-the-line iPhone has a 2.5X optical telephoto lens, so the 4X and 16X lenses on this Canon are huge improvements if you like telephoto photography. Samsung and Pixel Android cameras are little better, but the Canon still beats them at 16X.

I think this Canon camera is useful for casual photographers who want to take telephoto snapshots of wildlife, daytime sports, architecture, etc. This camera is small and lightweight enough to easily fit in a purse or coat pocket or even a big pants pocket and it takes better bright sunlight telephoto photos than most smartphones. The camera lets you wirelessly copy photos to your smartphone for editing and posting to social media.

What are your other options? Companies like Sony and Panasonic sell good compact point-and-shoot cameras with 720mm telephoto lenses and better sensors than this Canon camera. These cameras are a little more expensive and a little heavier, but about the same semi-pocketable size as this Canon. Of course, interchangeable lens cameras like SLRs or APS mirrorless camera will let you mount huge expensive lenses that can take fantastic telephoto photos, but are usually too big and heavy to carry around if your primary purpose is not photography.

I'm giving this camera 3.5 stars because of list of limitations is maybe too long for most people, but I think it does have its place for some people. I do wish they had used a bigger image sensor to improve the image quality and low-light ability, even if that meant making the camera a little bigger and heavier. Even many smartphones have bigger image sensors than this Canon camera.

This isn't a good first telescope, if the intent is to introduce and encourage someone to pursue the hobby of astronomy further. The images were fuzzy and distorted and varied in focus across the field of view. Any reflector telescope, even this small one, requires the mirrors to be precisely aligned (collimated) to get sharp images. Out of the box, the two mirrors were not aligned well. I did take it apart. I unscrewed the primary mirror holder from the bottom and drilled out larger diameter holes so that I could adjust the positioning of primary mirror I reseated the secondary mirror (below the eyepiece) which was not level. The 3 existing screws in the secondary mirror can be adjusted to adjust the alignment of the secondary mirror. After some manual collimation, the image is now much better. Stars no longer look like fuzzy balls. But this process isn't easily done in this telescope, nor is it described in the included instructions. Reflector telescopes can be quite persnickety because of their need to be precisely adjusted. My advice is to either spend more money on an reflector which has better optics which can be collimated, or choose a refractor telescope which I think is easier to use for a beginner and doesn't require such adjustments such as this one for not much higher cost:
Celestron 21035 70mm Travel Scope https://www.amazon.com/dp/B001TI9Y2M/ref=cm_sw_r_other_taa_QTn5zbPV2FBNX

I'm having a serious problem with the Denon DHT-T110 TV Speaker Base that apparently the other reviewers are not having. I called Denon Technical Support and after spending a lot of time behind the TV set making sure all the wires were hooked up correctly and then pressing different buttons on the Denon Speaker base, they can't figure out what is causing this problem. And the problem is this: No sound signal is going to the Denon speaker base through the TV from the Roku player. The Roku works just fine through the regular TV speakers and is connected directly to the TV via HDMI. When the input on the TV is set to stream via the Roku no sound comes through the Denon and it turns off. If I increase the volume on the TV speakers you hear sound. If the input is changed to TV with the TV sound off, sound will come through the Denon. Also, if a DVD is played on the DVD player which is connected to the TV, the sound comes through the Denon. It just won't put out sound when the Roku input is being used. And that's a real bummer for me because we watch a lot of Netflix and Amazon streaming through our Roku. I am using the digital optical cord included with the Denon Speaker Base. I have it connected to the Digital Optical "Out" on the back of my Sharp 37" flat screen TV to the digital optical "In" on the back of the Denon Speaker Base.

I will keep working on this problem, and if anyone reading this has any idea that might fix it please say so in the comments section. I would love very much to have it work and to raise the star level to 5. When sound does come through the Denon it's great! Loud, clear and no buzzes or rattles whatsoever like when the volume is turned all the way up when using the TV speakers. I love that it can get loud and there's no rattles or weird vibrations. and the night mode is very useful since the TV room is located underneath the main bedroom and my husband has to go to bed early since he has to go to work early. More than anyone, I really wanted alkaline charging to work like other rechargeable batteries but the sad reality is that they're just not made for it.

The reality of alkaline charging:
- Duracells seem to leak more than cheapo "Kirkland" brand from Costco.
- Energizers do not hold charge very well.
- All brands leak eventually.
- Takes a long time to charge.
- Unreliable even if successfully recharged -- usually, batteries are connected in series, which means that if one fails, the device will not work.
- Battery leak can happen while charging or while being used in the device, resulting in a very messy charger and messy device.

So after some dumpster diving (or at least, I raided the battery recycling bins at work), I came home with batteries of various brands. For a while, I really did use recharged alkaline batteries exclusively and kept my Ni-MH batteries in the drawer. What I found was that I needed to change the batteries a lot more often and I couldn't be sure that the battery would have a charge when I took it out of the drawer.

Leaking is a big problem. My charger now has one charging port that is stuck because the liquid got in to the spring mechanism and dried. I also have a couple of remotes and devices that had to be cleaned out because the batteries leaked.

In the end, I had to give up on the idea of recharging cheap alkaline batteries because of how long it takes to recharge and that it can leak at any time, potentially ruining your device (mostly, it's just oily and you need to clean it out with a tissue). I just couldn't trust those batteries.

So why did I still give this charger 5 stars? Although alkaline charging was a failed experiment for me, the charger is still a better-than-average Ni-MH battery charger. It has separate intelligent charging and LCD display for each battery and will trickle charge a battery even after the lights turn green. Other chargers that have the same features cost more -- and without the Alkaline charging capability. You really can't go wrong with this charger.

I picked this router up at another online retailer as soon as I spotted it was on sale. I had my eye on the Tenda 1800/1801 routers for a while before that though, as these seem to be the only decent Gigabit / AC routers that are directly compatible with Tomato right out of the box, that don't break the bank!

My router is essentially the same thing as the much more expensive ASUS RT-AC66U, but with less memory. Having less memory on a router is not really the same thing as less memory on a computer. In other words, most people (including myself) will not notice the difference.

Hardware Look and Feel:
This Tenda sports the basic router design, and includes wall mounting screw holes that are 6” apart, and 3 movable antennas that are easy to install. There is lots of good ventilation on the sides and bottom, and a glossy white top. Altogether, the router seems will made, and doesn't feel cheap at all. Glad to say that it doesn't have a gimmicky cylindrical shape, or a stupid upright design, with an even more stupid non-adjustable plastic stand. I don’t mind at all that I can't take selfies next to my neat looking stylish black router to post on Facebook; Boring routers are just plain under-rated!

Stock Firmware:
I spent about 5-minutes poking around in the stock firmware before flashing to Tomato. To me the stock firmware seemed like an unpolished version of Asus firmware. This is not necessarily a bad thing, but why settle for stock when there is a specific version of the very stable, configurable, and admired Tomato USB written just for routers just like this! Enter Shibby K26RT-AC...

Tomato Flashing Process:
No feverish searching the internet for firmware “that will work” with your router, simply go to the Shibby download page, find the latest version for your router, download the compressed file, and unzip it.
Then unplug your WAN cable, open your routers firmware page, go to tools, upgrade, navigate to the folder your just unzipped, select the .TRX file, click upgrade, and wait about 10 minutes. Once it is done, you might want to do a factory reset in Tomato to clear the RAM.

That’s it people, no messing around with cumbersome flash utilities, no 30/30/30 resets in restore mode while holding your nose and saying the alphabet backwards in Pig Latin while crossing your fingers that you won’t brick your router. This one is as simple as it gets!

Whoever designed this camera and its power source should find another line of work! Why? Here’s my list of reasons to perhaps pass on this camera, or at minimum, get a screw-in physical mount and extra batteries

1) It ships with a very strong magnetic mount that makes it easy prey for anyone wanting a free camera, or just wanting to vandalize something. UNFORTUNATELY, this is the default mounting that ships with it. Yes, Simplisafe does sell an attachable mount (screwed in), yet at this price point a physical, screw-in mount should be the default.
2) Reviews about great battery life—how long a charge lasted are not consistent with my experience. The battery runs down in three to four days, no matter how much or little sensitivity you set for triggering video. In my installation, this means running up and down a ladder a lot. The more traffic in an area, the faster the battery drains.
3) A compatible solar panel charger did not provide sufficient trickle charge to maintain battery function. Frankly, while this facilitates a very easy install, the constant battery charging is a royal pain! It would be great if the solar option worked, as the cameras have sunlight most of the daylight hours.

Best things are:
1) Slam-dunk easy install.
2) Clear videos.
3) Connects easily to the base station (brilliantly designed).

Final notes:
I have a complete Simplisafe system and I love it. The ease of the total install, the base station’s connection to cellular (a standard feature) is flawless, and better is it doesn’t cost anything extra. As for monitoring 24/7, it’s less than $30 a month. The speed of response to an alarm was under 60 seconds when last I accidentally set it off. That’s perfect!

My 3-star REVIEW is FOR THE CAMERA ONLY, and is strictly due to the default mounting system, and the lack of battery life. Recommend if you’re buying one, you get an extra battery or two and a better camera mount.

I was so excited to finally have a separate GPS again, as my Garmin one was from 2009 (OLD maps) and using my phone was unsafe because even with stuff disabled during driving, I was still getting messages and interruptions that would pop up, plus I like listening to something on the drive, and using it as a GPS makes that tricky. Having tried several Garmin models, Apple Maps, and Google Maps, I was excited to try TomTom. And I was disappointed.

Problems:
•Screen is VERY dim in the sunlight, and living in Florida, this is most of the time. It is NOT easy to see the map, which even in my ancient Garmin is much more visible and automatically switches from day mode to night mode. Likewise, my iPhone screen automatically changes brightness for the amount of sun coming in. And this? It looks horribly dim and takes a lot of effort to see.
•Routes don’t always make sense. I’m used to some amount of this in the other systems I’ve tried, but they’re really wacky on this thing, taking a REALLY scenic route that sometimes involves making a full circle for something that was literally as easy as just turning left in the correct place.
•Point of interest search is slow and ineffective. Even with my ancient Garmin (and obviously with my phone), it would never find most places, even ones that have been there many years. This after waiting an interminable amount of time for the list to compile. Did I get the long update on my computer and add it to the GPS? Yep. I thought that was the problem, did the update, and then discovered it was Not the problem.
•Doesn’t appear to take traffic into account. Neither does my old Garmin, but it should do better than a piece of tech that’s 10 years old and at least be comparable to a current smartphone’s GPS; otherwise, what’s the point?
•Hard to stop. You want to sometimes say, “OK SHUT UP. I know the rest of the way!”, and in all other GPS systems I’ve tried, getting to the “end route/stop” place is usually two steps, max. It is long and complicated, and I don’t want to die in a car accident, so I end up having to suffer through unnecessary and often over-complicated routes that make no sense.
•Doesn’t default to turn-by-turn. Sometimes it shows an aerial view, which is zero helpful, has no detail, and requires me to think a lot about “is this to MY right or left if my car is facing this way and the map is oriented North Up and I *think* I am moving East maybe, but I can’t tell because this stupid thing is both dim and also has an unbelievably zoomed out map view where I’m not sure Where my little dot is going?!?!”

So yes. Unless I sit in the parking lot and fiddle with it for a good while, nothing is quite right, and everything takes a long time to find or set up. I tried it for a month now, and my opinion has not changed. This is frustrating.

Good things:
•nice size screen
•fun voices

Overall rating: 2 stars. I like Garmin more, and I am quite unhappy with this. It is slightly better than my now failing 10-year-old Garmin GPS. *slightly*. I would not buy this or recommend it. The interface is cumbersome, the visibility is bad in the sun, and finding places is a pain and basically 100% of the time requires me to just search for an address on my phone and plug it in. Nope.

I received one of these as a review sample and for what it does it deserves a full five stars.However, I am docking a star because there is a learning curve, due in part to sketchy documentation. I''ll get the challenges out of the way first.

Even with the included documentation it's difficult to figure out some aspects of this case. Some examples: there is a pull strap on the hard, snap-in holder for the iPad that is held in place by two labels that say 'do not tear'. That strap is intended to remain as is and the friction and pressure of the iPad will hold it in place. The instructions do not mention this and I removed it anyway because it looked like a temporary shipping solution.

Secondly, there are adjustable straps on the right and left sides of the case that prevent it from fully opening and remaining open. They are probably unnecessary and do create confusion. This case is not designed to fully open like a conventional case - it's designed to slide the iPad in and out using the T-shaped track. If you do want to use this as a conventional case you need only unfasten the two side straps and it will operate as such.

On the plus side, this case if one of the best I have come across with respect to protection. You can literally drop it from shoulder height and it will protect your iPad. The shoulder strap is designed to function as a set of pockets as well as a comfortable way to carry your iPad. And the material from which this case is constructed is built to take a lot of abuse and last much longer than your iPad.

Bottom line: this is a little over complicated and under documented in my opinion. However it's also ideal for folks who need a fairly rugged case. While the video on this page implies the target customer is a business user I think it's more ideally suited to first responders and folks who work in harsh environments.

Thank you to all you wonderful Amazon reviewers. I'd never purchased a Bose product before, with the exception of possibly headphones at some point in time. We know the Bose sound is legendary, but I never really needed a Bose radio or CD player. The Solo caught my eye because I love my flat screen TV, but the speakers are only so-so at best. Like many other reviewers, I have trouble understanding some dialogue on TV. It's fine as long as there is someone around to annoy endlessly by asking "what did they say," but watching TV alone, I miss big chunks of the story & plot. The doctor says it's just "one of the vestiges of old age." Oh. Another one of those. Thanks, doc.

So, I wondered if the Solo speaker might help, and thanks to all my hard-of-hearing contemporaries here (or should I say THANK YOU), I saw all the reviews promising that I wouldn't have to ask "what?" every 2 minutes any more. I could jump for joy after hooking up the speaker and giving it a listen, although my doctor would probably advise against it. On my TV, unlike some others mentioned here, the TV speakers work along with the Solo speaker, so it's easy to mute the Solo and hear the difference between it and the TV speakers. It's amazing. The sound is rich, and big, and crisp in a way that my surround-sound system isn't. Most importantly, in answer to my wildest hopes, I can understand every single word of dialogue, even Christian Bale mumbling behind his Batman mask. No kidding. The Bose speaker took 20 years off my age, and reduced my waist by four inches. Ok, I am kidding about that.

As if all that isn't reason enough to get one of these gems, it has to be the simplest piece of electronics to hook up, set up & operate. It's simply two cords, one to the power outlet, and the other to the TV. They include all the cables in the box: digital optical, HDMI & RCA. Plug, plug, power. That's all. The remote is four buttons: power, mute, up & down volume. It's hard to believe that such intricate, complex sound can come from such a simple device. Thank you, Mr. Bose, wherever you are. Not only would I highly recommend this to my friends, I think everyone with a flat-screen TV owes it to themselves to get one. Seriously. This is the audio-visual experience I thought I was already having with 5.1 surround system.

I was researching the best way to get high speed NETWORK speeds to a downstairs room. The cable modem was installed into an upstairs room (left side of house) and the WIFI speed in the first floor room (right side of house) was sufficient for most internet streaming services (about 60Mbps) However I needed higher network bandwidth for accessing a NAS.

I sought out solutions that could avoid having to run an ethernet cable from the first floor to the second floor. First I tried ethernet over AC PWR. I received the same speeds as WIFI. Then I found these MOCA adapters, once installed they appeared to work great. I got sufficient speeds but not quite as fast I wanted (about 100Mbps) But once they were installed I would experience constant drops in connection across all devices. It would go out for anywhere from 30 seconds to 10 minutes.

Customer service was great and responsive via email. We verified my setup and hardware were all compatible with the MOCA adapters but the only thing that could cause issues was interference in the coax cables. Since those cables are all inside the walls already, there really wasn't anything else I could do unless I wanted to run new coax.

Ultimately I decided to run CAT8 ethernet upstairs.

I had my concerns because I've researched Powerline Adapters before, and there is talk about how your home's electrical wiring may cause your adapters to work or not work depending on where you plug in your adapters. For me, the process was pretty painless. I plugged the main adapter (GPL-2000PT) to a wall outlet next to my Frontier Gateway. Then an ethernet cable connects my Gateway to this adapter. BTW, the GPL-2000PT is the smaller of the two adapters. For some reason, my brain correlates MAIN as being BIGGER. So without looking at the model numbers on the device, I connected the bigger adapter next to my router initially and got it wrong, and had to start over. Anyway, so remember the smaller one is the one that gets tethered to your router. Next you plug the bigger adapter (GPL-2000WAC) to wherever you want to have the new wi-fi network. Press the Security button on the main adapter, then press the Security button on the other adapter.. wait for them to pair, and voila, you have a new wi-fi network. In my case, I was pleasantly surprised that everything worked because I needed better wi-fi in the garage, and there weren't any wall outlets available. Manual specifically recommends using wall outlets. I have these outlet boxes that the previous homeowner had installed along exposed 2x4 beams. I plugged the adapter into one of these and crossed my fingers, and amazingly, everything linked up. Speeds are super fast and snappy too.

The hiccup I run into, which is the same hiccup I run into every time I play around with gadgets of this kind whether it be powerline, meshes, or wi-fi extenders.... is the part where I would like to change the SSID and password. The default they give you is always something that's hard to remember, so you always want to change this. I can never get to their user interface with their provided IP's. The idea is that once you're on the adapter's network, you should be able to go to the provided address to access the user interface. It never works for me, no matter the brand. Either there is something about my network that I'm not understanding, or there are many consumers in the same boat as as I am. In any case, I will tell you what does work for me every time.. I simply go to my own router ADMIN. So if you're Spectrum, go to your Spectrum admin, if you're Frontier, Verizon, etc., go to their router admin. Then look for your new Nexuslink adapter. Your router would have assigned it an IP address. Type that ip address into the browser, and it will take you to the Nexuslink user interface. So whenever you can't get to a user interface provided the manufacturer of a powerline adapter, wifi extender, etc., just go to your own router admin and get the IP address that it was assigned. BTW, when you're browsing your router admin for the IP address of the adapter, you might not know what you're looking for since it may not be labeled by your router properly. So you'll need to find it through a process of elimination. All the IP addresses listed will show whether the device is connected by wi-fi, moca, or ethernet. So you can ignore all the wi-fi and mocas. Look for the ethernet connection that is unfamiliar to you. Mine showed up as "UNKNOWN." I have several devices connected to my network as UNKNOWN. I simply tried them all out, and one of the addresses eventually took me to the Nexuslink user interface.

If any network expert is reading this, I'd love for you to chime in below in the comment section and explain when it comes to this part regarding accessing the user interface of an adapter whether it be powerline, wifi extenders, etc., why the default given address in the manual never works for some of us. This hiccup doesn't deserve a star subtraction since I've experienced this with every other brand I've tried. Anyway, I can now access my garage camera blazingly fast, versus the 50/50 hit or miss connections before. This is 5 stars!

When I initially saw this camera it checked most of the boxes I look for when looking for security cameras. It is PoE, has H.265, ONVIF support allowing use with Blue Iris, Sony IMX274 Starvis Sensor. Once I received this camera and began digging into it I quickly realized certain important facts.

Most importantly, this is a rebranded Hikvision camera. This is among the companies that has been discovered spying on the US using their cameras - the firmware this camera comes with is long outdated and, in fact, can not be updated to anywhere close to what is current. This is far too risky for me to install on my system.

Any camera you install on your system should have the latest firmware installed and you need to have a good understanding of network security protocols. Cameras such as this one, that are older versions of cameras made by manufacturers that are blacklisted - while still being sold, people who understand the industry avoid them - are an invitation for hackers to invade your system.

While the specs on and price of this camera seem decent - this is not a camera I recommend. This poses far more risks than it is worth.

However, if Frontier set you up with both the Arris and the MEB1100, then I recommend buying both. You want the set-up to stay the same.

I do use moca adapters to bring internet to rooms with coax cable. These are the ones I use: https://www.amazon.com/Motorola-Adapter-Ethernet-2-Pack-MM1002/dp/B078HMDDVS/ref=sr_1_2?dchild=1&keywords=Motorola+moca&qid=1617140900&sr=8-2 With the Arris router, you do not need to put an adapter next to it. My connection is like this:

* Ethernet from ONT in my garage goes to WAN port of the Arris router in living room.
* Coaxial from ONT goes to a 4 way splitter, one line goes to the living room, I connect this line to the coaxial on the Arris.
* Coaxial line in my bedroom goes to the network coaxial port of my moca adapter. I then hook up an ethernet hub to the ethernet port of the moca adapter. Voila! That's how I bring ethernet to my bedroom.
* I do the same to the other coaxial lines in my home to bring ethernet hubs to those rooms as well.

This has been how my home has functioned. All connections were left untouched. I simply swapped out the Frontier Arris for this identical Arris. I then made sure to go into the new Arris admin and create the same wifi SSID with the same password as before. All your wifi and network devices will function as normal, no need to re-enter any passwords. I contacted Frontier, and they are sending me a box with pre-paid envelope to ship back their router, and I was assured I will no longer be charged with rental fees. I'm happy to report every customer rep I've talked to have been very nice and accommodating. The FCC ruling to allow consumers to use their own routers have been in effect since December, so I think they've been given a memo that they need to accommodate us, instead of selling us on why we should use their router, or say they cannot remove the rental fee. The process has been painless.

I have worked with a number of trackballs, my most successful being a Logitech M570 which served me well for years. I finally wore it out and after some research I purchased the Logitech MX Ergo to replace it. I have had it about three days, and it has already proven to be exactly what I had hoped and more. It’s not perfect but it’s close.

I was attracted to the fact that it works both as a wireless mouse with a USB receiver as well as a Bluetooth mouse. I have two computers on my desk, one being a Windows 10 system and the other being a Linux (Arch-based) system. My old trackball worked with both though I had to move the receiver between the systems, so I went with the assumption that this one would also work with both.

I connected the trackball to my Windows system via Bluetooth and it has been flawless in operation. It connects without intervention and it works exactly as expected - all buttons work as they should and the operation is very smooth and predictable.

I plugged the USB receiver into the Linux machine, pushed the channel button on the trackball and it immediately started working on the Linux machine, even though it was still paired to the Windows system via Bluetooth. It works exactly as it should and I have had absolutely no issues with the trackball on my Linux installation. So now, I can switch back and forth between the two systems with the push of the channel button and without having to connect or disconnect anything. It simply works, and the switch-over is fast. The take-away for me is that I no longer need two mice on the desk.

I friend came over with his MacBook and there was no issue at all with connecting the trackball via USB. We did not try connecting via Bluetooth.

The trackball has a metal plate on the bottom that is held in place with magnets, and depending on how the plate is attached the trackball can be tilted to ease wrist strain. The plate serves another purpose too - it adds a lot of weight to the trackball. Even without the plate, the trackball is hefty and has some mass to it, but the plate just makes it even more so. For me that’s a positive; others may dislike the added weight.

One of the things I have missed has been a tilting scroll wheel. This trackball has one and I have been enjoying getting used to that feature again.

One thing I did notice is that there is no CD/DVD in the package for loading drivers. This isn’t a big deal, and it’s easy enough to get the drivers from the net. That said, the trackball just seems to work when you attach it, without any issue. For me it has absolutely been plug-and-play, on every system I have tried.

If I could change one thing - I would have made this trackball a little bigger. I have big hands and I struggle to find a trackball that’s an absolute perfect fit. This one is close. For the large majority of people it’s going to be spot on.

I am very happy with this trackball and have no issue with recommending it. It works great, connects easily, when connected to two different systems it switches at the press of a button, it has a bit of heft to it and the tilt is adjustable for wrist comfort. It’s really all I could ask for.

When I pulled this little camera case out of its box, I immediately thought it was going to be too small for my Fujifilm FinePix Z700EXR camera, but it fit perfectly! This is a sturdy, classy, soft-leather case with soft grey suede inside. The little inside pocket for carrying an extra battery is tight and out of the way; I'll probably use it to put identification inside in case I ever leave the camera lying on a table somewhere. With my camera's side strap sticking out of one side (which I prefer to running it through the top hole because access is quicker), it's like a little mini-purse. The cutout in the top happens to be right over the USB cable port on my camera, so if I had to (but I probably won't), I could run the USB cable to it without removing the camera from its case. Another thing I could do if I wanted to is use that little hole to loop an ID tag or small ID/credit card holder through using one of those beaded lamp-pull type thingies. Then I really could travel light.

Little things mean a lot to me, and I have to say I just love the magnetic clasp underneath the low-key silverish AmazonBasics logo on the front of the case. The magnet is not so strong as to be annoyingly hard to pull apart, but it's strong enough to do the job without slipping. The little circular magnetic piece in the clasp has a small center button that fits into a recession in the other part of the clasp; when closing the cover, you hear a satisfying little click when you slide it into place, so you know it's snugly closed.

I was thinking when I got this (not paying great attention) that the holder "clip" on the back was actually a clip suitable for clipping to the edge of your pants or a coat pocket, but it's not. It's actually better than that, because we all know how quickly those clips break off our cell phones. This one closes with strong velcro so you can loop it through a belt loop or other strap or onto a belt. The part of the holder that does not have velcro on it is not quite an inch wide, though, so it wouldn't work as well with wider belts. With the camera in it, it would be too heavy (at least for me) to want to wear around your neck, but you could definitely put it on a lanyard if you wanted to—and then perhaps stick it in a breast pocket so it's not dangling. One nice thing about the velcro is that, even though it is sewn on very well, part of the piece that is sewn to the camera case actually lifts up as you pull the velcro apart. This should extend the life of the case because you're not pulling against case stitching when you're trying to get it apart. This is not wimpy velcro, so you have to tug a bit to get it open.

After flashing the SSD firmware from a bootable CD, putting a 120gb SanDisk Extreme in a (Dell GX620 sff/3ghz Pentium Dual Core w/2gb of RAM) was a walk in the park and so was installing Linux Mint 13 Cinnamon on the SSD. Enabling the Trim function as described on various Mint/Ubuntu websites went without a hitch. I've enabled a few other basic tweaks and they also have worked without any problems. Be sure to use the the EXT4 file system when partitioning, Linux Mint 13 uses it by default. Do not use the Linux Mint 13 KDE release, not even Orkin could kill all the bugs on that turkey.

At this point I am using the swap partition and browser caching on the SSD, but will be moving those to RAM as soon as Amazon gets my memory delivered to bump my computer up to 4gb. A note to other Dell GX620 owners. The Normal mode in the BIOS is in fact AHCI mode, as such it does fully support the Trim function. Linux can also emulate the Trim function using CRON if you do not have an AHCI capable box.

I'm telling you all this because getting the information to determine whether an SSD would work on my computer was like pulling teeth. User Name "SpeedStep" on the Dell forums was a lot of help.

Buy an SSD, you'll like it. Unless your Mac or an XP user, it isn't that big a deal.

I've had several pairs of Sennheisers before the momentums namely a pair of HD580's from back in 1999 & much more recently a pair of HD650's. Let me start off by saying I'm not an "audiofile" I'm not a headphones snob. I don't name drop as to act like I know everything about all "cans" as they're referred to as. But I do know music & I know MY TYPE of music, which is pretty much everything except Country/Western. I listen 100% through my iphone or iPods.

I come from an LP, then 8 track (yuck), then cassette, then CD background so when I finally went all compressed format I didn't realize what I'd be "missing" I just thought, "Wow what a convenience"!! Anyway, I ended up ditching all my CD's (about 1400 total, originals!) & ripping them into iTunes, total of about 7500 songs. I long ago sold my HD580 back in 2005 & just listened from earbuds. I got tired of these real quick. So I saved up & did my research & just knew I had to have the Senn HD650's but I knew I had to have a good amp so I bought both (used) & I was thoroughly disappointed. I didn't hear this "wide open" expanded 3D imaged sound that everyone bragged about. After "damning" these headphones for being overpriced I realized, after my anger, I was being angry at the wrong item, it wasn't the can's it was the compressed format that removed all the subtle nuances of the original recordings!

So back to the drawing board to look for a decently priced (new) set of headphones. I bought a pair of in ear headphones from Sennhesier of course & these sounded good, better than than the Apple buds. Then I ran into the Momentums! I did my youtube & google research & the Momentums appear to be the one's I've been looking for. It has the controller but are "can" style headphones not earbuds! The cord is just long enough so i can stick my iphone in my pocket but no so long that it'll get caught on a doorknob or something else. The only drawback is it was hard to find the black with red from any type of discount. I got the brown ones reluctantly but I couldn't argue the price I got them for and for what it's worth the brown looks pretty clean & euro with the brushed aluminum.

I knew as soon as I started listening to some of the typical songs I play that I found my pair. They're paired perfectly for the portable MP3, phone or tablet's. You don't need an amp of any kind, they have great sound quality even for a sealed back design an because they're sealed you won't bother anyone sitting next to you at moderate levels. I was kind of put off of how small the ear surroundings were because my ears are not huge but they do stick out a bit, once I found a good position my ears fit fine.

All I can say is that I"m finally happy with a pair of headphones. I think the challenge is to match your style of music with headphones. Don't listen to name droppers & snobs who only talk about Gredo, AKG's HiFiMan & even Sennheisers. People knock Beats by Dre but hey if your music is like 99% current day hip hop & Dance then the Beats are probably the best suited for you. They're not for people who listen to live rock or classical. I had to find that out the hard way those higher priced headphones that require DAC's & AMPS aren't necessarily suited to my music. I believe the momentums are a great "in betweener" set of headphones. For that person who's aged a bit where they're not looking for LOUD & BOOM any more, they know & want detailed sound but they're still at a stage where they're listening to their music in a compressed 256k or less format, mp3 or wave format & not CD's anymore, but want that CD sound brought back.

I ordered the 'Nomodo U Wireless Wearable Bluetooth Speaker, Rechargeable and Portable' for review and would like to share some of my thoughts and experiences.
First off, out of the box this Bluetooth Wireless Speaker not only looks interesting but it is beautiful. I say interesting because I have never had a Wireless Speaker like this, and I wonder where would I use it and would it be practical. Well after some time with this device I must first report that it really does sound amazing. The sound is clean and immersive. It is hard to describe the incredible sound sensation while wearing it. It is almost as if you have speakers floating on either side of your head (pointing directly to your ears) and it is nothing like I have experienced before but it is pretty cool. I have been trying to think of how this Speaker would actually fit into my life. It's not like you are wearing headphones that only you can hear. While wearing this speaker, everyone else around you can hear it too but it's just not as immersive as it is to you. It's hard to describe, but what I will say is that it really is an incredible experience. If the volume is down low you can still hear your surroundings yet when you crank it up, surprisingly your surrounding sounds seem to disappear. Personally I have decided that this would be best worn while alone in your home while doing simple household chores. Like doing dishes or folding laundry. The Nomodo U speaker stays put pretty well for the most part due to the rubber neck pad, yet if you are constantly bending over or doing anything where you are moving around a lot and twisting your head and body, it tends to need re adjusted. Sitting in bed listening to Music or listening to an audio book works really well with this device as long as you wont be disturbing your partner. As for watching movies, for me this really doesn't work. I can't find anywhere where it says what version of Bluetooth this is using but I don't think it is Bluetooth 5.0 unfortunately. There are noticeable sync issues and this just gets annoying. Speaking of the Bluetooth, it connects/pairs effortlessly to all of my devices and that is a bonus. I am disappointed however that it uses Micro USB (the cable is included btw) for charging. With this being a new device it should have USB Type C. I always have to mention this with any new devices. Call quality is acceptable. Those on the other end can hear you just fine, as long as you are not in a loud environment. This is pretty typical with most wireless headphones. Overall I do love this device and think it is a great value for what it is.

This MOTOROLA MDC100 FULL HD (1080p) DASH CAMERA (Black) suits my needs perfectly. It’s mounted on the windshield, behind the rear view mirror, with an extremely strong suction cup. The suction cup is made of something that sticks to the windshield, and a ring tightens the suction cup so that it really, really sticks. The dash camera itself plugs into your car’s repurposed “cigarette lighter” outlet, and video recording turns on automatically when you start your car.

The camera requires a micro SD card (not included) for recording the video of your auto trips. I installed a [[ASIN:B00M55C0NS SanDisk 32GB card]] (the maximum size), and filled about 15-20% of the card with an hour’s driving. So the maximum size should record for 5-6 hours before it starts recording over the oldest recordings. The camera’s internal software allows you to “protect” designated recordings (or still photos) if you don’t want them to be recorded over.

Using an adapter, I inserted the micro SD card into a Windows 10 PC, and the PC was able to play the .avi videos without any problems at all. I also deleted selected videos that I made while learning to use the settings. The camera has a “delete” function, but it’s easier to use a PC for deleting selected files.

The camera has three modes--recording, photo, and replay. In photo mode, you can take still photos; in replay mode, you can look at your recordings and photos. You can replay the videos at various speeds (up to 8x maximum). You can also fast forward and fast rewind your videos as you replay them.

The camera takes excellent high-definition footage when it’s set to the highest (default) setting. The camera’s on/off functions for both power and recording are a bit confusing at first, so I strongly recommend that you sit down with the camera and familiarize yourself with all the settings and features before you install it in your vehicle. Of course, the camera is easy to uninstall/reinstall if you want to leave that step for later.

One very important thing to know is that if you turn recording off manually (by hitting the OK button) for any reason, you must turn recording on again manually when you’re done with Settings or whatever made you turn recording off. Otherwise the camera won’t start recording automatically when you start your car.

The camera has a built in battery for holding the settings and powering the camera while the vehicle is parked. I didn't test the Park function, which is disabled by default, because I don't like to leave an electronic device in plain sight when I'm going to be away from my car for a while. The battery can be used to replay videos or to look at photos, but it doesn't last long when used this way.

NOTE: I am writing this review for the 1TB platter-based Passport drive.

I have a 250GB Passport I bought several years ago and it has served me well, though it has gotten close to full over time (I never imagined at the time that I would fill that thing up). I have had good fortune with it so I expected the same from this 1TB version, and so far I have been right. In addition to the larger capacity, it is very definitely a speed upgrade from my old Passport.

This is a small drive in terms of physical footprint, approximately 4”x3”x0.5” in dimension. That’s a double-edged sword. On one hand, it is small enough to stuff in a shirt pocket which makes it an excellent on-the-go storage solution that’s almost as convenient as a thumb drive. But, that also means it is easy to misplace or lose (or have stolen if left unattended).

It comes with software that allows you to password-protect the drive which is a nice deterrent in the event that the drive is taken. It’s certainly not foolproof, but it’s sufficient to keep the large majority of unauthorized access out. To be honest, since the drive does not leave my home I have not used the software at all.

When you plug in the drive to a Windows or Linux system, the OS immediately recognizes the drive and it is available immediately for use. In the case of Windows, you can immediately explore the drive and read from it and write to it. For Linux, it depends on how you have configured automount and which desktop management software you use, but the kernel does register the presence of the drive and you can display the partition table.

This is a USB 3.0 drive, making it a huge speed upgrade from my older 2.0-based Passport. This is a great solution for storing all of your pictures, movies, important documents, and as in my case large downloads and purchased software packages. With 1TB of space, I don’t think I am going to run out of space anytime soon.

As a bonus, this is a very quiet drive.

I put this drive on a USB power meter to see how much it draws from the USB port. At rest it pulls 0.17A. When actively reading, it peaks just under 0.6A which is surprisingly low. My concern was that this would add some strain on the USB port over a longer period of time but this seems to be an unjustified concern. That said, I am more likely to connect it to a USB hub instead of directly to a USB port.

So far I have no complaints with this drive. It’s a big step up for me from my older Passport, being larger, faster and more quiet. It’s not cost prohibitive either which is just a bonus. If you need a decent backup drive with large capacity and a small footprint, this one is worth consideration.
