I often eat at my desk, which is not the greatest thing. Croissant flakes, bits of cheese and even rice grains often find their way into the crevices of my standard keyboard at work. It gets really disgusting. A few times crumbs got stuck inside the keys and stopped them from working properly. I've used compressed air cans and mini vaccuums but they don't do that great a job. I often end up having to flip the thing over and give it a shake. In addition, I remove all the keys and use a Q-tip to wipe up dust and dirt that get encrusted in these tiny spaces, which is time-consuming.

So you can tell I was relieved to get this washable keyboard. This thing is made for the Oscar Madisons of the world (like me). While you can't use it underwater while scuba diving (the instructions say you shouldn't submerge it in more than 11" of water, and no more than 5 minutes at that), being able to do a wash and rinse (as if it were a dinner plate) is more than enough to get most dirt and crumbs out.

I also like the fact that there is no additional software to install - just plug into the standard USB port, wait a few minutes until your computer recognizes the hardware, and then you're off. The keyboard is about the same size as other computer keyboards, except that the keys feel more like ones you'd find on a laptop. They are round and smooth and make me feel I'm pushing buttons. Because they lay flatter on the surface of the keyboard, you get a softer sound when you type as opposed to the hardier tapping of regular keyboards.

It took me awhile to get used to the feel. The buttons lack the slightly concave ridges that keep your fingers nestled so my fingers felt slippery on them, but not enough to have a problem.

Despite these reservations, however, I think this is a well-made product that is very practical, especially for people like me, who'd rather write than clean. Now all I need is a washable mouse!

The main feature we wanted from this was to pull the photos from our iPhone without having to sync all the time. Sometimes our phone gets filled so quickly with photos and videos that we can't take any more and we're not near our syncing computer. That's where this comes in handy.

In order to use it fully, you have to download the compatible app (which is free), connect the device, and let the app and device access your photos, contacts, and calendar. We have a few microSD cards lying around, and so far our brands (Kensington and SanDisk) worked fine, even though the packaging is adamant in having you buy their brand of cards. ;)

The app itself is pretty easy to use, but I'd rather have the main syncing buttons appear on the first page. When you open it up the app is split into three "pages" that you can swipe through to select. At the top are icons to select the app and card memory (though I'm not sure why you'd back up the phone to the app over the card), and then at the bottom you get features to sync to other apps. Those aren't why we got this product, so when you swipe right you get the buttons to sync the photos, contacts, and calendar. You can sync selected ones or sync them all to the card. We usually just select all, even if we know only pictures and videos have been added since the last sync; we just like to be cautious.
Syncing takes only a few minutes. To confirm that all the photos and videos have been synced, I removed the memory card and plugged it in to both my computer and an Android device. I was able to navigate the folders in the card without issue (that is, no restrictions as I thought there might've been since it was an Apple's synced history going into Windows and Google machines) and see all the photos, etc. You can also navigate the folders via the device in the iPhone, but the thumbnails sometimes take a while to load.
Initially I didn't think the videos were backed up, but that's because they didn't have that little play icon on them as other videos usually do. When I scoured carefully through the dates, however, I found them all, and no noticeable resolution loss. Perfect!

So far this is exactly what we wanted and it works just fine.

I bought this so I could play Blu-Ray movies on my computer or my laptop.

Interestingly enough, the drive itself seems to be recognized by Windows, and Windows can actually see the files on the discs, so the drive seems to work in that respect. However, the drive comes bundled with an older version of CyberLink's media playing software (PowerDVD 12), which is supposed to be able to play Blu-Ray discs.

However, the software just doesn't want to play Blu-Ray movies. I popped in "The Equalizer" and it showed me the thumbnail icon for it, but when I tried to play, it just took me back to the home screen of the PowerDVD 12 player. I tried updating the software with no luck, and I tried it on a different computer that is almost brand-new, and got the same results. I even installed CyberLink's "Advisor" tool that analyzes your system to see if there are any items that could cause issues with playing such content, and it told me everything passed.

From what I've read, it sounds like you need to constantly upgrade to newer versions of PowerDVD (up to version 15 now, which is an extra $99 upgrade fee) in order to play newer movies.

So while this might be a good drive for data-driven usage of Blu-Ray discs, just be aware that the packaged software is just too old to be useful nowadays. You'll need to account for another $99 upgrade charge to watch more recently-released movies unless you already have a newer version of that software.

As of today, if you can find a version of PowerDVD that is version 13 or 14, the upgrade fee to version 15 is $49, I think, so the included version is just one version too old.

It's unfortunate, since the drive itself seems like a really nice piece of hardware. It's very convenient in terms of being able to be plugged in, it's very small, and seemed very quiet, too.

This is a dual review, as I own both the Contour + 2 and the Contour Roam2. I don't work for nor do I have any affiliation with Contour. I've had the Roam2 for more than 6 months, but held off writing this review until I had the +2 to compare it to. Although I don't own a GoPro, several friends do and I do their video editing so I'll chime in on the Contour vs. GoPro at the end.

MOUNTS:
Contour uses the same proprietary mounts across their lineup, so interchangeability between the two should be fairly easy (but doesn't always work out that way). I've found some to be flimsy(hat mount), while others are damn near bomb proof(suction cup)! The rotating lens means you can mount it in just about any position, however it is difficult to know that you've framed the shot with the correct orientation! Had an important video recorded upside down - laser level only lets you know it's level, not if it's upside down! One of the best features I've found is the ¼ by 20 thread on the bottom of the Contour, pretty much universal to all modern cameras and there's a TON of mounts out there reasonably priced.

SOFTWARE:
The Storyteller program needs to be installed on your computer and is fairly easy to use, but not intuitive, you need to play around a bit before you can figure everything out. The editing ability is extremely limited. (I use imovie). Software is free, and although you can use the camera(s) without first updating I suggest you do that first! The +2 also has an app that I use on my iPhone 5 - it too is free and pretty easy to use - but not as capable as the Storyteller program. The downside is you HAVE to use the Storyteller program to change settings on the Roam2, AND you have to use it if you want to use any of the GPS data with the +2.

ROAM2:
Got this for Xmas last year and immediately swapped the included 4GB micro SD for a 16GB. SUPER easy to use - charge, point, and slide the slider to the on position. Video quality is good, first few outings I had it set for 1080@30 and was very happy. In editing I found one clip I had to slow down and was slightly disappointed at the quality - since then I've got it set for 720@60 and haven't had any issues - video quality is still good (even in slow mo). Low light does induce more "noise" to the video, but if there's ambient light (streetlights etc.) you can still get decent vids. Sound quality isn't all that, it's usable, but in high winds or at speed - forget it. Battery life is really good at around 2 hours. The camera itself is very well built, one of my first uses it got throw (by an idiot) about 8ft into about 4 inches of water over concrete - few scratches, but still kept recording. This led me to look for something to help protect the aluminum body - Glock Tape, works amazing, adds some protection, but most importantly gives it some GRIP!

[[ASIN:B00C7WXTJS 6-Pack Glock Grip Tape - Pistol Grip Tape. * Use on handguns and rifles * Not gritty like sandpaper or skateboard tape. * Does not scuff clothing, holsters, furniture or car seats like those sandy tapes. * Makes chambering a round easier for arthritis s...]]

CONTOUR +2:
Only had it for a week or so, really wanted it due to the Bluetooth (to help frame shots) and was wanted the waterproof housing (worried about watersports damage on an upcoming trip) the GPS would be a plus. Once again amazing build quality - this things tough as nails. First thing I did was hook up to Storyteller and get the latest firmware update - less than 5 minutes later I was off and running! Pairing the Bluetooth took a couple of attempts, but once connected has excellent range (20 or so feet with obstructions - close to 50ft line of sight!). Using the app you can check status of battery, GPS, and memory as well as change settings and start stop recording - wish you could watch videos but oh well. The app has about a one second delay between what the camera "sees" and what you see on your phone - pretty amazing! Attached to my suction cup mount and went for a drive - took about 30 seconds for the GPS to lock on the first time (since then it only takes maybe 5 seconds). GPS is accurate. The video quality is great! Uploaded vid into storyteller and the GPS data was also great - until I exported it then there was a lag of about 5 seconds between the data being displayed and the video. Waterproof housing is bulky, yet seems a bit flimsy - still not sure it could survive 200 ft of water. Came with HDMI to hook up to TV - works really well. Haven't used the mic adaptor yet. Battery life seems to be around 1.5 hours, but spare batteries are cheap.

[[ASIN:B007PUC1UU Wasabi Power Battery and Charger Kit for Contour 2350, 2450, 2900, C010410K and ContourHD, ContourGPS, Contour+, Contour+2]]

COMPARISON:
Even though the video specs are the same between the +2 and the Roam2, the video quality of the +2 is noticeably better - even in low light. Sound quality on both suffers in high winds or speed. They both have the proprietary T-rail mounts on both sides, but the ¼ by 20 thread is about an inch further back on the +2. The Roam2 is waterproof without housing to about 3ft, but the +2 has the waterproof housing. The +2 also allows for filming while charging. The +2 has the HDMI out, as well as a jack for external mic. The +2 has the Bluetooth app, plus GPS - that combined with replaceable batteries and the better video make it worth the extra money.

CONTOUR vs. GOPRO:
I absolutely love the form factor and the mounting options available for the Contours. The Contour line has their own proprietary mounts, but the ability to use the ¼ by 20 thread mounts for other cameras (even the GoPro mounts) plus the rotating lens means there's just more ways to mount the Contour. That being said the GoPro Hero3 flat out destroys the video quality of the Roam2, and slightly edges out the +2. Of course this difference (even over the Roam2) is completely removed once video is uploaded to Youtube or other sharing sites as they compress the video during upload! I've yet to see a GoProH3 recording 1080 go for more than 75 minutes. Sound quality between all three is about the same. The GoProH3 app uses wifi - and has about a 3-4 second delay - still works for framing shots, but not much else. The GoPro also has the advantage in that you can change settings in camera - but it is a complicated affair(the +2 only allows you to choose between two predetermined settings). GoProH3 doesn't have GPS, or rotating lense. Contour recently lowered the price on the +2 it's now $50 cheaper than the GoProH3. Also it seems they changed pricing on their mounts - I went with the Contour line because of the simplicity of their system, more mounts, cheaper price, and the form factor. Now that they're cheaper it's a no brainer.

I selected the Meade 20225 TerrStar telescope as my youngest son is often asking me where to find certain constellations in the sky and has always been interested in celestial events. I thought this telescope might be a good entry level scope with which to foster his interest. While it does work, I would hesitate to recommend it, mainly on the basis of its build quality but also for its usability.

My son decided to assemble it himself and it was done by the time I got home from work. He had no issues putting it together and he managed to get it assembled correctly without any assistance. In short, it's easy to put together. However, his very first comment to me was that it was very cheaply made, and it did not take long to determine what he meant. The whole assembled unit is slightly wobbly and a little unstable though it does not feel like it will tip over without a little help - I would be more concerned about it breaking outright. There is much more lightweight plastic than metal and there are numerous opportunities to break components which all feel cheaply made.

One of the packing decisions made was to put the lenses in the carry bag which is folded up in the box. So, until we realized this we thought the lenses were not included in the package. While this is not a major problem - all the parts are there - it does show a lack of understanding of the consumer who is likely to call the support line first before searching the carry bag.

We took the telescope outside and started looking for objects in the sky, and we discovered a serious issue. Once we find something to view, the scope's positional setting is so loose that even the very slightest bump either knocks the object from view or causes the scope to shake which makes viewing impossible. At a minimum the scope itself should be mounted tightly and should move only with deliberate effort. I have found no way to tighten this up which is very unfortunate.

I have trouble recommending this telescope. It's very cheaply made and this shows all through the product from assembly to use. Research other options before selecting this telescope.

I purchased this HDMI Capture USB device to record a Windows desktop session. What I noticed is that the passthrough video quality is very bad. What is clear text coming out of the computer becomes blurry by the time it gets to the TV. What this means is that you can't keep this device plugged in permanently to record when necessary. You'd have to settle for plugging it in only when recording. Perhaps for gaming devices that have larger text and buttons, it wouldn't be a big problem.

This device can also be used to live stream by plugging it in to the USB port on your PC. A few problems here:
-- This is only USB 2.0
-- The USB port is also used as the power supply for the device. This means that if your PC doesn't provide enough power through its USB port (especially if you have an external drive plugged in to the device), you won't be able to use this function. They did not include those two-headed dongles to provide additional power.
-- The drivers are bad. I was able to get OBS to preview the device only after a lot of changing inputs around. VLC will not work with it.

What I do like about it is that while the passthrough quality is pretty bad, the resulting recording isn't. You can certainly tell that it is a recording, probably due to the video compression but all of the text from the 1080p desktop is readable.

I also like the fact that you can record directly to a USB drive with scheduled recording capabilities. The UI of the built-in software is straight out of VHS days but it does the basics of what you need. The convenience of being able to press record on the remote to start your capture means you can set up your PC how you need it without having to also manage your desktop recording software.

In my opinion, this unit makes the GH4 into a professional video camera. However, it's certainly not perfect. I begged the Nikon guy at NAB 2013 to build something like this for the D800, but nothing yet. Panasonic is listening. I'm commenting here because as of June 4, 2014, you cannot download the YAGH manual from Panasonic's website for details you may need.

1. Cost

It's more than the camera body, which is to say, really expensive. I can only hope the YAGH will fit future GH5 and GH6 camera bodies. Please, Panasonic: don't obsolete this thing.

2. Power

There is no internal battery. It has to have external power, supplied via the industry-standard 4-pin XLR. This is good and bad. Stated power requirement on the bottom plate is 12VDC at 1.4 amps.

Power is applied to Pin 4, Ground to Pin 1. (Pins 2 and 3 are not used.) The manual says voltage can vary from 11VDC to 17VDC. This means any professional AC camera supply or brick battery like an Anton Bauer 14.4VDC. (I'm using a 12VDC battery pack built from ten NiMH D-cells and supplies 10,000 mAhs.) You'll need a 4-pin extension power cord and drag the power supply with you. Hello battery belt? Sort of going backward. It would be great to have the ability to add lith-ion batteries somehow but perhaps it draws too much power for smaller cells.

The external power powers both YAGH and the GH4 body.

Once the YAGH is attached to the camera, an "Interface Unit" menu appears on the "Motion Picture" tab. There are many options. One setting allows you to set low battery warnings at 11, 12.5, 13.5 and 15 volts. This is very professional.

UPDATE Sept 26,2014: I built a 12VDC power supply from a computer monitor power supply and a 4-pin female XLR jack. I also have a 14.4 volt battery power supply. I found that if I leave the battery warning set to 13.5 for the one power supply the 12VDC power supply won't work. The battery warning settings actually stop the camera from working. Be sure to set the battery warning levels to match the batteries you are using.

3. Fan

Yes, it has a fan. You can barely hear it (can't hear it six inches away), but hot air blows out the left side when it's plugged in. I assume there's a lot of electronics inside to supply all the outputs. Have not demonstrated the fan can be heard by the camera-body's built in stereo mics.

4. Inputs:

a. the 4-pin XLR power plug

b. two, 3-pin XLR audio inputs, switchable between Line (0dB), Mic (-50dB) and 48VDC phantom power. A stereo/mono switch sends the signal from a single mic to both left and right channels. You can select which mics to use: the built-in stereo camera mics or the XLR inputs.

c. time code-in on one of the BNC connectors

d. the micro-HDMI plug that transfers the HDMI camera output signal to a full-sized HDMI on the YAGH unit. This HDMI interface is implemented clumsily; I hope there is a better reason than engineering laziness. It's basically a short Micro-to-Full HDMI extension cord. The dovetailed arm that sticks up on the unit holds the micro-HDMI cord with a plug. You mount the camera to the unit, open the rubber door on the camera's left side so that it sticks straight out of the camera, then slide the YAGH's dovetailed micro-HDMI plug into the camera, then tighten the tiny thumbscrew. The rubber door disappears into the dovetail arm and is not removed or abused by being bent back too far. This sturdy plastic arm with its metal dovetailed very definitely protects the extremely fragile Micro-HDMI socket on the camera body. (I personally would not directly connect a cable into the camera. One yank and your camera is broken. I thought the Mini-HDMI plugs on Canon 5D's and Nikon D800's were bad. This Micro-HDMI is even smaller and weaker. The YAGH solves the problem.) It would have been better if Panasonic had routed the signal through the bottom of the camera, but that would mean another 15 pins down there, and it's already crowded.

e. One drawback of this HDMI interface method: if you screw the dovetail in, it takes up the whole left side of the camera and you cannot pivot the flip-out viewfinder down at all and upwards only about 5 degrees. The whole point of the pivoting viewfinder is the ability to frame low- or high-angle shots. If you don't need to remote the HDMI to the YAGH (say you're using the audio interface and DC in and not monitoring via the HDMI) you can let the dovetail hang there, flopping in the wind, and allow the viewfinder to rotate.

5. Outputs

a. full-sized HDMI socket under a rubber door on the left side outputs 4:2:2 8bit or 4:2:2 10bit. You can't record both internally and externally if in 10bit. You access this setting while in "Creative Video Mode." The 8bit is good for sending to an external monitor while recording to the card.

b. 4, SDI BNC connectors under a rubber door on the right side, marked 1, 2, 3 and 4. They output different signals based on the resolution of the recorded signal.
- any of the four BNCs can output a 1.5G HDSDI signal if resolution is set up to 1080-29.97p.
- 3G-SDI is output on BNCs 1 and 2 if you record in 1080-59.94p or 1080-50p
- 1.5G-SDI Square Division (whatever that is) is output on all four BNCs as a group if you want to output the Cinema C4K (4096x2160-24.00p) or Broadcast 4K (3840x2160-24.00p/23.98p/29.97p). Apparently you will need all four BNCs to get enough bandwidth to send the 4K signals to an external monitor or recorder.

UPDATE: the four BNC SDI outs supply "QuadHD" -- that is, each delivers one fourth of a 3840x2160 picture or, four 1920x1080 streams. If you have a device that can accept QuadHD, you're in business.

6. Plug and socket covers

Minor point, but of some concern. The camera is not waterproof but is touted as "splash proof." To achieve this, rubber doors seal the camera all over. The bottom of the camera has two rubber seals that cover two sets of contacts -- one with five, one with 18 contacts. The YAGH unit has quite exposed corresponding spring-loaded pins sticking up. When you attach the camera to the YAGH, you obviously need to remove the four covers. There's no place to store them. You will want them if you split the units apart, especially the camera seals.

7. Audio Controls

a. two 8-segment LEDs indicating level: 4 green, 3 yellow, 1 red.

b. two approx. 1/2" diameter knobs to adjust level, shielded by a clear cover so they won't get hit accidentally yet are easy enough to adjust during a take without shaking the camera or making noise

c. brightness is adjustable to either "Hi" or "Low" via the Interface Unit menu item under the Motion Picture tab

8. Mechanical

a. two locating pins register to the camera body and are held tightly via the 1/4-20 tripod socket. It really becomes a single unit

b. Both 3/8-16 and 1/4-20 threaded tripod mounts on the bottom. There's also a hole for the tripod plates that have an anti-rotation pin. Having both 3/8-16 and 1/4-20 allows you to use two screws to mount the YAGH to your tripod plate so it cannot rotate.

c. two 1/4-20 threaded holes are supplied on the lower front of the YAGH to allow mounting a set of matte box rods, once some third party supplier starts making the rod/rail adapter. The two holes are exactly 32mm apart and centered 85mm below the optical center of the lens, conforming to the 15mm Light Weight Support (LWS) standard.

d. It's still not too giant for hand holding, but it's getting there. It's really designed to be tripod mounted.

e. Because the YAGH extends forward of the camera and slopes downward, if you use one, the Metabones Speed Booster tripod foot must be removed for the adapter to fit the camera while attached to the YAGH. Fortunately, Metabones allows this and supplies necessary Allen wrenches and caps.

Overall, the YAGH is useful -- allows (well, requires) external power for long runtimes, protects the camera from HDMI socket damage, outputs all kinds of signals up to true 4K via SDI, allows timecode input and allows professional audio inputs.

However, if you don't need external power, SDI-out or HDMI-out, a simple audio interface like the JuicedLink Riggy [[ASIN:B009YLRZFE JuicedLink RM222 Riggy-Micro Dual-XLR Preamplifier with Phantom Power]] or a Beachtek [[ASIN:B009R89SNQ BeachTek DXA-SLR MINI PRO HDSLR Audio Adapter]] might suffice to get pro audio in.

USB hubs are one of those computer extras that don't get a lot of attention or thought until one runs out of ports. When needed, though, a hub can greatly expand the USB capabilities of a system. This particular hub is one that comes with its own power supply, which is in my opinion better for most uses.

This is an unassuming little device, about the size of a small harmonica and about as solid. Its small size allows it to take up a small amount of desk space, tucking easily behind a monitor or case (or, if being used with a laptop, behind the whole system). In my specific situation I have it plugged into a laptop with an external monitor attached to it so I have the hub just at the base of the external monitor where it is out of thew way but still easily accessible.

In use, it works as it should. My one real test for the hub was to connect up an external USB hard drive, which does not work well with my other USB hub (coincidentally, also a Belkin product). When I attached the hard drive, the system immediately saw it and assigned a drive letter to it, just as if I connected it directly. This is how a hub should handle such a drive and I was pleased when there was no issue.

The one complaint I have with this hub is that the power cord is not snug. When the hub is moved while attached it is very easy to disconnect it from the power supply. My workaround was to use a twist tie to attach the power cord to the USB cable that attaches the hub to the system, after which I can move the hub without any difficulty.

This is a decent USB hub that works as it is supposed to work. Other than the less-than-secure plug for power I have no complaints.

Bose headphones are noise suppression first, sound fidelity second. If it’s sound fidelity you want, buy a comparably priced studio monitor headphone without noise suppression.

I’ve owned and worn out every iteration of the Bose noise-canceling headphones over the last 20 years for jet cabin noise suppression. Commercial airplane cabin noise is a proven travel fatigue-inducing component. A 2-17 hour flight with noise reduction headphones delivers noticeably less flight fatigue.

The QC-35’s are nearly worn out after another ‘million miles.’ They got 5 stars for the Bose attention to long-wear comfort. They’ve been beaten about, dinged, I’ve replaced the ear and head cushions twice. I suspect I have a wiring failure that’s about to reveal itself fully. I use the Bose most frequently without music for just the noise suppression. They work great as a sleep aid in hotels with and without music. Noise suppression is my #1 priority in this category. I have tested 2 of the latest Bose noise suppression headphone competitors. For several reasons, mostly head comfort and suppression extent, they still have a way to go to meet the Bose total experience.
The ambient noise suppression that these new 700 headphones provide is a significant improvement over the QC-35’s. The bass quality of Bose has always been a question mark easily revealed in a sales counter testing for comparison. Honestly, after an hour, the bass issue disappears in the Bose sound ambiance.

As to music reproduction, Bose does not represent the product as a monitor grade headphone. I happen to have a pair of Blue Ella monitor grade headphones. It is an error to compare the Bose work-horse noise suppression headphones that the 700 series represent with studio monitor grade fidelity. There is no question that studio monitor grade headphones deliver superior fidelity for the time they are worn.

Can I comfortably wear the Blue Ella’s on a trans-con flight? No (plus they are prone to a five-finger discount). They simply aren’t designed for hours of head comfort. The Blue Ella’s are fantastic for a couple of hours but are no way suitably head comfortable for a 17-hour flight to Australia.

The Bose 700’s are a clear step up for the QC-35 users. These are lighter on the head, and though they don’t have hingey elements of the QC-35, I’ve not experienced a flexibility problem from this lighter weight and flexible design. They are an improvement in the Bose reputation for the best designed, long-wear consideration.

Ok, so I have to admit at first I was wondering why someone would spend this much on a Bluetooth headset that isn't a feature-rich entertainment one like those from Sony or a major fad brand like Beats, both of which I have some experience with. But this, no... this is actually something different. This is a serious tool for serious use with serious built quality and seriously useful features. Seriously.
For example, the telescoping mouthpiece means you'll get unparalleled mic quality compared to headsets that pick the mic up by your ears (looking at YOU, airpods!), both in clarity and isolation from background noise. You can also physically bend it out of the way, or use the button on the mic itself to mute. Try doing that with airpods. Then there's the button based features. Shortcuts and touch-sensitive buttons are cool on aesthetic devices, but the physical controls on this are an ergonomic user experience DREAM. Everything is easy to access and control, no apps or press-and-hold or counting LED blinks, etc. Sort of makes me miss the old days of phones with physical switches and buttons. When you want your equipment to get serious, this is the sort of user experience you expect. Then there's the charging rack. OMG I love that, I can store it on my desk and it's charging automagically. Pick it up and put it on, ready to go. Never needs to be charged because it's been charging in between uses. Finally, I'm really impressed with the USB dongle option. You see, the one thing I really dislike about wireless headphones is that you usually need to pair it with a device, then unpair it to switch to another device. For example, using my Sony headphones on my phone and tablet, if my wife wants to borrow them for a zoom meeting, I need to pair with her device but then also unpair with mine so that it doesn't keep trying to reconnect to it. Sometimes we just give up and use a wired headset to avoid that mess. Non-bluetooth wireless headsets have a dongle, which makes it easy to swap what you are connected to (no unpairing needed, just move the dongle) but then you can't connect to devices without a USB port like a phone. This is the best of both- you can pair it with your phone, but ALSO use the USB to quickly connect with your desktop or laptop without going through the process of pairing and unpairing. This is the kind of usability and professional quality I would expect from a brand like Plantronics, and all the while it works well as a stereo headset for music/gaming/etc as well. Very comfortable to wear for long hours, I'd highly recommend it for serious users.

First thing's first, it is important to understand what you are getting. This isn't a VR headset - you aren't going to be bringing these on a trip to play some beat saber. These are simply a screen that you can strap to your head.

Now that we have that out of the way, lets go into the things I love about these. Plugging these into a device is (usually) a breeze and you can get to consuming your content on a virtual screen in no time. The included blackout shade is a great addition, giving you the choice between maintaining situational awareness of your surroundings, or closing yourself off to the world and immersing yourself in the content.

I particularly like using these on a plane. It is great to be able to shut out everything that is going on around you and just watching content without your seatmates peeking over to see what you are watching. I do recommend using in-ear headphones since on or over ear types of headphones can get uncomfortable when combined with the glasses.

If you wear glasses, I suggest purchasing prescription lens inserts - it will really make your experience just that much better.

I think it is really smart that these are powered by whatever device they are plugged into. This allows the device to be less bulky and lighter; hence more comfortable for long term wear. The downside being, your device will consume power quicker. This can be mitigated with a wireless charger (since your glasses are plugged into your device).

This is an impressive little drive and operates quite fast on USB 3.  No install or drivers needed as it is ready to use; just plug in the provided USB cable and it is ready to go.  It might be a little pricey, but not much more expensive than typical USB sticks of the same capacity (256 MB).  It doesn't seem to provide you much more value than a regular USB stick, at least not in terms of storage space.  The value is in the speed.  It is quite heavy compared to a USB stick and about 2 to 3 times larger, as it is encased in metal, so probably far more durable than some storage devices.  The size is still small, at 4 inches long, 1 3/4 inches wide and 1/2 inch thick.  It also comes in an attractive metal storage case that would be great for transporting it.  This would be an ideal external drive for your data.  You can then detach it and move it to another computer easily, just by unplugging the USB cable.  If you are traveling, it should travel quite safely in the metal storage box it comes in.  The capacity is a little low by today's standards, but larger solid state drives do get expensive.  This would be ideal in a 1 TB or larger size and I think we will see bigger solid states drives in the future at affordable prices.  I would not hesitate to recommend this if 256MB space is large enough for your needs.  This would also be great as an off-site backup.

This is one of the modems that's on Comcast's recommended list for my cable system here in California. When the cable guy showed up to install my Internet service, he checked it out and said "It will work fine." After about an hour of pulling wires around my house, he hooked things up to the modem and I had very high speed Internet service. Pretty sweet.

I chose this model because its upload and download specs are well above what my cable Internet service needs, and because it has advanced features like IPv6. So I'm assuming they got the basic stuff right as well. Other reviewers have said this model runs hot, but I haven't observed that. I have it in my utility room which is in the basement where it's pretty cool to start with.

The lights on the front of the unit show what's going on, which is mostly useful as it boots up. They work well, and are also attractive to look at -- they had a good designer for that. The unit has only 3 connection ports on the back, one for power, one for the incoming cable, and one Ethernet RJ-45 out. If you want to hook up more than a single computer, you'll need to connect this single Ethernet port to a router, or wireless router. I have the cable modem connected into a 5-port NetGear switch downstairs, which is connected to an 8-port NetGear switch upstairs, which is then connected to my Linksys wireless router. My computers then use the IP addresses that the wireless router provides. (It won't work to plug additional computers into the switch that I connected directly to the cable modem because the cable company provides only one IP address. It's the wireless router that hands out additional IP addresses. Each computer that you're using requires its own IP address.) The wireless connection works well for my 2 computers and my Roku box for Netflix. (And the bandwidth available to Netflix is amazing. It spends virtually no time at all buffering before it starts streaming HD video.)

Oh, and of course I had to reboot everything (including the modem and the wireless router) for the new modem to be recognized. For now, I'm keeping my old DSL service as a backup Internet service. Not sure when I might decide to give that up.

I’ve had this SSD for a few days and I also have a 1TB 970 Evo Plus and 1TB 860 Evo and all of them are great! But they do have their drawbacks too.

However, if you do heavy workloads like video editing, file transfers, etc,. where you are regularly moving large (15GB+) files around this is NOT the drive for you. If you are a “heavy” user I highly recommend the 860 Pro. It can keep up those high R/W speeds without slowing down after ~15GB. It will maintain full speed throughout the duration of whatever you are doing.

With that said this is a great drive for light/moderate workloads (gaming, web browsing, small work files, etc.,) and it is at a price that gives you excellent value and quality for your money.

Just got this and started playing with it, but first a little background.

I also have two 5 Blacks and a 7 Black. I drive a truck (truck, not peekup) and use these to record my trips and the traffic around me. I record several hours of video every day. With a minor amount of effort, these work much better than typical dashcams. I use them without batteries inside the cab, with USB-C cables powering them. They tend to overheat with the batteries installed when mounted inside the windshield. The 5s still overheat sometimes without the battery. The 7 seldom does. They're often in the sun for hours at a time, so this isn't really a fault. It's not what they're designed to do. The 7 stays connected to the app much better than the 5s do. It's just a much more capable camera all around.

The Hero 7 Black TimeWarp and stabilization are first rate. The first video I took using it on my Jeep, a friend thought I'd bought a gyro-stabilized mount. It's that good. I assume the 8 is at least as good. I expect it to be better.

I've also owned a cheaper "Action Camera". It actually handled the heat better, until the battery swelled up and destroyed the camera. If you're looking for a toy, those are fine. If you want something that lasts, GoPro, with all its faults, is just about all there is. Nothing else does what they do while taking a substantial amount of abuse.

There is a dive case with external battery available from Suptig (on Amazon) for the 5, 6, and 7, but not for the 8. I use this case for the 5s when I mount them outside the truck. I use a Panavise mount with tethers outside the truck. The Panavise mount is heavy enough to hold the heavy battery with the camera mounted on it. I've also used this setup on my Jeep, but not as much as I'd like. There are dive cases for the 8, but not with external batteries that I've found.

The main feature of the 8 that I was drawn to was the ability to switch from TimeWarp to Realtime and back while recording. Unfortunately, this control isn't available on the app, only on the camera screen. I'll just have to mount the 8 where I can tap the screen easily while driving. Not optimum, but not a deal killer.

The app could be a lot better, but GoPro insists on using it for marketing. The app is useful, but I've already bought four GoPros. The cameras sold themselves. The app lacks a lot of features I'd like to see on it, though it is much better now than when I was given my first GoPro 4. The 4 still works fine, by the way, and I still use it where I'm afraid I might lose the camera, such as under the Jeep.

The battery door and charge port on the Hero 8 Black are completely different from the Hero 5 Black and Hero 7 Black. If you plan to use the camera for long periods without the battery, you'll need to get a battery door designed to allow connecting USB while closed. I've ordered one. Just search for "Hero 8 battery door." The alternative is to leave the battery door open, or off. I really don't like that choice. Either way, the camera isn't waterproof without the original door in place and closed.

I can't recommend any of the GoPro 6 series, because for a bit more you can get a 7, and for a bit less, you can get a 5 Black. I bought the 8 instead of another 7 because the price dropped to within $40 of the 7, and there are several improvements. Before you buy any of them, do some research into what each can and cannot do. There are various video modes on each. The older models drop in price every time a new model comes out.

Has 1/8" spring steel rods with 8mm ends that fit normal speedrings well. The other end of the rods have smaller ends if your ring has smaller holes.

My unit came with heat vents on the horizontal sides but not on the vertical sides. In other words, it will vent heat better when positioned horizontally. I think this is for higher-wattage modeling lights, but I've seen some boxes made of a very similar fabric that are suitable for hot lights if mounted very carefully and vented properly. The Bowens speedring is well made and has 12 holes in it for various shaped softboxes. At first, as the box is 31"x47" rectangular, I attached the rods in its ring at the less-than-90-degree (X) position, but found the rods did not lay in the seams properly. Refitting the rods in the holes that are 90-degrees apart (so the rods are in a perfect + shape) caused the rods to lay in the seams of the box perfectly.

Interior is bright silver. I find if I sew the rod ends into their pockets it's a lot easier to assemble and the rods can't come out and get lost.

Grids and speedrings alone usually cost twice as much or more than the whole price of this box, which has two diffusers, a grid, rods, vents and a Bowens-type speedring. Fabulous value.

The only thing that would improve any of these softboxes -- expensive or not -- is a speedring that would help you assemble and especially disassemble the box. The nature of softboxes is that you can get the rods into the holes on the speedring fairly easily but getting the rods out to break the box down is a real pain. The [[ASIN:B00093GGMY Calumet Quickring Speedring]] folds in half and locks. I believe the Calumet ring will do the trick. Undo the lock and all the tension will relax. Chimera makes a quick-release ring too, but it's $87 for the ring alone.

We have a couple of other pairs of binoculars; one cost $300 and the other cost $100. This set is far cheaper that our others and you get what you pay for. On the plus side, I have a larger face and I have no problem focusing these binoculars despite what some other reviewers say. However, despite the binoculars having adjustable eye cups, they are not adjustable enough for me to focus while wearing eye glasses. I have to take my glasses off then adjust the eye cups all the way out to get a clear image.

In bright sunlight, these binoculars give me a reasonably colorful and clear but not especially sharp image. There is some distortion and chromatic aberration, even in the center of the image. In lower light conditions, like around sunset when the wild animals I want to watch are more active, these binoculars give me dim image with poor detail. All compact binoculars degrade quickly in lower light conditions, but cheaper ones like this especially so.

The field of view is advertised as 342 feet at 1000 yards. That number is printed on the front of the binoculars. However, in use the field of view is much smaller than our Nikon 10x25 binoculars that also advertise as 342 feet field of view. These Pronite binoculars are semi-sharp and clear over a much smaller portion of the field of view than our Nikon as well.

In summary, you get what you pay for. These binoculars are near the cheaper end of binoculars that I would consider usable. They are somewhat usable, especially if you don't need great clarity. These binoculars can help you figure out which way a road or trail heads through the valley ahead. They may not be able to distinguish one species of bird from another if you are looking at the shape and colors of the bird.

We have an old DVD player in our basement that tries to up convert but it is not always that great. It has some nice features that were great when we got it, but we wanted another one to replace it that did not take up so much room.

WHAT THIS WAS USED TO REPLACE
The DVD machine this replaced was a really old Philips. It played all regions. No fancy settings, except a sleep timer setting that shut it off after so long. The menu was ancient and very clumsy to navigate.

DID THIS PLAY AS WELL AS THE OLDER ONE?
This DVD player played DVDs as well as the older one. So far we have not had any issues with it. It was only hooked up to the HDMI and the used a mini USB to USB cord the plugged into the outlet. We made sure that it was powerful enough to run the player.

PICTURE
The picture was comparable to the old DVD player- perhaps a bit nicer in some cases. I am actually surprised that it has performed as well as it has.

TRAVEL
I have to say that traveling to a cabin we go to occasionally was nice. We are able to bring this DVD player with us to plug into any TV and watch some DVDs if we want to. It is without TV service so DVD is the only way to really have entertainment if we want it.

DOES IT PLAY BLURAY?
This is not designed to play BluRay.

ANY ISSUES?
This is not a top of the line DVD player with super high definition. If you are looking for that, this isn't it. Is it good DVD quality? Yes. I think so. If you have the right set up, it is a great way to take up little room and still be able to play DVDs. I am not sure I would have this as my permanent player in my bedroom or anything. But it is great to use once in a while at home or travel.

THE BOTTOM LINE
Although this is not fancy or super high quality, it plays DVDs as well or better than our old player so we are happy with it. The footprint is small and it is portable.

MY RATING
FOUR STARS. This is a decent player and so far has been good in a pinch to use for playing DVDs. I like the small footprint and portability especially when we have to go somewhere for a while. It is nice to be able to tuck it into our luggage/bags to take with us. The remote is a bonus.

Smart watches have gotten more popular with the release of the Apple watch. They tend to have a standard set of functions, such as access to instant messaging, email, time, alarms and a lot more, typically tied to your phone. Not all smart watches are alike, though, and offer different sets of functions, better connectivity and other various differences from one another. This particular smart watch offers the mainline set of functions, setting itself apart through the user interface which is more polished and clean than most others with which I have worked. That said, I have a couple of quibbles with it, leaving room for a little improvement.

This is a standard-sized watch with a rubber wristband that can actually fit a larger wrist like mine. I have trouble finding watches and watch bands that fit me, so the fact that this one fits me is a pleasant surprise.

Powering it on, the user is immediately greeted with a complex and fairly complete visual menu system with tiles for every function available to the user. This is a standard presentation for a smartwatch, but this one looks a bit more polished and clean than the others I have seen. Switching to other menu screens just requires a swipe gesture, as to be expected. I have big hands, and this means that, for me, using a stylus makes working with this watch a lot easier. This is not the fault of the watch but a reality of working with a small device.

My first issue with this watch came when I paired it to my phone. The date and time on the watch were off, so I expected that it would grab the time from my iPhone when I paired it. It did not. Instead, I had to dig for the clock application and manually set the time. I dislike this and think that having it set itself when it is paired is much more accurate and cuts effort on the part of the user. For Android users, there is an application to allow for syncing up the time, date and more, but iOS users are out of luck for now. To the manufacturer's credit this is made clear on the product listing so this is not a surprise. Regardless, I am of the opinion that the watch should fetch the time, not rely on being sent the time. In the grand scheme of things, though, this is an annoyance, not a deal breaker.

There is a fairly comprehensive list of functions provided by this watch in addition to time/date and phone answer. Through the menus the user has access to call logs and function, Bluetooth functions, a remote finder function, a pedometer, a sleep monitor, a reminder function to get up and move on occasion, calendar and clock functions, audio functions, video functions and a few more.

One of the interesting functions that this watch offers is a camera. So, I tried to use it and it complained that there was no memory card available. Reading through the limited documentation included, I was unable to find anything about a memory card. I finally noticed that the back of the watch has a small groove where it can be popped off, and when I removed the back I found the battery which is removable (replaceable - another pleasant surprise). Under the battery is a slot for a micro SD card.

Adding a memory card comes with a big catch. It requires removing the battery to get at the holder which in turn clears the clock and resets it to midnight 01-01-2015. So, adding the memory card requires me to set the time again. And again if I remove the card.

Although I think the time sync functions of this watch are lacking, it is otherwise a good smartwatch. The interface is professional and polished and the whole provides access to a large number of useful functions. It's priced well too. Overall, this is a solid offering worth a look if you are wanting a smartwatch.

These other systems had so many false positives I ultimately turned them off.

Pros: But the Ring Bell filled several voids in these other systems. One, the false positives are almost nonexistent due to the ability to mask the alert area of the camera. My existing security system may alert me, but then I had to log into the camera system to see what was going on. The time it takes to do that could make a real difference. But the best part is being able to ignore solicitors and screen people before you answer. It’s as easy as answering a phone call and the live image is instantaneous. The fact that it integrates with my SmartThings hub is just icing on the cake.

I was able to install the Ring Bell Pro in about 15 minutes following the simple instructions. It is extremely well thought out. The video quality of the Ring Pro is excellent! It does not have a very wide angle and there is a slight fisheye distortion, but it should be more than sufficient for most applications. The mobile app is also very intuitive. As I mentioned, when you get an alert, you can immediately see who is at the door and you can choose to answer and speak, or just watch.

Cons: I was confused by the wall plate not having the mounting holes line up with the existing wall plate holes. This required drilling holes above and below the existing holes to mount the plate. I could see no reason for this.

The unit can easily be ripped off the wall with one hand. Because the main unit mounts onto a plastic wall cover, it would take about 2 seconds to remove and disable the unit. But at least you will get an alert and when you went to log in you would know something was wrong. However, the Ring Pro has a unique purchase protection that sates “If your Ring™ Video Doorbell is stolen at any time after your purchase, Bot Home Automation, Inc. will replace your Ring™ Video Doorbell at no charge to you”. That’s pretty impressive!

If you want to keep your Ring History, you have to sign up for their paid service. Otherwise you only see live views. Prices vary by plan, but they do offer one free month for new customers.

Overall: There is no perfect security system. Each one has its plusses and minuses. But the Ring Pro should be part of every home security solution. Also, if I had to choose only one component for a complete home security solution, this would be high up on my list.

I have been working with security camera products for over 20 years - over that time I have installed systems for businesses, corporations and individuals - from enormous multimillion dollar systems to single camera nursery monitors. I’ve consulted on large projects and written about security vulnerabilities within networks for trade publications.

This is a field I know well. Over the years the technology has improved and become less and less expensive to produce. It is now practical to install security systems that would have only previously been used in commercial settings in residential.

I have tested and reviewed many wireless doorbell systems. Typically I always advise to avoid any wireless cameras due to the inherent security vulnerabilities but this is often not possible with doorbell cameras. That being said there are key components I look for in wireless doorbell cameras: clear picture that provides a wide viewing angle, it either be hard wired or have excellent battery life, when chime button is pressed alert is sent and app can be opened and responsive in a quick time, 2 way audio communication is clear on both ends, motion sensitivity is adjustable and accurate.

I have thoroughly tested this product over the last 4 months and in comparison to the others on the market around this price point this product has proven to be clearly the best.

In terms of what is excellent - the internal battery is long lasting and dependable - I have found that it will last nearly 2 months on a single charge. The vast majority of wireless doorbells use proprietary batteries which forces users to purchase secondary batteries typically costing $30-$50. This factor is a huge bonus.

The camera is quite good. Images are clear and the wide angle provides a full view of the area in front of the doorbell. The AI Smart Human detection is without question the best I have found. This is a huge feature that helps prevent constant false alerts.

The base station holds up to a 128GB SD card for video storage. This is awesome for multiple reasons. If the camera was stolen the evidence will be saved on the base station within your home and all of your recordings are stored locally. This is an outstanding system.

Unfortunately, as with many similar products, while the hardware is good the software needs some work. As is typical, I can not find any way to force this doorbell to work with better software. It is obvious this was designed on the Tuya platform though I have not found any way of integrating it. I would much rather use the Tuya app where I have the bulk of my automation set but this will not migrate.

The lag from the time the doorbell button is pressed until you can see who is there is mediocre. The FASTEST I’ve been able to get this to work is 18 seconds - and I’m using an iPhone 13 Pro Max with 512GB on a super fast 1G mesh WiFi with a node located within feet of the doorbell inside the door.

The 2 way audio is spotty. It sounds like ordering through a drive through where every 3rd word is audible. Since I don’t use these to have in depth conversations it isn’t a huge deal but should be noted.

This is definitely among the best wireless doorbells I have tested for a while. It is not perfect, the sound leaves room for improvement as does response times but overall this is a quality unit.

While the vast majority of the doorbells I tested I advised to avoid all together this one is one worth using.

I've had problems with Pixmas in the past, mostly having to do with wireless networks and having to reinstall the software over and over to try to get them to hang on to network settings. I can't guarantee that this printer is going to be any better in the long run, but the set-up actually works pretty well if you use the standard version, not the WPS... and I'm getting way ahead of myself on this one.

To begin with, the printer requires a lot of time for set-up. You're not going to be doing this on the fly, so set aside an hour or so to: 1) remove all the tape of which there is much, 2) read over the instructions 3) install the ink, 4) run a print alignment 5) set up your wireless connection (about which more in a moment) 6) install the software (which takes a good 15 minutes or more), and 7) put the machine (and yourself) through its paces. Yeah, it's going to take a while.

Now I know you can read about the features on your own, so I'm here to tell you about the things that work for me and those that don't. First off, the wireless set-up is confusing. Choose Standard instead of WPS and save yourself some headaches unless you're a computer whiz kid. After the third error message in the WPS set-up I went to standard, entered my pass code and had the connection up and running in about a minute.

Once that was done and the software was installed I fired up the Canon Image Garden. First I scanned an image and attempted to rotate, crop and fix any deficiencies I found. The scan was over sharp and looked a bit jagged, but a little fiddling with the Canon software fixed that. Canon software also rotated and cropped perfectly. One really nice feature is that they remind you to put the printing side of the paper down in the paper cassette. How many pieces of paper will that save?

The biggest complaint I had was that it didn't give me a choice of which paper cassette to use for printing, so I got a ridiculously truncated image on the first try. I believe it chooses the paper based on the size of the image, which I get, but at the same time that limits flexibility in printing. I opened another photo processing program and it allowed me to print from whatever cassette I liked. Coupled with a better suite of applications for correction and enhancement, I think it's safe to say that I'll be using the Canon software almost never.

Printing on plain paper is clearly not going to be as satisfactory as it is on glossy, but in some cases I found it surprisingly good, good enough to give you an idea of what sort of image you're going to end up with when you switch to photo paper. It's also more than good enough for printing out emails and web pages.

Scanning and printing are both pretty fast, another plus. And the copy function works pretty seamlessly without any sort of computer interface. Just punch a couple of buttons and Bob's your uncle! It does take a bit of time to warm up and is a little noisy but no more so than any Canon printer I've ever used. It's not bothersome, in my opinion. You might feel otherwise.

Inks are easy to install, but you'll find refills pricey, no question. I suspect off-brand ones are available or will be soon enough.

In short, it's a good, inexpensive printer for a home or home office. Use photo paper and settings and get the full quality the MG5420 is capable of producing; I think it's pretty remarkable. The photos I printed out are as good as or in one case, better than the original. That's a powerful recommendation in my book.

I have worked with a lot of different sets of headphones and ear buds and have gotten a good feel for what sounds right and what doesn’t. Specifically with ear buds I pay attention to the fit as well as the sound, which are two areas where many manufacturers get it wrong. Anker did a good job with these though there is a soft spot in the sound profile.

I used these with an iPhone 7, and initial pairing was very quick and painless. The buds found each other (another issue I have seen with other sets on occasion), and these paired without much fanfare or issue at all. That’s really all you could ask.

These fit like a dream. The package contains several silicone plugs of different sizes so you can get just the right fit for yourself, but I found that the ones already on the buds were actually a perfect fit. I popped these in, gave them a turn to lock them in place and they sealed perfectly. I am especially happy with how well these fit in my ears and actually stay there.

The sound isolation is on par with what you’d expect. When not powered on and streaming music they are the equivalent to a cheap set of ear plugs – enough to block out some sound but not completely silence the world.

The sound quality is very good but the sound profile could use a tweak. The bass is strong but not overdriven to the point of causing headaches. There is a tendency to overdrive the bass, so having good bass that’s not overpowering is nice. The highs are bright and clear too. The midrange is another matter and feels weak (though not non-existent). Music played through these buds lacks the warmth and fullness that the midrange brings to the table (and if it was overdriven everything would sound like it is coming through a tunnel). I would rather have under-driven midrange than overdriven, but it’s still soft enough to be noticeable.

They case in which these buds are stored also serves as the charger. What is interesting about these is how the case itself is charged. Instead of MicroUSB, this case uses a Type C connector which is not unwelcome but up to this point is unusual for this kind of device. There is a cable in the box so there’s no issue.

These are good ear buds and they have some nice features. They fit superbly and they pair to a source without problems. The sound profile is imperfect, though not terribly so, which is the only complaint I have with them.

This is a fairly standard surge protector with 12 outlets with only two of those set apart for the larger adapters. The selling point that it attempts to sell consumers on is the usb ports, including one type-c so this review will concentrate mostly on those ports.

As far as the surge protector portion of this product, the face outward, which means that the longer style chargers that comes with some electronics will not plug in without taking up an extra socket. With only two set farther apart for power adapters, this power strip will not work well for a location with routers, modem, and NAS.

Now on to the USB ports. Five USB ports share a total of Five amps. It means that is the power strip is completely filled, it will only deliver one amp to each port. The type-c port is only useful if that is the only cable you can find because it does not support any fancy features such as quick charging or type-c pd, although it does support up to 3A so some phones may actually consider this "fast charging". Do not expect to replace a true 5-port usb charger with this power strip.

Problem #1: Camera eats up normal AAA Energizer batteries quickly. Maybe get 5 pictures and then it quits. Change to AAA Lithium Entergizer Batteries. Now, you are OK. The sensor on the camera trips just after a few underwater photos.

Size, and functionality seems comfortably nice. Not too technical to get started using this camera. Found this camera a great first step for beginners who want to document their scuba dives, take photos on surface, on the boat, on the shore, etc. But, hold on... when you want to go scuba diving:

Problem #2: Does not have an underwater setting for diffused lighting. Only Flowers and Landscapes. What dah? Is this not for underwater use? Hello! All of my underwater photos could have improved by 100 percent if there was a setting for underwater lighting. The sunny days at the shore, boat photos, trees and countryside photos, ok. These were nice, the detail in the landscape photos were good. You can even use the camera without its plastic shell. The protective casing makes this an excellent choice as a first step scuba camera. But, how are the photos underwater? This is a $100 camera, so please do not expect high quality photos from your squid, lobster, or grouper ... posing for you underwater, even at 25 feet. This makes a great first step camera, getting your feet wet with underwater photography.

Problem #3: strap holder is on right side only (for right hand use.) Better if there was a strap holder on both sides, for those who need on left hand side (underwater.) Why? My first hand experience is that you want to use this point and shoot camera using either your right hand or your left hand. Not both. This camera is a quick shot camera, not "oh, wait a minute, pose, look this way, now smile, ok, cheese ..." This camera sits on your right hand or left hand while diving. Now, if you see that nice fish, and want to take a picture, you try with one hand. If the strap is on the wrong side, it blocks your ability to use the left hand to hold the camera. So, this camera is ONLY FOR RIGHT HANDED folks. But, do not let go of the camera underwater, you may loose it. Right? Not really. Nice thing about this basic camera is that it float to surface (rather than sink into the bottom.) Wow, did that save me a few times. Dropped off my wrist. Then floated for a few feet, and I got it back. If it sunk down 300 Feet, I could have kissed this baby --- good bye.

I have taken about 50 surface images, and 50 underwater images, using this Intova. All 50 surface photos, with reasonable sunlight, were excellent considering this camera. Of the 50 photos underwater images, about 10 were acceptable, the other 40 were blurry and not acceptable. Yeah, I had to spend another 15 minutes per each of the 10 photos to convert the poor colors into something more exciting, adding RED, adding CONTRAST, adding BRIGHTNESS using a photo editor. But, I did get 10 acceptable underwater photos. And that was great. Really Great. These photos were generally above 25 feet.

Scuba divers need to know the difficulty of taking photos underwater while attempting to swim around reefs, wrecks, squid, lobster and other photographers. Buy this camera as a first step. Just correct that battery issue, take lots of pictures, and learn the responsibility of underwater photography is the PERSON BEHIND THE CAMERA. For $100, not bad, eh?

Great board. Install was simple. Most ports are in decent locations with no real trouble with cable routing. First boot was normal and got me right into the bios screen. Make sure you update the bios before doing anything else. I made the mistake of setting my memory to DOCP1 (to get my DDR5 set to 6000) before updating the bios which resulted in black screen, no post. I did notice that once I had had Win11 installed, my boot times were slow. Did some research and found that there's a bios setting "memory context restore" that needs to be changed to enabled. After that the boot times improved drastically, but still not as quick as my previous AM4 system. I'm sure it will improve with future bios updates. With a 7700X cpu, Cinbench R23 multi-core score is 20k (about the same as my previous 5900X). Timespy score with an RTX4080 is 29k, which I got to 30k with a quick oc. So far so good, it's a fast and stable motherboard.
I do have one con: CMOS battery was DOA! I found this out when I removed power from my sys to setup another pc. I had to go back in and setup all of my bios settings again (then saved my profile until I could get a new battery. I recommend swapping the battery (CR2032) before you set it up and to save your profile in the bios. I guess it costs extra when buying a $500+ motherboard to get a working cmos battery. -1 star.

I am an audiophile who is determined to get great sound without spending large amounts of money.  It is esy to get world class sound if you are willing to spend over $5,000.  I will never do that, however.  In the 1970's, I worked part time in two high end audio stores -- hence I know what good sound is and is not.  I was interested in the Motion 4's because they are Martin Logan speakers and Martin Logan has been a leader in producing remarkable speakers for decades.  And I was interested because of the technology employed in the Motion 4's. I got a pair of the Motion 4 speakers about one week ago after auditioning them three times at my local Best Buy. In the store, they sounded far superior to any other speaker even close to their price range.  Once I got them home, they sounded even better as I hooked them up to a Denon 3805 receiver.  I got the 3805 used for $200 after doing much research on receiver performance vis a vis 4 ohm speakers -- which the Motion 4's are.  This is a big deal -- matching you amp to your speakers -- since there are many amps that simply fall apart sonically under 4 ohm speaker loads.  Many receivers won't even rate their output into 4 ohm loads because of their embarassing performance. This particular Denon receiver, however is a throwback in terms of build quality and handles 4 ohm loads exceedingly well. The Motion 4's are not big speakers but they will fill an average sized listening room quite nicely. There is not much low end but that did not surprise me and it wasn't needed since I have a subwoofer. The midrange and the high end, however, are nothing short of glorious.  They are spacious and very open and incredibly detailed. I absolutely was hearing more and better sounds than I have heard in years. The folded tweeter -- a smaller version of the incredible Heil Air Motion transformer of 30 years ago -- clearly is amazing. Any high frequency -- cymbals, pianos, acoustic and electric guitars, etc -- simply come to life with a sense of immediacy and aural acceleration lacking in any other speaker near its price range and size.  The only possible reason anyone would find these speakers lacking is if you installed them in a very large room that they couldn't possibly fill OR if you hooked them up to an amp that could not handle 4 ohm loads -- and beware, there are a lot of amps out there that have this problem.  Otherwise, buy the Motion 4's with confidence.

Purchased the Amplify HD from Ubiquiti Labs. Very first Mesh router.

I did however buy the main rougher first and next month adding the mesh points. I wanted to see how good was the coverage on the solo unit before dropping the full amount on 2 mesh points. I'm running ATT Fiber, and wasn't use to using a forced gateway modem. (had to look up connecting a unit to my gateway) My speeds are 300 down and 300 up. Directly connected to the unit I get full speed up and down sometimes lowest down at 280/290 but always full amount or more up stream. Its blazing fast, the app is smooth and the unit has a soft touch that's hard to describe, almost like felt/metal/plastic. Feels premium. As others pointed out, by tapping the screen, you can cycle threw connections (direct connections), time, up and down speeds to see how much data its pulling or reveal the units ID.

PROS: Easy to connect, open and set up. REALLY GOOD RANGE. Much better than the default hardware provided by ATT. I will update the review next month when I get my mesh point. By the looks of other reviews, it shouldn't be an issue.

WARNING: if you're running 1000 down and up. You have to set the router to hardware NAT to ON. Keep in mind this is for direct connections, not Wifi speeds. If you're using 1000 down and up, its common sense to be directly connected. From what I read in thier main forum not using it caps at 500 down and up. You also may NOT need to turn it on. ONLY if your not getting the full speeds in test. So it may work like normal. It also has a built in BRIDGE MODE. If your gateway doesnt have bridge mode. (MOST DO).

#MY SET UP ATT 300 FIBER

As a general rule, I hate hands-free handsets.

I hate it when I begin speaking with someone, and I think they're agreeing with everything I say, and then it turns out they're actually talking to someone else using their dratted ear extension with the flashing blue light.

I hate the fact that my ears are the wrong size and shape for the majority of headsets.

I hate it when my untrained (clumsy) fingers hit the wrong part of the headset when I'm simply trying to stop it from falling to its death from a height of just over 5 feet, and I either redial the last number or hang up on the one person who hates being hung up on.

Plus, they're UGLY, and don't accessorise well with any wardrobe!!

HOWEVER,

I hate it even more when I have to pull over and park to take or make a call.

And I especially hate it if I DON'T pull over, and then get busted by the only policeman on the entire empty highway who has insomnia and a full book of blank tickets waiting to be filled in.

SO,

Hands free it shall be -
But ONLY when I'm driving.

That said, this device fits most of my basic needs, and throws in some convenient extras. The EASYGO Headset was indeed very easy to set up and even easier to use. Sound quality was good and the spoken connection status and audio volume adjuster are useful features.

The headset is also relatively small and stylish (as hands-free headsets go) without any flashing lights or buttons that attract unwanted attention (or cause an attack of photosensitive epilepsy, or signal the letters N-E-R-D in morse code.)

The most impressive feature of this headset has to be the long battery life, which is great because the miserly charger cord is so awkward to use that you don't want to have to use it more often than necessary. Besides, as I only use it in the car, it lasts me several trips, depending on how often and how long I prattle.

Admittedly it is more comfortable to use than I expected. The extra ear hook prevents suicidal leaps from ear to earth, and it doesn't weigh my head down on one side.

In summary, for a simple headset, it delivers.

I have been working with security camera products for over 20 years - over that time I have installed systems for businesses, corporations and individuals - from enormous multimillion dollar systems to single camera nursery monitors. I’ve consulted on large projects and written about security vulnerabilities within networks for trade publications.

This is a field I know well. Over the years the technology has improved and become less and less expensive to produce. It is now practical to install security systems that would have only previously been used in commercial settings in residential.

If you are new to home security camera systems, I recommend going with wired (non-WiFi), NVR or computer based recorders run with systems such as Blue Iris. This type of system is infinitely more secure and stable. While initial setup costs are a bit more the security it affords is worth every penny. It always pays to research the products, discuss them with those in the field, understand vulnerabilities and PLAN YOUR SYSTEM PRIOR TO PURCHASING ANYTHING. If you are at all tech savvy at all you can do it. While there is a bit of a learning curve it is not awful and in the end you will be thankful for the time you spent in the beginning as it will save you time, money and endless frustration.

I have set up, tested and reviewed more security systems and individual products than I can possibly remember. Without question my go to solution for home security solutions is a computer based, Blue Iris system with POE cameras run off of quality POE switches. This type of system is not only easy to operate but is highly secure.

As with any component there are a host of factors to consider. In terms of cameras more megapixels is not always better. For instance 2MP cameras often perform better in low light while 5MP will allow for more detail when lighting is good. One disadvantage of higher megapixel cameras is the recordings will take up more hard drive space. Depending on the number of cameras, this can become a larger concern.

When I saw this camera at this price point I knew it was something I needed to check out. I appreciated the fact it was 2MP because with this lens you are not going to want to be eating up the hard drive space required for a 5MP.

I was able to get it set up within my Blue Iris system after playing with it for a while. Typically this takes me no more than a couple of minutes - this camera required much more extensive programming in order to have it functional.

Once I did have it up and working image quality is substandard even compared to other cameras with similar specs.

I figured it still could be utilized as a tertiary filler camera but it kept going offline for absolutely no reason. When a camera is connected via PoE to Blue Iris this simply should not be an issue unless there are issues with the camera itself.

While the price point is excellent on this camera, unfortunately this is an example of getting what you pay for. In my four months of testing this camera has proven to be unreliable, difficult to connect and keep connected and the images captured are far lower quality than expected from cameras with similar specs.

This is a product to pass on.

What I Don't Like:
*The camera quick-access patch. While it almost certainly won't dump your camera out (it secures at the top with a plastic latch & velcro) the zippers 1) don't completely close off the opening. Dirt, bugs, moisture can easily get inside your backpack. 2) the zippers are attached to each other with a loop of nylon. This is going to catch on things (branches, chairs, doors, etc.) and open. Again, you probably won't lose your camera but if you don't notice the zippers opening and they open VERY easily, you're going to have even bigger openings for problems to get in. You can remedy this somewhat by putting the loop under the latch it still allows the zippers to slide down several inches.
* The rain cover comes in a small pouch kept in one of the back pockets. It could easily be lost.

All in all it's an okay backpack but not a great one. There's room for everything you could want to carry but the quick-access patch... that just ruins the backpack for me. My camera gear is expensive and dear to me, I want to protect it the best I can. Having an opening that doesn't seal completely and can easily be opened wider by accident is a poor design.

I bought one of those very small ASUS VivoMini UN62-M037M computers. It has an HDMI out port to connect to either a monitor or your nice HD TV. (I have mine connected to my TV.) I am running Windows 8.1 on the computer.

Microsoft has acknowledged that there is a bug in Windows 8 and 8.1: When you turn off your TV but leave your computer on, the OS will always give you an Out of Memory error message. There is no software fix whatsoever. Many people are complaining of this issue on boards over at Intel and other places.

The only fix is to either never ever turn off your TV, or always turn off your computer when you turn off your TV, or fool the computer into thinking there is that HDMI monitor connected even when said monitor is powered off.

I bought this ConnectPRO for just this purpose...and it works.

Out of the box I did not get a green light, per the instructions. The light was orange, which implies it had a memorized EDID from the factory.

I reset the box and cloned the EDID from my TV.

I can now leave my computer on always if I desire and turn off my TV at any time, and no more problems.

Sad that Microsoft never offered their own software fix via an update, in spite of the fact they confirm the issue, which forced me to have to spend an extra $70.
