So I decided to go for MSI after doing much research on Nvidia Pascal-Powered laptops. I do a lot of 3DS Max work, and I'm a gamer since the 80's, so I figured, this may be the best route. I didn't want to get a laptop which, in a few months, would already be obsolete, so I skipped some of the other current gen models from the likes of Alienware with 970/980 m cards. I didn't give Asus a shot because I've had a not-so-good experience with my current and previous desktops. My current desktop (which is quite powerful so no qualms there)... had a keyboard issue, and I was only 3 months into ownership. Asus refused to replace it as their one year warranty only covers the PC itself, not the keyboard which I'm sorry, but is part of the system.They said if I paid for shipping they would give me a new one at cost. How generous - after the price I paid for that system.The keyboard is backlit red which matches the red-lit system and impossible to find. My previous Asus had a cheap motherboard / power supply, which overheated only a few months after my one year warranty was up.

This is my first MSI computer, and I have to say, the laptop is stunner. The Steel Series keyboard is a pleasure to type on with its generously- spaced keys, and backlit configurable color spectrum while the non-reflective IPS screen is gorgeous, sporting good viewing angles with colors that truly pop. I love 17" screens for gaming when I'm sitting on a recliner, as I don't feel like being hunched over a desk all night. I haven't used it for VR yet, but I did run the Steam VR Speed Test to see where it stands. On my Asus G11CD Desktop (16GB i7-6700 3.40Ghz and Nvidia 970), the results showed my system just making it into the VR ready green band. The same test on my MSI Laptop had the VR Ready indicator near the very end of the green band, almost off the chart. As for Windows 10 itself -- it's up within seconds thanks to the 128 SSD. There's not much to comment on the touchpad. I never use them - they're the spawn of Satan. I always hook up a wireless mouse.

I haven't had a chance to test all of my games yet, as my laptop less than a week old as of this review, but the few I've tried ran smooth as glass. I downloaded the demo of the updated System Shock which has a 2017 release. Using FRAPS FPS counter, I was clocking in 92-120 FPS. Same download on my Asus was roughly 75-83. I've been heavily involved with the Planet Coaster (Alpha) which is more taxing than most high end first person shooters. I am running large simulated theme parks, with very advanced lighting effects and all graphic options maxed out. With Nvidia GSync (this monitor supports it) enabled, I'm getting a solid 60 FPS .98% of the time. In comparison, my Asus using the same dense parks using V-Sync gave me an average of 45-50 FPS

Thankfully, there is not too much on the bloatware end. Most of the included extras are MSI tune-up/tweaking programs and surprisingly, quite useful. Norton Security however, is bloatware in my opinion. It came with my Asus, it came with this MSI, and on both systems, it was the first thing I deleted. I don't need it. I never will. Stop it.

As far as the audio, the Nahimic 2 Virtual Surround is super impressive. I've had other laptops in the past, and they've always sounded like tin can alley. The sound that comes out of this unit is rich, and at times, the surround effect is quite effective. The max volume could use another notch or two, but it's still quite competent. Definitely game and epic movie-worthy sound.

The system remains fairly cool and quite capable of dispersing heat properly. Running the power hungry Planet Coaster Alpha no doubt generates a ton of heat, but it all seems to flow out of the back vents, so no keyboard hot-spots. One issue: I use a very thin, rigid laptop mat so the back vent heat winds up flowing to my knees which can be uncomfortable. The one way around this is pulling the laptop toward you, allowing for about an inch of the mat to stick out of the back as a kind of shield. A welcome addition is the turbo fan which you can easily access from a button on the left side of the laptop. I usually turn it on for about a minute and it diminishes the heat fairly well. One of the included MSI utilities gives you more access to the fan's options. Besides the fan, the MSI Dominator Pro has additional buttons that handle quick access functions like sleep mode, sample keyboard color layouts, and other options. Oh, and if you're thinking about lugging this around to your local coffee shop, forget it....unless you want to attract a crowd of wide-eyed onlookers. Also, It's pretty heavy, as in home gym bicep curl heavy. Unfortunately, the one area I haven't tested (my apologies) is the battery life as I am not one who travels with my laptop. I keep my laptop powered through AC in my living room.

Any regrets? None whatsoever - my jaw is still on the floor, but I have a very minor gripe.

The Laptop has a huge sticker on the base, in front of the keyboard. It's one of those highlighted specs stickers that all laptops generally boast. On the list it shows 120mhz display, yet, the on-line specs shows it being a 60mhz. At first glance, your heart will skip a beat and you'll be thinking... WOW even better than I imagined! That is, until you look close at the tiny word under that feature which says (optional). Really MSI - If you're going to slap a "Look what I have inside me" sticker on my laptop, at least leave out what is absolutely not included.

My parents used to have a Polaroid camera and it was everything that we remember those old cameras for – it spat out a white square of plastic that slowly developed into a grainy, faded-looking picture within a few minutes, it was bulky and it had a very distinct sound. It was a great old camera but when Polaroid quit making film for it it became a paperweight. It's nice to see that some of these old cameras are available with film again. That said, there are some oversights with this package.

I will start with the two negatives (no pun intended). First, the way the camera was packaged for shipment was sub-par and the package was partially crushed when I received it. It did not appear to be damaged beyond the packaging, but it was a disappointment to open the package and find the merchandise box partially crushed. Second, the camera comes with no film or batteries at all. So, the camera by itself is still a paperweight. It would have been nice to have at least a lower capacity pack for film to get started.

The camera came out of the box without a mark on it. It looks to be brand new, in spite of being an older unit. Some of the other reviewers have complained that the camera they received either was scratched up or was partially damaged, but mine is pristine. It's a simple, straightforward device too, and it does not require much thought to use.

In use, it works just like it would have when new. It fires the flash, spits out one exposure with that same distinctive sound I remember and the film develops in front of you. The exposure still looks grainy and old when it is all done, but it is a real photograph that does not need a separate printer or software to get a hard copy. This is not the kind of camera a photographer would use, but rather it is for the tourist or enthusiast.

Why would you want a camera like this? For me, it is a trip down memory lane to a time years ago, when candid pictures were a part of daily life and the exposures were lined up on the pinboard for all to see without needing a computer or tablet. It is not going to make pictures that look like they could be in a magazine, but it will produce pictures you can enjoy right away.

This is supposed to improve the sound quality, but I could barely tell any difference. It has a little too much bass for my tastes, but others might find it acceptable.

Probably my greatest complaint with this Philips MP3 player is the included ear buds. They are the type that hugs the ear, but they do not contain a foam cushion and thus are not very comfortable or very good at blocking outside noise. The good thing, of course, is that an accessory like this can be replaced, which I recommend doing if you purchase this product.

MP3 players are nice and Philips GoGear Vibe 8 GB MP3 Player is a good MP3 player, especially for the price. There are certainly better MP3 players out there, but this is a good one for beginners or those with basic needs. I'm torn with my overall rating because of the division between the pros and cons. So, I will award this device with a middle rating of three stars and a modest recommendation.

On the other hand, the highs and lows are practically seamless, with a slight emphasis towards the mid range, so if you listen to jazz, blues or some forms of rock and Americana this speaker will probably please you.

One review discussed bluetooth range issues so I specifically tested that. Even two rooms away, which normally causes drops in quality, I was able to get crystal clear streaming with no drops in the music quality streamed from a Samsung Note 3. The distance is approximately twenty feet, but definitely not line of sight, so I am happy with that aspect.

While the product specs claim six hours of music, you can realistically expect somewhere between four and four and a half hours if you have the volume cranked. If you drop it to about a quarter - perfect for near listening up to two or three meters - you will get the claimed play time.

I got this because I needed a basic router that could handle multiple connections and not break under the strain. I needed all 4 ports for a desktop (gigabit Ethernet destroys wireless for ping on multiplayer games!), PS3 (same reason), and two networked printers. I also have three or four devices that connect wirelessly. This router was easy to set up, had good security options and seemed to work fine for a couple of months. But I found that YouTube on the wireless connection with a Windows Update running means that my Android smartphone net speed slows to a crawl. I pay for a 20mbps connection and Speedtest shows that this isn't giving it to me.

This router cannot handle multiple connections very well. Downloading large open-source code packages via P2P networks chokes the pipe to a crawl OR kills it altogether until an unplug and restart. I have a 1000 square foot apartment with this in one bedroom and when I'm on the other side of the apartment, I don't get full signal.

This is a good basic router for a single user who primarily streams YouTube or Netflix to one laptop at a time. If you are a power user or really need good range, then you need to spend more money on a N600 or N900-level router. Additionally, since this router does not specify compatibility with IPv6, a more expensive router might be more future proof.

From there, the process was fairly easy, BUT it should have never been so difficult to get the phone to recognize the SanDisk in the first place. It should NOT have been that difficult to plug the device into my phone however!  I will also mention, not that it's a big deal, but the device is considerably smaller than it looks to be on the Amazon website (less than .75x1.5").  At least I have an additional backup, but not as easily as I would have liked.  Given the issues I had with it I don't think I would purchase this particular device again.

When I received my review sample I tested it on a legacy system (a ThinkPad T61 running Windows XP) and a phone running Android 4.4.2. I tested the USB 2.0 compatibility on the ThinkPad and USB 3.0 on the phone using an [[ASIN:B00GLKI258 [OTG HUB with SD card reader] Unitek usb3.0 hub with OTG adapter Bus-powered HUB ALL IN ONE USB 3.0 HUB OTG Function]]. As a previous reviewer warned it's not advisable to plug hubs into bubs, but I wanted to text the transfer speed.

In the case of the ThinkPad I plugged in an extra keyboard, mouse, flash drive and camera (the latter for transfers only). The load of devices did not exceed the 500mA that this hub kicks down to for power consumption when connected to USB 2.0 ports. this can support up to 900mA when connected to USB 3.0 ports, but note that it's still only viable for lower power peripherals. Plugging a single USB 3.0 external drive into this into USB 3.0 ports can eat your entire power budget, rendering the other ports in the hub unusable. Be aware that this limitation applies to all unpowered USB hubs, not just this one.

I tested the USB 3 speeds using the set up described about to my Note 3 phone. This hub, even daisy chained into another hub, supported copying 10 GB from the phone to an SD card reader in about 30 seconds. That is blazing fast.

While this is not the prettiest hub on the market (there seems to be a trend towards brushed aluminum these days), it performs per USB specs and has an integrated switch that I like. I had no issues whatsoever with either of the test beds I used. As long as you heed the limitations of unpowered hubs this one is worth considering if you need to expand your ports in a cost effective manner.

The Android system works well for plex and jellyfin, which I have installed. I pre-ordered this product 6 months before it was released. Three different release dates came and went until finally it arrived at my door without notice. When I opened the Amazon box, I saw the first problem. Although I ordered it in black, I received a white one. I was replacing a white one so I figured, what the heck, let’s go with it. I opened it up, looked at the very sparse instructions, plugged it in and within a few minutes it was up and running. However I wanted to use this as an access point and not any of the other three options offered on the setup wizard. More on that later.

Prior to this arriving I would comb through the dozens of questions people posted on the pre order page. One of my favorites was repeated by several people, “Do I still need internet service if I get this”? OF COURSE YOU DO! That’s like asking if you still need food if you get a new refrigerator. If you are asking this question, I highly recommend you enlist a qualified professional to help you assess your needs and get you set up. With that out of the way, let’s get into what this little guy can do.

As Wireless Range Extender (Repeater):

Think of this as a relay race where one runner reaches a mark, hands off the baton to the next runner, who then takes it to the next mark. This assumes you already have the first runner and of course the baton. So to use this as a wireless repeater you need an existing internet connection and wireless router. You will put the Almond 3 somewhere in your house where you get a good wireless signal using any other device such as a smart phone, laptop or tablet. Check to see you have most of your bars on your device, find a wall plug and fire up the almond 3 and follow the on screen directions to set up a “Range Extender”. (The device is just for checking the signal, not for setting up the Almond 3) If you put the Almond 3 too far from your existing wireless router, you will have the same crappy wireless speed you do now. Only you will be confused because you will see you have all the bars on the device which will be coming from the Almond 3. Remember, the Almond is only handing off the same signal it gets. If the signal is bad, that’s what you will get. So keep the Almond 3 as close to the existing wireless router to the point where you just start losing bars on your devices. However don't put it too close to the existing wireless router, or the signals may compete with each other.

As A Wireless Router:

This assumes a few things. First, that you have an existing internet connection. Second, that you are comfortable replacing the main router in your house. This means you will be taking the internet connection from your provider, disconnecting and turning off the the main router and plugging this in its place. In the case of cable internet, you will have to at least have a cable modem from your provider. (NOTE: Only qualified network engineers would ever have two routers in one home). If you set up the Almond as a router and you already have a router, you will start experiencing all kinds of network issues up to and including completely crashing your network and internet connection. Once you have put this in place of your existing router, simply fire it up and follow the on screen wizard.

As A Mesh Network:

If you don’t know what a mesh network is, then do not attempt to try this. Just use one of the above choices. If you know what a mesh network it, simply fire up the Almond 3 and follow the on screen prompts.

As An Access Point:

Again, unless you know the difference between a router and an access point, you are better off choosing one of the first two configurations. To start with, an access point assumes you have an actual Ethernet cable coming from an existing router somewhere in the house. This could be next to the router, or anywhere in the house using a switch or a switched port on the main router. If you are already lost, stop here and choose one of the first two options. If you know what you are doing, then follow these steps. Connect the Almond as a router with your network cable in the WAN port. Configure the setup wizard as a router (its ok to do that for now). When you complete the setup, go to the home screen, select the MORE icon followed by the Access Point icon. Once that’s done you can set up the SSIDs the way you want. It’s unfortunate that Access Point is not an option at startup. It seems an obvious deficiency.

Once You Are Set UP:

Once you get through the first setup screens you get the option to configure the Almond trough an App on your phone. I would download the Almond App before you get started on any of the above options. That will make the final steps of the wizard go much easier. Follow all the prompts to configure the App. (NOTE: this does not connect your phone to your new wireless connection; it only connects the App for future use). Once you get your phone connected to the new wireless connection and get the App set up, you can configure some of the more frequently used options right from your phone. Also don’t forget to update the firmware by going into the setup icon from the device. Finally, make sure you password protect the Almond 3 display so no one can change you configuration.

The App:

The app is a great tool for many reasons. With the optional smart home dongle you can connect all sorts of devices to automate your home. But right out of the box, you can track your family coming and going using their smart phones as sensors. You can be alerted every time someone connects to your network. You can turn on a “guest” network when you have company. The guest network is segregated from your home network so you don’t have to worry about prying eyes on your other network devices. . I am not sure how much I trust this, but a quick test did in fact block traffic from the guest network to the rest of the house. Just make sure you remember to turn it off or your neighbors will be stealing your internet. Finally you can rename your wireless connection from the App for both the 2.4 and 5.7 MHz connections. I suggest using the same wireless name (SSID) and password for both. (NOTE: never name your wireless connection your real name).

The Range & Conclusion:

The range is outstanding! I have a full 5 bars everywhere in my house. My wireless speeds in my bedroom went from 10 to 15 Mbps to 65 – 70 Mbps. My wife is very happy about that. Happy wife, happy life. There is no perfect electronic device and this is no exception. I am using Samsung’s Smartthings for my smart home, so I may not ever get around to playing with that feature on the Almond 3, but one never knows. For the price, the features and performance of this device is far superior to anything I have seen on the market to date. It rivals some of the $800.00 Cisco Meraki enterprise wireless devices we use at work. The free App & cloud service is just icing on the cake.

Whether you are a network engineer or complete novice, most people should be able to get this to work if they select the right options at startup. I am very happy with this purchase and so far it was well worth the wait.

A lighting manufacturer at NAB 2013 explained to me that LEDs put out most of their energy in the UV spectrum. The way they emit visible light (at least some of them) is to excite tiny amounts of phosphors placed over the LED itself, similar to how a fluorescent lamp excites phosphors deposited on the inner surface of the tube.

It also means that to be safe, manufacturers need to build in a UV filter. I sincerely believe that we instinctively realize such bright LED light is bad for our eyes and react with a squint.

Then again, your poor subject also has 640 very bright point sources searing their eyeballs.

The diffuser helps spread the light a bit, and it works as far as it goes, but my plan is to cut arcs of additional diffusion material and attach them to the light, over the LEDs, under the diffuser sock.

Pixels per inch is where it's at!

I bought the 24" 1440 model for one reason: Pixel density.

I'm not a gamer. For me it's all about legible screen fonts for easy reading. And pixels per inch is where it's at. The higher the pixel density, the clearer the type looks. Fonts on a larger monitor with a lower density won't look as clear as a smaller one with a higher number of pixels per inch.

The density on the 24" model (2560 x 1440 resolution) is a little over 120 pixels per inch (ppi). A Kindle Paperwhite pixel density is 300 ppi. So if this monitor is a bit over twice the distance from you as a Kindle Paperwhite, the density and clarity will look about the same.

There is one thing I do want to mention: brightness. Wow this thing is bright. In the early days of LCD and LED monitors, brightness and color accuracy were issues. The brightness issue has certainly been solved, and maybe too well. I have mine set on just "5" on the on-board brightness setting. Occasionally I have dialed it down to "0" and it's still readable.

I waited almost six months to write this review because I wanted to "cool off" from my installation experience that would have caused me to rate this 3 stars. I am also now able to fairly assess this tablet after a few months' use.

I wanted a highly-rated unrestricted (open) tablet that provided great graphics and sufficient screen space. I purchased this to use on a Wi-Fi network only for when I didn't want to boot up my laptop to check mail or see a movie, etc. I also did not want an Apple tablet because my boyfriend has an iPad 3 and the Apple products have restrictions. I also was not impressed with the graphics on his iPad. I was considering a Kindle Fire HD 7" but that tablet was too restrictive as well and was geared to Amazon junkies. I am an Amazon junkie but I also do not like restrictions on products I purchase. During my July 2014 research, I discovered that the Nexus 7 tablet was the highest rated Android next to those more restrictive tablets.

After I received the Nexus, I wondered if I had made the right decision. First, I was surprised that this came with no documentation (other than the business card sized diagram of where all the ports were and a warranty and safety agreement in both English and French). The documentation didn't even say how long I needed to charge the unit. I charged it overnight and then had immense trouble getting this connected.

The router I was connecting to has MAC filtering enabled so I needed the MAC address. However, I couldn't get the MAC address without setting up the device. Also, I couldn't set it up because I couldn't get the MAC address. I could have fussed with the router and turned off MAC filtering/security temporarily but I had to get to work in the morning right after the unit completed charging. I then tried connecting via three other networks (my library for one, my work another, and another Wi-Fi connection). It still would not connect. Because I didn't want to wait until I got home 12 hours later to fuss with my router I wound up asking a tech support person where I work. He connected me via his personal MiFi mobile hotspot.

Apparently, Google Nexus only connects to certain networks if the first time setup has not been done. I tried several open networks. My co-worker's MiFi mobile network connection, although I suspect mine would have connected had I temporarily removed the security on my router, was the only one that would allow me to run the automatic setup so that I could connect. After setup was performed, I was able to get the MAC address from the settings "about" tab. I was also able to connect to the three other networks I tried previously and after inputting the MAC address, I could also connect to my router. It was apparently the initial setup process that prevented the connection.

This Google Nexus would have gotten five stars if they enhanced the user experience by:
1 - Providing a MAC address either on the unit or on a piece of paper for those that have MAC filtering enabled.
2 - Providing a documentation pamphlet with the unit that:
* Tells the user how long they need to charge the unit the first time.
* Explains to the user that setup cannot be run on all networks and sometimes they will get an error message. Therefore, they might say something like "using your own network is advisable" or provide an explanation of why certain networks (including totally open ones that allow all connections) would not work. Perhaps there is some sort of technical protocol that is not available on all networks; I have no idea.

Other than the above, I absolutely love my Google Nexus. I've been using this for almost 6 months and it has met my every expectation. It charges in less than four hours; lasts about 3 hours if I'm constantly using it; lasts about 3-4 days when I'm using it for about 10 minutes daily. I've used this for email, movies, web surfing, pictures, etc. App availability is unending (Kindle, LinkedIn, Battery Doctor, etc., etc.) I tested the screen image next to my co-workers Kindle Fire HD 7" and there is no discernible difference in quality or resolution. OK I admit it, I am leery of Linksys wireless routers. I have had four routers in my life (the E4200 being the fifth) and only the Linksys router gave me headaches. I vowed to never get another Linksys in my life, but I like Cisco so this was a dilemna and so far I am have been happy with it.

Design

This is a very slick device. I love the low profile that lets it hide on top of the cabinet it is on. A nice looking piece of hardware.

Setup

I have never had an easier set up on any wireless router. I installed the software onto my MacBook (mac friendly) and it self-discovered and prompted for the rest of the set up. Very nice setup, although a little long from beginning to end (7 minutes or so.) I loved that it prompted to personalize the SSID and password right up front. Software was slick and straight forward. Once set up I had all 7 wireless devices in the house on-line in about 20 minutes. Even my wireless printer worked instantly. - Five stars on Set-up

Functionality

I have only had the device installed for a weekend now, but I spent that time backing up my hard drive to a wireless SAN, watching streaming netflix and uploading a new website. No hiccups at all. About the only thing I did have an issue with is trying to set it up with my Ooma. I needed to rebooted the router and modem after removing the Ooma. No blame here, the Ooma doesn't seem to want to play nicely with any router or cable modem.

I really like the ability to have a guest network. It is easily turned off and on so I can easily provide a connection to visitors, but turn it off and totally deny the Brazilian students next door (actually it is password protected so it is not wide open, but less secure.)

Speed

I may not be the best to judge speed. I am not the type to watch the throughput numbers, but I can say that netflix streamed Mars Attacks wirelessly to my Wii without any issues. I have no issues with the speed at all.

Conclusion

I am very happy with the router. Who knows, two years down the line, I may be able to let my prejudice against Linksys go. If things continue to go well, or if they take a turn for the worse, I will update this review.

I have mixed feelings about this stylus. Overall, I like it. There are some very good things about it, but it has a few issues.

I'm using this primarily with my iPad Pro, and to a lesser degree with my iPhone 6s. This is my first experience with a fine-point stylus, although I've considered purchasing one for awhile.

First, the pros:
-- I was able to get it charged with no problem
-- Using the included quick start guide, I found my way to the Wacom website to get more details on set-up and apps that I might want to use with my iPad Pro.
-- Found the apps in iTunes App Store and downloaded a few of them to my iPad, got them installed and ready to test.
-- Pairing went smoothly -- no hiccups or issues at all. This was a pleasant surprise, as I've had problems in the past pairing things with the iPad.
-- Was able to get it up and running with both Bamboo Paper as well as Sketches and ibispaint.
-- Nice look and feel -- since it's the size of a fairly standard pen (ball point, gel, retractable, etc.), it feels "natural" in use.
-- Surprisingly long battery life -- I used it almost constantly for 3 hrs, and still had a lot of battery charge left.

Cons:
-- it skips. My iPad doesn't have a screen protector, so the pen is operating on the bare glass. I thought maybe the problem was the glass, so I cleaned it -- twice. Didn't seem to help. It skips in all three apps, and in different parts of the screen each time. Still haven't figured out if it's operator error or problems with the apps or something with the stylus itself. I'll keep playing with it and see if I can find a common denominator cause. When it skips, it's only a short distance -- maybe 1/4" or so -- but it's enough to be annoying.

-- the tip has an annoying tendency to retract during use, especially if I'm using it for writing longhand. In 3 or 4 lines, it has already retracted over halfway. I'm not exerting much pressure on it -- only enough for it to "register" on the screen, so I think it might be the combination of the motion -- writing loops, "twisting" to make some of the letters, etc. -- plus the minimal pressure. What it means is that I have to stop periodically to twist the pen to move the tip "out" again. Otherwise, I end up trying to write with the hard plastic external edge of the tip, which doesn't work that well.

So why the 4-star rating? Despite the issues, I still like this stylus. I'm not a professional artist, but I do like to sketch, to annotate photos, etc. and it really does work nicely for that even with the skipping (I just move the image a bit and try again). If I were a student and I was looking to use this to take longhand notes in class or something, I'd probably drop the rating to 3 stars. But for my use, it's OK. I can work around the issues. So I DO like it.

Wow! Talk about an effortless, totally-bubble-free installation of a screen protector on a large tablet! Also, the protector sheet is made of stiff plastic that makes it easy to handle. You just place the sheet gently on the tablet, using the camera and light sensor cutouts as a guide, and then apply light pressure to the black edges to secure the adhesive. If you get the placement wrong, you can try again, because the screen protector is removable. It can even be removed, stored away, and reapplied at a later time.

Once the screen protector is installed, it's virtually invisible. There is no loss of touchscreen sensitivity, and the protector itself is crystal clear. I've installed a lot of screen protector film--on cameras, cellphones, and 7" and 9" tablets--and until now I thought it would be impossible for anyone to make a screen protector for a large tablet that would go on bubble-free and also be invisible after the installation. This Moshi iVisor XT screen protector has proved me wrong.

Apple and Google smartphones use the PD fast charging mode. In my testing, it charges up my gadgets as fast as any other charger that I have tried and it is smart enough to reduce the charging speed as the devices become fully charged to reduce overheating (this is part of the PPS protocol, if your devices support that).

I really like that this charger has an ETL electrical safety certification printed on the bottom of the device. ETL is an independent safety testing laboratory. Many US companies will not buy electrical devices that do not have ETL or UL safety certifications.

This product is tough to rate. I will go into detail because it really depends on what you need out of a case.

Pros:
-It’s pretty.
-It’s rugged.
-It feels like it has some drop protection.
-The weight means it doesn’t tip easily.
-The magnet is very strong, and the outer case is sturdy. My last iPad Pro died when it got bent, and this feels like better protection.

Cons:
-This is extremely heavy. I’m not sure it could be heavier unless they made it out of lead.
-You cannot charge an Apple Pencil if the pencil is in a sleeve because they cut a slot that fits the pencil exactly with no margin.
-It’s a strong magnet so don’t keep hotel cards etc, near it. It's definitely not safe or OK for those with pacemakers etc.
-The back covers the iPad completely, trapping some heat near the machine for those who run it hard.

It's a great case but I can’t overlook the weight. It can be a plus in that you are unlikely to forget your ipad is there and treat it carelessly, but it also makes carrying it around a literal pain in the shoulder. If you don’t want to feel like you are lugging around a laptop, I would look for a different case. If you are worried about it being bent when you forget it's in your bag or if it’s going to be mostly at home and a magnet on the back appeals to you for things like sticking it to the fridge when referencing recipes, then this may be a good fit.

Personally, I would rather buy a separate stand for when I need it than carry around something this heavy even if it works well.

[[VIDEOID:f8be83e3530c313d3485906c32dd0520]] Typical web cams built-in on laptops and phones have gotten pretty good, but those of us that spent some time with old school video or SLRs know that that best zooms are optical (instead of digital) and the best lenses are large enough to allow a lot of light to pass through (making low light images more natural). This camera embodies those old school concepts with a 5.5x110 mm lens that's got aperture settings up to F1.6 (depending on zoom settings). These are impressive numbers by any measure. Where modern technology shines in this camera is in the electronics and interfaces, etc. Auto focus, remote zooming and panning - and multiple outputs as well. When you bring all of this together into a very usable camera like this one does, you've got a winner.

First, the obvious - the picture quality is excellent. Certainly suitable for conferencing or a video blog, and in fact, will look great in any type of performance videos. If you want to put your best face forward by emitting a professional grade video, you should use professional quality equipment like this.

Second is ease of use. I confess that when I first set this up, I simply plugged it into a monitor - that doesn't work. You need to plug it into a device with appropriate software. Once I plugged it into the USB drive of my older Lenovo laptop, I simply pulled up Skype and there it was. I was able to run it through some simple paces without any further action. And again, the picture looked great. I even dimmed the lights in the room to see how well it would handle it - beautifully! Just for fun, I zoomed out to show the room and then zoomed in to show my whiskers... all presented in GREAT detail (the autofucus struggled just a little to lock focus on my whiskers when zoomed all the way in, in a low light setting, but I switched to manual focus and was able to tweak it right in). And the real beauty of this system is that it's all controlled by remote.

Another nice feature that was immediately obvious - the gimbal that the camera's mounted on is, of course, motorized - but it runs in complete silence. Nobody's going to want to watch a video of they can hear the sounds of a camera being manipulated. This is yet another feature that separates the pro equipment from the rest.

The base is solid and usage is straightforward. My only nit would be that the manual is a bit sparse, giving technical specifications about various models of cameras rather than detailed info about usage - but so far, everything I've tried has been fairly straightforward, and I've managed without any further detailed instructions. I have a growing interest in photography and I have been learning as I go. One of the things I have discovered is that a good camera bag – sufficiently large to hold the camera, lenses you need and any accessories – is absolutely essential. I have a messenger-style camera bag that works well enough but I have run out of room in it and it does not have the capacity to hold all of my extra lenses and filters. I looked to this camera bag as a solution. It definitely holds more than my old bag, it seems to be made well and there are some nice features to this bag.

This is a backpack style bag and it is about the same size as a small travel backpack, though it is an order of magnitude thicker. There are zippers and pockets everywhere. There's a lot of padding to protect the camera and multiple movable partitions.

The main compartment is large enough to hold a small laptop if all of the partitions are pulled out. There are three small partitions and two large ones and these can be arranged in any configuration to accommodate a wide array of accessories. As shipped, the partitions are arranged to allow for the camera lens and camera to sit through the middle of the pack which maximizes the padding and protection for the most valuable parts of your setup, and the smaller partitions are about right for 2-3 lens kits. I have a smaller camera – a Samsung NX300 with the 18-55mm lens – so I need less room for my camera and rearranged the configuration to permit room for several filter kits, a telephoto lens, a fisheye lens and a few smaller accessories, all in the main compartment. I have not yet purchased additional lenses but will rearrange when I do.

The main compartment also has a pocket that is suitable for either a thin book or a tablet. So, even with all of my other gear in the main compartment, I still have room for my tablet. I really can't ask for much more than that.

There is a smaller zippered compartment on the front that has room for even more accessories. In this I have loaded up a spare set of macro lenses that would not fit in the main compartment. Inside this compartment there is yet another pocket suitable for holding a tablet as well as a mesh pocket for loose items, my choice being a couple of pens. However, the most interesting item in there, attached by a tether, is a waterproof nylon cover for the whole bag. So, if you need to go out in the rain with this backpack, you can do so without fear of getting your equipment wet.

On the sides there are two small pockets, sufficient for holding a couple of small items like a filter or two or even a very small flashlight.

On the front there is one more zippered pocket that is well suited for thin items, like a map, magazine or papers.

The shoulder straps are adjustable and padded so getting the pack to fit just right is not an issue. However, there is a carrying handle loop on the top of this bag and I prefer carrying this bag using that instead (I have always preferred carrying backpacks this way).

This is a very nice camera bag. A lot of thought went into the design and it can hold a lot of equipment for its size. It has replaced my other camera bag outright.

I have had the opportunity to review more iPhone cables than I can possibly remember and over the years I have found there are certain characteristics that I look for in a cable that will increase its chances of being a high quality, long lasting cable. I knew as soon as I saw these cables by Maxrock they had those characteristics and after using it for the last 6 weeks I have been nothing but impressed.

I’ve found long, over 6.6’ or 2m, cables have to have increased shielding in order to not lose speed in data transfer and be especially well made to resist unraveling and the stresses from being that length. This cable suffers no noticeable loss in speed from its length during either charging or data transfer.

The primary failure point of any cable is where the cable meets the plug. Due to the strains constantly put at those junctions this is where electrical shorts are most likely to occur and thus cause eventual failure. As is clear with this cable this area is protected by the manufacturer utilizing reinforced plugs making it so the cable can not put the same strain at that weak point.

One additional feature added to this wire is a way to keep it coiled when not in use. This is definitely a nice feature especially for an extra long cable.

This is among the best cables I’ve had the opportunity to review and I definitely recommend it.

When it comes to hands free devices, I am pretty particular about what I need to have handy. I like to have ear pieces like this handy when I am shopping or out doing errands should I need to receive important business calls. I also have to be available due to health issues of family members. Let's see how this one measures up.

WHAT IS THIS EARPIECE LIKE?
This hands-free earpiece is black. That does make it harder to find in a pocket of a purse or carry case. The outside of the entire unit is black.

LIGHTS
There is a green battery light on the outside and a blue bluetooth light on the outside when you turn it on. When you turn it off, the battery light turns to red so you know that is what you are doing with it. I LOVE this feature.

EAR BUD
The ear bud is only one size. There are three ear covers in this set. Two of them have an ear circle in them which allows you to wear it with or without the ear loop that hooks over the entire ear. One of them has no ear circle (the kind that fits into your hear cartilage).

EAR HOOK
There is one ear hook connected to this ear piece and then there is an extra in case you break that one. This fits around the outside of the ear hooking it into place for added security.

Mini USB
The charging plug on the outside is pretty uniform.

CORD
It comes with a 12 inch cord that goes from USB to mini USB for charging. You will need to have a receptacle to plug that into.

INSTRUCTION BOOKLET
Instruction book is minimal. This is a basic set which I LOVE. It is pretty straight forward. You turn on the phone, turn on the ear piece and they pair. Then to turn up volume, you press one side of the bar, down is the other side and muting is both at once. To hang up press outiside of earpiece.

BATTERY TIME
This thing stays charged a LONG time. I rarely have to recharge it, although I do not use it daily. It also holds a charge when not used for a long time as long as it it not left on endlessly.

RECEPTION/MICROPHONE
Here is where my review gets difficult. The first few times I used this, the caller at the other end complained because the sound was so bad. I was even told that the old handsfree speaker in my car was better and that was like a tin echo chamber.

I was all set to write my review, after all, it was pretty cut and dried. Then for some reason I could not write my review, and I had to use the earpiece to call someone again. WOW, the comments:

"I am so glad you are not using your ear piece, that thing was awful. Your voice has never sounded so clear."

"WOW, your phone is so CLEAR. I can not hear anything around you. Where ARE you?"

That second comment, I was shopping in a loud area. Now I had a dilemma. It was like I had two different earpieces! People were commenting on how wonderful it was now, but previously, these SAME PEOPLE could not stand it before. Nothing had changed. Same phone, same earpiece, same people.

So, I tested this quite a bit and the more positive feedback outweighed the negative, so I will say that this is a fantastic OMG marvelous earpiece sometimes and other times it is not as good.

STREAMING MUSIC
This is a decent earpiece for streaming music or programming on the phone, but I tend to use it more for temporary phone answering when I am not in my car.

COMFORT
This is not as comfortable as other earpieces I have had. I still prefer my older plantronics ear piece as it is so comfortable I don't notice it is in my ear after a while. This one is a bit too large. I actually prefer to wear it without the rubber cushion on it if I have to use it for any length of time. The ear hook helps it stay on pretty well. Once in a while I will use the rubber cushion and it is not too bad.

THE BOTTOM LINE
This is a solid performer as a hands free earpiece. It has potential to deliver fantastic phone calls much of the time, and once in a while not as nice, but it still works. For comfort, I have had better, but this is not too bad. It has extra pieces which I love, and the colored lights on it are fantastic.

MY RATING
FOUR STARS. This is a nice solid hands free ear piece. Despite a period of time when I was not so sure, longer term testing brought out its good points and solid performance. I would get this again.

Power isn't everything. My intention was for the A90 to replace an old portable DAC/Amp combo that is only rated at 1.6W total at 75Ω. I figured the massive increase in output power paired with a much higher-end DAC would sound heaps better than the little DAC/Amp combo I've been using for the last 7 years. Sadly, the A90 made everything sound a bit thin and lifeless. It's like it has the negative characteristics of an overly clinical sounding amp without any of the positives like extracting detail.

It's not a horrible amp. It's just not a great amp. Maybe the A90 would sound better when paired with muffled/veiled or extremely warm sounding headphones. For Sennheiser HD800's or HD820's though, which are inherently bright, it's a horrible match. The A90 sucked the soul from the music with those particular headphones.

The chain I tested with the A90 was a Naim ND5 XS2 streamer > Nordost Silver Shadow BNC > Schiit Gungnir Multibit DAC > Cardas Clear XLR > Topping A90. There's usually a Schiit Mjolnir 2 at the end of the chain and it sounds amazing. I didn't expect the A90 to outperform the Mjolnir but I did expect it to outperform my little DAC/Amp combo, especially when being fed such a good source

All I can really take away from my experience with the A90 is DO NOT pair this amp with bright headphones. Can't comment on other headphones but avoid this amp if you've got HD800's or 820's.

This MP3 player, which I was given at a discount in exchange for my honest review, is sleek and lightweight yet potentially—via a firmware upgrade that I hope Lonve will consider—very powerful. (See my photo of the player lying on top of my MacBook Pro trackpad to get an idea of its size.) It can be listened to without hooking it up to anything else, either with wired headphones or through the surprisingly good-sounding on-board speakers. The view screen when the player is powered on is quite readable, and I love how the surface of the screen becomes a classy grey-bronze mirrored surface that is so clear you can use it to check your appearance. The ability to add up to a 32GB SDHC card you've preloaded with music or video is a great feature.

The included wired headphones are better than some I've listened to, although I prefer another pair that fits my tiny ears better; unfortunately, those are Bluetooth, so they won't work with this player. I will likely listen to the player my itself, with no headphones, through its speakers.

I can't five-star love this player because I can't set the time to a 12-hour clock and it doesn't allow for adding playlists, which I was thinking it did. Maybe I'm missing something, but I can't even start an album folder playing by tediously navigating to it in the Explorer; it appears you have to navigate all the way into the files in the folder and then start it playing, although I haven't even been able to get this to work. It takes too many steps and is so very aggravating that I usually just quit trying to play either music or video.

What really shines on this player is the radio. I'm sure reception will vary depending on where you are, but in Lexington, KY, I can pull in NPR very clearly and easily. It would be nice to be able to store favorite radio stations—if there's a way, I haven't figured it out after days of fiddling with the player—but I'm happy that I can leave it sets to my main station and it always comes back there even after I've powered off and then back on. If you're a person who likes to listen to the radio at night with the lights off, going to sleep, but don't like fooling with headphones, this will be a great little player for you.

The Game feature has a neat little Tetris-style game that's amusing while stuck waiting somewhere. The Photo feature is nothing to write home about, but it can be used to show off a few photos of your pets or kids or maybe a logo or graphically produced emergency contact info. There is an Autoplay Time setting you can set in the Settings/Photo. The text feature allows for reading text files, so you can take along a grocery list or study notes. I started to knock off an extra star (down to three) because of something I really dislike about this player, and that is the dedicated left-side button (one of only three) that seems to serve no purpose but to turn on the voice recorder. When I press it by mistake or forget that the On/Off button is the button on the right, not the left, the Recorder comes on. Then I get a file format error when I try to get out of it. It would have been better, I think, had they used that button for something more likely to be used constantly (Explorer with the ability to set either the internal C: card or the external D: card as the default for the button maybe) or, better, allow the user to define the function of that button via a Settings selection. I want to be able to disable the Recorder completely, although I know some people will want to have a recorder. But I hate it.

I am director of a small publishing house. I got accustomed to the trackpad (I switched the scrolling direction) and haven't used a mouse since I got my Mac. I do book production and cover design on it, sitting in the living room recliner (too far from an electrical outlet to use the adapter) but the battery runs down pretty quickly.

I wanted this Chromebook as a second machine for starting and ending my day: browsing and doing the cloud-based work I have to do, like accounting in Wave, managing social network-based marketing, ordering books, searching for cover art, reading manuscripts in Submittable, handling email, etc. My Mac with Adobe CS5 is essential for the actual book design and production, so I basically reserve its battery now for that.

What is amazing to me is how similar this Chromebook keyboard is to my MacBook Pro. The only time I realize I'm not on my Mac is when I hit what, on the Mac, is the caps lock key but on the Chromebook pops up apps. (There is no caps lock key on the Chromebook; supposedly you can press both shift keys at the same time to effect caps lock, but I guess I don't have the right touch because I can't get it to work.) Another slight difference is in how click and drag works; on the Chromebook, you hit the trackpad with your thumb, then drag.

Those who have already gotten accustomed to using Google-related commands for email, clearing the cache, and the like will be good to go without any learning curve. Chrome extensions and apps, of course, work as expected. (I am SO glad I had the prescience to realize a year ago that I definitely wanted to shift to a cloud-based approach!)

Now, a word about the quality of the monitor. I find the type on the screen to be MORE readable than on my Mac. It is much crisper and high-definition. The colors don't match between the two computers, but I'm not sure it's the Chromebook's fault. The Chromebook does seem to be able to sense how to adjust brightness based on the conditions of the room, which is helpful. Sometimes, however, my eyes start smarting, something that happens when I'm working on the Chromebook, but not on the MacBook Pro. I don't know what accounts for this. The sound is better on the Chromebook than on my Mac, especially if I use good headphones. When watching a movie, the color is a bit washed out compared to the really garishly brightly colored sets, but I prefer that.

I'm probably more of a power user when it comes to the user end of a computer, but I don't try to get in and hack things like some people do. Developer mode, need for static IP address, etc., I'm clueless about. But this is a well-built, fast, mostly no-fuss, low-cost and very light-weight piece of work with a long-lasting battery, which is exactly what I wanted. That I also got a seamless experience shifting from one machine to the other for a quarter of what my MacBook Pro cost? That's priceless!

I got it up high enough into the recession on my porch roof that you can't see it from the sidewalk - at least if you're my height - but it can see you. And you have to be discreet in a nice neighborhood: I don't think people want to feel like cameras are a necessity. But you never know. And good theives would be scoping your property out ahead of time, so in my mind a purposefully discreet camera would say, "there are lots of security features here you probably don't know about".

Anyway, it works with my off-branded NVR, which I believe to be a Uniview OEM. I have it so the cables go into a hole in the fascia and the camera covers the hole (I was able to make a generous sized hole, thankfully, due to the large mounting plate (not too large, but basically the diameter of the camera). I really needed that larger hole to pull my cables (this is a very old house, so getting the cables run inside columns and underground and all hidden was really a feat).

It has what I'm not gathering is standard equipment on a good PoE camera - 3 cable ends - one for RJ-45, one for external power if you're not using PoE, and one for a reset button which I hope I won't need since it'd be a bit of a pain to get to.

If you can't hide your cables completely, you can also run them out the side of the baseplate. The camera is essentially infinitely adjustable with very large range. This seems basically the same standard design as all my old analog cameras from my last system on my last house.

I believe you can get this to show up on an app all by itself if you don't use an NVR, which is an awesome feature if you only have one camera or a few by the same brand. I'm also sure I can get this set up with my QNAP NAS if I wanted to, but when I played around with that on my last camera, I wasn't super-impressed (plus, I'm not about to pay for additional licenses on this stystem that is going to be augmented many times). Since I knew I was going to use the NVR, I just went right to it with this camera.

The NVR way sort of automatically makes a VLAN on your network so your cameras aren't taking up IP addresses and getting in your way. I paired this up with a Onkyo TX-NR809 home theater receiver and i'm extremely pleased. Its a bigger improvement sound wise from my RSW-15 sub from klipsch . I've owned the Klipsch Reference line since around 2002ish and they sound just as good today as they did after a few hours of break in. The reason why this middle brand 12 inch improved the sound quality in my room is purely my hearing style preference. I love front firing subwoofers my old one had a passive 15 inch behind and front firing but air flowed behind so the sound felt strange, In this unit, the bass is very deep for a 12 inch and has 3 options. Movie, music and flat settings . Each one can be customized. My room is large or slightly under a large. It fills everything with tight bass.

I have to run it on +3 volume on the subwoofer with my receiver set to reference (dead center) if I want extra bass.. Even if the sub itself set to 0 (dead center reference) it still produces tons of large bass. Especially with bass tracks and movies. For me to listen to bass music like drumming bass, Deadmau5, DJ baby Anne I have to set the subs volume to -8 so it doesn't disturb neighbors and I STILL GET BASS! One of the reason I went with this 12 inch was to control the deep bass from extending and having cops called on me. It didn't help. I have absolutely no problem with this.If anything it reinforces its a good subwoofer.

TIP: for many of those using receivers that do auto calibration. Its better to do yours subwoofer settings by hand and personal hearing preference. Many auto-calibration systems like Audyssey have a tendency to ask you to lower the subs volume on the unit and mutes the bass sound. This is normally done to adjust the speakers hertz frequency and measure the room but system like Audyssey do not take bass into account. So your speakers will probably get shifted to see itself as "large speakers" even if you have towers. This reduces overall bass tracks your subwoofer plays because it thinks the other speakers can reproduce low bass. To fix any lack of bass, change the hertz settings of each speaker at a starting point of 80hrz. This will feed the subwoofer bass tracks that the others speakers can not reproduce. Satellites speakers crank it up to 120hrz or more.

-LFE (low frequency effects) in your receiver settings to 120hrz. Sub crossover or LFE settings are in the receiver itself.
-all speaker herz settings to 80 or test by going higher. Some have a setting for small and large Set them small even if you have towers unless they have powered subs built into them.(this is normally in the settings of the speakers in the receiver) Not the sub itself.

This allows your receiver to control where bass gets redirected. If you set the receiver to control every speaker, you would disable similar settings on the subwoofer itself, That way you don't get the sub and receiver having a double filter effect. The only thing you raise up and down would be the subs volume control and equalizer settings IN THE SUB. I avoid lowering and increase sub volume from the receiver , instead ,do it by hand on the unit.

I’m a big fan of the Panasonic Lumix line of point and shoot cameras. I’ve been using one for years and, while it has limited features by today’s standards, it has yet to let me down. This latest one in the Lumix line offers a huge range of capabilities, provides outstanding image quality, but continues to suffer from a less than ideal user interface.

The camera comes with just the basics: the camera, a single battery, lanyard and a charger (plus manuals and software). I was a little disappointed right off the bat when I saw the charger. Unlike the older Lumix chargers that had a wall plug built into the charger than flipped out, this has a separate power cord. While that does make it easier to plug into the wall, it also means I have to remember to carry the cord with me to charge it.

Initial setup is straightforward, with the usual time/date setting. Since this has a GPS there’s also the need to go through initializing that option as well. All of these steps can be skipped, but you’ll be reminded to do so every time you power on the camera. It also displays a warning on screen about the waterproof limitations of the camera (and provides ample documentation as to what it can/can’t do re: underwater use).

The view screen is wonderful. Sharp, clear, and easy to read in all lightning conditions. The menu system will be familiar if you’ve ever used a Lumix camera but, if not, it’s still pretty straightforward. I still think Canon has the lead when it comes to having an intuitive point and shoot menu system, but Panasonic does a decent job. I like that with most options there’s a scrolling line of text that comes up to explain what the option is/does. That’s very helpful for options you don’t often use and need help with, but it does not interfere or slow down operation should you know exactly what you want to select.

I won’t list all the camera specs in this review since those are easily available in the listing and the Panasonic web site. Suffice it to say this offers a huge range of options and capabilities that cover pretty much any shooting situation. The Intelligent mode shooting scenario options (of which there are many) are helpful when you just want to point the camera and have it do everything else for you, including compensation for specialized lighting/scene situations. I especially like the macro option, which produced some impressive close-up shots that were sharply focused and clear even though I didn’t use a table-top tripod for stability but relied on the image stabilization features of the camera.

The video recording image quality is excellent good for a point and shoot cam. The performance of the built in mic is decent as well. This won’t compete with a dedicated HD cam, but for casual video shooting it’s a small, simple and easy to use setup that gets the job done pretty well.

The WiFi setup was surprisingly easy. I was dreading that since it often can be a bear, but this was quick and easy, and the included instructions were easy to follow. I use the WiFi option a lot since the USB port to connect to a PC is inside the camera (located under the battery compartment door). It’s done that way to maintain a water-tight shell, but is also means it can be hard to get to easily.

What has not been improved, and actually has slipped a bit, is the overall user interface (e.g., the buttons on the back). They continue to be small, hard to read, and don’t provide solid feedback that they have been pressed. Given that the camera is designed to be used in “rugged” conditions, larger buttons would have been a big plus, especially for zoom and the main menu keypad since those are used so often. Using the menu buttons is hard enough with bare hands; it’s impossible if you have gloves on.

I would certainly recommend this camera if you’re looking for a rugged point and shoot for outdoor use, but also if you’re looking for a high feature camera that never leaves the house. The performance and feature set are both excellent. The user interface brings my rating to four stars but performance and option-wise, this camera offers a lot for the price point.

This Honeywell smart home security starter kit has a great video and is easily expandable.

When opening the box I was pleased to see that it was packaged very well. The box even has a magnetic closure. Maybe a little over the top but a nice feature to make it feel like more of a luxury product. I also have the Honeywell thermostat and that box wasn’t as nice.
Each item in the security kit was simple and clear to find since they were labeled in their own little box. There is an instruction sheet that is quite large for the info that it holds. The instructions have nice graphics and it is spaced out well so it is very easy to read. The instructions are simple for initial set up. Though I would appreciate another manual to help with the “extra” things it can do. I relied on the Honeywell videos and reviews (video and written) by other people to get it functioning with all the bells and whistles. I could see the need for a manual for those less tech savvy.

The base station could be a little smaller but it looks very nice in my kitchen and blends in very well. It’s a nice design with only one button, for the speaker. You can touch the top to check how it is working and run your finger around the top to change the volume. The camera is small and has a privacy ring that can be twisted to block the camera. It would be a nice feature if I could twist the camera from the app in case we forgot to open it when we left.
The middle mesh part is the speaker and it has a good range of volume and the sound is good.
The bottom has a light inside and it changes colors when you choose the different settings. It also lights up to help when you set up new devices.
The base has a backup battery. You will get an alert when it doesn’t have power. This has been handy when there is a storm so I know when the power goes out and when it is restored.

To start the set up I downloaded the Honeywell app. It was easy to use and is a nice looking app. The main page is very simple. When you go to the settings that’s where all the extras are.
My husband also has the app on his phone so he can use it just as I can.
Set up was very easy besides having troubles with it connecting it to my WiFi. I decided to wait till the next day and it worked after a couple tries. I don’t have a fast internet so that might be why. I haven’t had any issues with the connection since set up. Besides the WiFi wait it was about 15 minutes to set up the app and base.
The key fob was very easy to pair up and only took me a couple minutes to have it ready to use. Nice to have when a babysitter comes over.
The access sensors were very easy to install and set up. I didn’t need the extra piece. It only took me a few minutes to stick them on and pair them. I did use painters tape to attach them to my doors and frames. I am worried about the tape they have ruining my stained trim. I haven’t seen any comments about it. I also wanted to try it on other doors and windows first.
When you open a door or window in home mode it chimes and sends you an alert. When you open in away mode it will sound the alarm. I wish the door sensors were a little smaller or gray. They stand out too much on my wood trim and door. If my trim was white they wouldn’t be very noticeable.

The camera is very clear and has a wide angle so if you position it right you can see a lot. You can switch the video to full screen and the picture is still good. You are also able to zoom in on the video in the app and it has options to take a snap of the video, talk through the base or have an alarm go off. Sometimes it takes a while for the video to load or it will just turn off. I am assuming this is from my slower internet. Usually after a few tries I can get it to work. Also there is a delay in the video and the movement is jumpy, this could be due to the slower internet also. You still get a good picture of who is there. I was impressed with the night vision.

The motion detection is a nice feature when you are away. I have been trying to figure out the best setting while we are at home. It will send me alerts all the time when we are home. Most of the alerts are during the people detection time. Maybe because our camera covers so much of our main area. I do like that how the people detection can let me know who is in the house and I don’t have to look at the video. When it detects motion it will take a short video clip and save them below the live video. You can scroll down to look at the older ones. It looks like the clips are saved for a day. The people detection is limited to 2 hours. But I did notice that you could set it for the morning then when that time was over you could change it for later in the day. You would have to remember to change it but good to know if you wanted it on for longer or multiple times in the day. Not sure why they don’t have an option for more time.

The geofencing didn’t work well for me. It would switch to away mode even when the phone was close to it. We’ve decided to turn that feature off. It’s easy enough to turn it to away with the app, key fob, or talk to it. We are at home a lot so it makes more sense to do it manually. But I could see it being a great feature for people gone more during the day.

The kids like the Alexa feature that it comes with. They can ask the weather, time, kids jokes. I use it for the timer and to ask it questions. We had problems with playing songs. It wanted us to subscribe to amazon music. We have found other ways of playing music but it’s not very easy. Alexa seems limited but still useful. This is my first Alexa enable device so hard to compare.

I like that the security base links to my Honeywell thermostat (it was very easy to pair it) and I can tell Alexa to turn it off or change the temperature or use the same app. I would like to get other devices that link to it. This is a great starter kit and I like that it is expandable for your needs.

You are able to do two way taking with the app. It’s not always easy to understand and you have to talk slower.

The box says you get free 24-hour cloud storage. I’m not sure if that’s for the video clips or what you are actually storing. I haven’t found where the cloud is accessed.

Overall it is easy to use and looks nice. It’s nice that you can have a security system that is easy to use and it doesn’t have a monthly fee. I don’t usually need all the security features that this security system offers but it’s nice to have it set up and ready for when I do.

I don't think there is any other lens from any manufacturer that satisfies all of those things except this one. (Sigma has the 10-20mm but no stabilization, lower optical quality, and more money! GOOD: Excellent optical quality for the price. This lens is noticeably sharper and has less distortion at 10mm than my kit lens 18-135mm has at 18mm. Stabilization works very well. Focusing is very fast and silent. I don't hear it even with the built in mic when shooting video (on a Canon 70D). Extremely lightweight and fairly compact.

BAD: Maximum Aperture. This is NOT a fast lens. F/4.5 maximum is not that great and you lose it pretty quickly as you zoom in since the max aperture ranges from 4.5 - 5.6. You need to have some decent light to shoot with this lens. But given the lack of competition in super wide stabilized silent EF-S lenses (or any Canon mount lens) and the price of anything vaguely similar, I think it's a reasonable compromise.

This review is for the Uniden BCD436HP I see reviews here for other radios, so not to be confused.
I used Amazon Prime Now to get the radio to me, in less than 1 hour (about 45 minutes) the delivery person was knocking on my door with my new receiver, wow, I was highly impressed and I will always check to see if Prime Now is available for all my deliveries from now on.....
So, the radio....
This receiver has a 4 gig SD card preloaded with every known frequency with text for the entire US and Canada. They have software called Sentinel you install on your PC and this is your gateway to all updates and firmware and it can control your radios SD card any way you like. Sentinel has an extensive database of all frequencies and let me say this again, all frequencies have text description included which is the most highly advanced scanner database system I have ever seen and I have owned scanner receivers most of my adult life, (long time)..
This is a digital receiver using the latest technology available. It can monitor any analog or digital TX (with some exceptions, like encrypted signals) and gives you extensive control over what you're listening to. There are FCC laws regarding what is legal and not legal to monitor and Uniden has got us right up to the maximum legally allowed to be monitored by civilians. If you are law enforcement persons you will have much more powerful receivers available to you capable of Cell phone conversation monitoring etc., things no civilian should even be interested in.
There is another version of this Uniden radio, the BCD536 which is a tabletop version. If you have large powerful outdoor weatherproof antennas the BCD536 is a good option and it is completely transferable to vehicle dash mount and back from your work desk to your vehicle.
I like this handheld BCD436 best personally for my purposes.
This is basically a plug and play receiver. It comes with 3 2300 milliamp rechargeable batteries, load those, charge them or just leave radio plugged in, enter your zip and you're in. Well theoretically that's how it works, in the real world? No.
When you first receive the radio I would suggest positioning yourself in front of your PC. Have the paper manual, the radio, you and your PC right there in front of you. Get ready to read and learn your radios keyboard layout and what these great, well thought out keys can do for you. You will learn, trust me, you will quickly come to love this radio.
Some cons:
No wall charger adopter included. You can charge from your PC's USB ports but you will need a wall charger with USB port. Most of us have several of these around the house from old cell phones etc. They work fine.
This unit should come with a nice wall charger adopter. That's really the only con, not to bad really.
Antennas:
Your ability to scan and receive signals on any scanner is proportionate to your antennas. The more robust and correct (correct meaning size, materials used etc).. You will need some nice antennas for this nice radio to increase your scanning powers. Amazon has some nice antennas, scannermaster.com has some also. Your local radio shop retailer will have some also. The included rubber ducky antenna is garbage, toss it from across the room to your garbage can, see if you can make a rim shot. Like I said, I have been playing with scanners for many years so I have many antennas to pick from.
Verdict:
This is without a doubt, the most powerful handheld scanning receiver available from any manufacturer. It is the luxury sedan of the scanning receiver world. It is easy and robust. It is backed up by Uniden's Sentinel software which will future proof your radio for many years to come.
I give Uniden 5 stars for this winner.
I give Amazon 5 stars for Prime Now 1 hour shipping, also a winner.

Edit:
Okay some people are wondering what the best accessories are for this receiver.
Go to scannermaster.com and look for the Austin Condor All-Band Portable BNC Antenna and the SpectrumForce Desk Mount for One Portable Scanner.
The Condor all band antenna is unsurpassed.
The desktop stand holds your handheld at the perfect viewing angle, you can listen and see all text clearly right beside your computer.

This is a nice smart watch offering a host of different functions. Most seem to be accurate or at least as accurate as alternate methods of measurement allow. Counting steps/distance has always been a bit dodgy in my experience, but if you're not looking for an absolute number, you'll be fine with this measurement.

But what surprised me, shocked me really, was the marked difference in the pulse oximeter reading between this watch, measuring at the wrist, and a fingertip oximeter. I'm currently suffering from dyspnea and while the fingertip measurement is sometimes harrowing, the wrist measurement is always a comforting 96% approximately. I've asked several medical professionals why this is, and I've googled a bit on my own and the only thing I can tell you is that I simply can't tell you why the measurement can be so different at different parts of the body. Nevertheless, I'll take the higher measurement with gratitude because it doesn't add more stress to the mix.

My best advice, across the boards, is to make baseline measurements on all the functions, and compare them to recent or baseline measurements from other devices. That way you'll have some point of reference whenever you make a reading with your smart watch. Beyond that, enjoy the watch and its colorful presence. It isn't all business after all. It might just make you smile.

I've been using a clip-on light for my Kindle Touch when reading at night. It works, but I don't like that there's a separate piece of equipment I need to keep track of. This all-in-one solution has proven to be an effective way to light up the Kindle without having a separate light.

The case itself is nicely made. The cover is soft and cushy; the interior is a nice "suede" type material that wont harm the screen. All the stitching is even and tight. The Kindle fits in easily and is held securely. The cover has what I assume is a magnetic closure. It works well, and keeps the case closed in transit, but opens without having to undo any snaps or zippers.

The light is attached on the back of the case. When needed, you undo a protective flap (has a snap button), flip the light over the top and secure it in place with a "hook" that's built into the top of the case. The on/off switch is on the side of the light housing. Takes only a couple of seconds to get it into position.

The light is more than adequate for reading is a dark room. It uses 2 button batteries (CR 2032).

IMPORTANT: my case came with a plastic protector on the batteries to ensure the batteries remained fresh in transit. This must be removed before use or it will appear that the light is non-functional. Unfortunately, there are no instructions about this (I guessed it was the issue when the light would not turn on).

While it's great to always have the light as part of the case, the downside is that the light housing creates a bulge on the back side of the case. That makes this more cumbersome to toss into a briefcase since it increases the width. But, for me, it's a fair trade-off since I don't have to remember to bring the light with me.

I'll give this 5 stars, but 4.5 is a more accurate rating since it should come with instructions with regard to the battery. I also think the battery cover should be thicker (no problems so far, but it's a thin plastic) as well as the lens cover (very thin plastic that bends easily). Those quirks aside, I'm finding this to be an excellent case for my Touch.
