First off, for those of you buying this product expecting the e-ink experience, you are wrong. This isn't an e-ink screen, if that is what you are looking for, go with (a) the original nook, (b) the kindle, or (c) any of the other e-ink dedicated e-readers on the market.

This iteration of the nook is marketed towards certain select categories of readers:
-The Magazine reader
-Students with text books that have graphics
-Childrens' books with lots of pictures
-Comic book readers

If you notice, these are categories of readers that benefit from the ability of the reader to handle color graphics, which is something e-ink can't yet do!

PRICE
For the price, you are getting an android tablet with limited functionality, though, with some technical knowledge, it is possible to unlock this device to be able to fully take advantage of the android market (though it may void your warranty, so do it at your own risk). Similarly sized android tablets go for prices starting at double the price of the nook color, but they come with full functionality. Another device this has been compared to is the iPad- which runs at about twice the price as well for the very base model. On the price point, you are definitely getting a decent deal, though, you are sacrificing some of the functionality for the the reduced cost.

Also note, you are not getting 3G access or any other cellular service to access the market- unlike the original nook, that came with the free mobile access to be able to make purchases from the nook market on the go. The likely reason for the lack of mobile access is due to the fact that this device runs a lot faster and features a full web browser- this increases the speed and easy of the user to access web content- which would be undesirable to any phone service that hosts access because it would reduce the service that their paying customers get. Instead of mobile data service, users have the option of accessing the BN market and the full internet through wireless. With today's cell phone technology, many phones are able to be set up as wireless hotspots that users can use to get access on the go- when they are away from their home network. Overall, this isn't a big deal to me, but I am sure some original nook users depend on that free mobile service to get access to the BN market, so this would be a draw back for you for sure.

WEIGHT
Honestly, this device does run a little on the heavy side, however, I do believe that it is slightly lighter than it's predecessor. Still, for the e-reader market, it is heavy. For the tablet market, it is a little more reasonable. The weight is a sacrifice, but as long as you aren't trying to read while laying on your back, you should be ok.

USER FRIENDLINESS AND EXTRA FEATURES
I find this device to be quite simple almost immediately. Every function that I have looked for has been where I expect it to be and everything has worked smoothly for me. The page controls while you read work great, and I love that they now give you the option to tap to turn the page rather than having to swipe like you did with the last version of the nook.

The full web is pretty easy to use once you get used to typing on a touch screen keyboard (which is always annoying).

This device also integrates with your facebook, twitter, and google accounts. This is great for the avid readers that want to be plugged into their social media.

Another feature that is nice to have on the reader is Pandora- it is a nice added bonus to have internet radio available on the reader.

One thing I wish this device had was access to android market, but I guess you can't have everything.

OVERALL
I like this tablet. I think it was a good buy and I would buy another one if this one broke. For the price, you are getting an underpowered tablet, but it still has access to the full internet- which you can use multiple windows in. It is primarily a reader, which makes me wish it were as easy on the eyes as e-ink, but for the market it is being geared towards, you can't really complain about that!

I received the unit pulled it out of the box and started playing with it everything works well, then I turn off the stereo and I hear a very faint buzz coming from the unit. Since I work with electronics almost daily (component level repairs) I knew that the power supply will die soon, (it was a sign of a cheap ps).
I decided at only $130 im not going to send it back I will fix it myself (i don't really care about warranty).
Under the cover there are 3 boards. 1 relay outlet board, 2 power supply, 3 controller. The controller board (the one with the display) was ok, it didn't look bad at all. The relay outlet board I have found 2 cold solder spots, that would cause malfunctions with an outlet down the line. After fixing it I pull out the power supply and OMG, that this looks like someone was first learning how to solder, the board had a ton of faults, remaining flux and cotton from swabs. I decided to throw the power supply out instead I installed 12v to 5v converter for the controlls and connected 12v for relays. Installed external plug for a 12v ps and it works great with no problems.

This unit is ok.
It should have a good power supply (a $5 ps from china is 100 times better than what it came with)
It should be using solid state relays (it would be silent, and it would last much longer, also you would only need 5v to supply it)

Good Luck

I live in a family compound which is an old house divided up into several apartments. What makes these walkie talkies useful on a daily basis is the water situation in the compound. All the apartments are connected to the cold water line and a couple of the apartments share a hot water line. That means if you are taking a shower and anyone anywhere in the house turns on a cold water tap, not only will your shower lose water pressure but the cold water flow will abruptly decrease, leaving the hot water hotter than ever. For the apartments that share a hot water line, the same kind of thing happens. Suddenly you are taking a cold shower in a a trickle of water. These walkie talkies have solved that problem. With the group call button you can let the whole house know you are going to take a shower so no one will use any water till you call in that you are done.

Nor is that their only use. Several times a year our town will get a tornado alert. Should a tornado actually appear in our area, the whole family will head down to the storm shelter behind the basement apartment. With the walkie talkies we can make sure everyone got the emergency alert and knows that they need to be ready to move fast if the sirens go off.

One our family members has been sick the last couple of days and these units were in an easy way to check in on her throughout the day to see if there was anything she needed. By assigning each apartment its own channel and having everyone on the same group channel, it is easy to call one apartment or to reach them all, whichever is appropriate for a given message.

The units are easy to use and even our least techie family member quickly got the hang of it. The sound is clear even when calling from apartment to apartment. There is a flashlight function that is fairly bright, one that will come in handy in case of emergency. All in all, our whole family is well satisfied with this product and it deserves a 5 star rating.

The touchpad can also feel a little bit cramped and somewhat insensitive when it comes to dragging, which is a tap and hold to start a drag. It does have the standard two-finger tap for right click and two-finger drag for scrolling (the scrolling direction is opposite of what I'm used to). While this touchpad will not be preferable over a tablet's touchscreen, it does work very well on machines that do not have a touch screen, namely a FireTV stick.

That is where this product shines. The two scenarios I listed were Typing with a tablet and typing/mouse with a FireTV. This product can do both with the press of a button. Able to be paired to three devices at once, I have a single, portable keyboard/touchpad that works with my three most-used devices. The trifold design makes this thing easy to pack into luggage or to simply stow away at the coffee table and easy to bring out when performing a search on the FireTV.

Slept two nights with these headphones in their stock configuration and decided I could create something far superior.
For several years I’ve owned and extensively used a pair of the original wired SleepPhones. They are extremely comfortable. The drivers are only 2-3mm thick and sandwiched between two layers of felt. The fleece headband stayed in place without feeling constrictive. It was also easy to wash - open the hook and loop closure on the back, pulled out the speakers and wires, wash, dry, re-install.
By contrast, MusiCozy uses thicker drivers (granted, the frequency response is better than the SleepPhone drivers) then adds a rubber cover, then covers that with a thin jersey fabric. The headband was painfully tight, and I don’t have a big head (22.5”). After the first night, I stretched the headband over a small throw pillow for a day and that helped a bit. But the second night, the thick drivers hurt my ears so bad I took the whole thing off. I mostly sleep on my side and stomach. It’s also tricky to charge because the port is only accessible if you line up the slit in the jersey fabric just right. Some simple product testing would have identified these issues. But for $20, I couldn’t be happier….. why?
SleepPhoness wants $100 for their bluetooth units. I’m sure they are top-notch but I didn’t want to spend that much. Here’s my solutions: The entire MuziCozy headband was disassembled….all two components. The bluetooth receiver / battery compartment and speakers come out easily enough. UPDATE: Since the review below this paragraph, I have put this up without a backup, and it's been a fire and forget mission. No problems with wireless network service. My "OK" review still stands, but I'm still optimistic some firmware upgrades or a big "that's it!" on my end could get everything working better or even flawlessly.

I have an extensive wired gigabit network in my home, so it has not been my top priority to replace my antiquated wireless B/G router (although I do use it much for casual surfing, mind you). Because I've been very busy when at home lately and in no mood to deal with nuisance computer/network issues, I put this new router in parallel with the old so that if issues came up, I wouldn't have to deal with them immediately. After about three weeks, albeit with only casual and sporadic "trying to make it work right", it's still not ready to run solo, obviously reason enough to just rate average.

This is unfortunate because it has a lot of cool touted features. The funny thing is when I was first setting it up I was thinking how they really have it idiot-proofed - even the WAN port is color coded to the included network cable (they don't even call it a WAN port, BTW).

But as is so often the case, by trying to make something useable to the masses, it actually becomes more difficult for advanced users to do simple tasks: I sort of want some Network Attached Storage (NAS), but have been too cheap/lazy/power misery to want to bother dealing with it, so I thought it would be great to try this router with its USB ports - ideally, I was going to put some hard drives in my gun safe, which is beside my telecom closet, and attach them to the router via USB, and have them both set to turn off when not in use. But it's just not working. I could go into a rant here about how Windows tries to set up a GUI so that people ignorant to computers can access their media when I all I really want to do is access the root of the drives and then do what I want without interference, but I'll save you my usual rant because I don't want you to misinterpret that it is indeed the router's fault that it rarely recognizes my attached devices (although interaction with various versions of Windows is the fault of both companies). The fact is, from the router's access page, you can see that my drives are often not recognized at all, or the router still thinks I have something attached that I've detached a while back (and sometimes even after a reboot). Clearly, I'm not about to put these drives down in a safe on another floor; it's easier just to deal with them locally. I was unable to EVER access these from a tablet or a phone; I wasn't about to waste that much time when I couldn't even rely on it to work with decent Windows machines.

The gigabit Ethernet ports are a great feature, and the wireless portion works better, but there have been a few times where I've checked my machines and they've reverted back to my legacy network, meaning that the new router obviously went down, if only for a short time. Thus, I'm not ready to put this machine up solo and deal with any headaches that I may have to incur.

With some cool features like QoS (Quality of Service) and port forwarding, etc., it sounds like it could be a great router. I can't begin to test these well when I'm still frustrated with making it look like a real seamless network. These are probably things that can and will be fixed with firmware updates, but they should have had this ironed out before release. If I hear of a good update, I'll give it another go if I'm still interested and will let you know how it works out.

I upgraded from a year-old, previous-generation Paperwhite, mostly to gain the new inverted white-on-black screen mode that Amazon insists requires new hardware and to have built-in Audible playback over Bluetooth.

This unit ticks most of boxes, and after some debate I've decided to give it five stars, but there are some imperfections worth knowing about. It's mostly good, though, and often great.

Battery life
No complaints. In several long international flights, I've yet to run it down more than about 30%, either in long reading sessions with the front-light or in lengthy Audible playback sessions over Bluetooth.

Audible content
The Audible player works brilliantly. Excellent sound, simple controls (including playback-speed adjustment). It does work best if you don't have a screen password enabled, though-- that will get in the way if you just want to rewind a few seconds to catch something you missed. Playback proceeds even if you have a case closed, which shuts off the front-light and saves battery charge.

There's no headphone jack-- this is for Bluetooth only. Fine with me. I have Bluetooth-enabled hearing aids (cochlear implants, actually) and it's a true joy to be able to listen to books on this device. Thanks, Amazon.

Screen
The screen is pretty much the same as my previous-generation Paperwhite's, meaning not bad but could use more contrast when reading in a dark room using the front-light. Outdoors or in well-lit areas, it's fantastic and mostly glare-free.

More seriously, the lack of contrast mars the new Paperwhite's valuable ability to invert text to white-on-black. This is a marvelous accessibility feature for those with "floaters", vitreous separation and other vision issues. Unfortunately, when used with the front-light in a darkened room, such as when reading at night or in a darkened airplane, the black background is more of a medium gray. So this new feature is less helpful than it could be. In fairness, poor contrast is characteristic of today's e-ink displays, which provide perhaps 8:1 contrast. If Amazon can significantly improve the contrast, I'd upgrade again in a flash.

The screen is plastic and will scratch. Keep it clean and use a case. Even with a case (I prefer one of the various "origami" cases available here, which allow the Kindle to prop itself upright) it will fit nicely into a pocket.

The touch-screen user interface is the same as the previous-gen Paperwhite's. I'm not a huge fan of it; too easy to touch it when you don't mean to, and end up on the wrong page. But, the earlier button-driven Kindles had sort of the same problem, so whatever. I recommend a simple fix, perhaps as a Settings option: require a double-tap rather than a single-tap. How about it, Amazon?

Connectivity
The 4G/LTE capability is a nice speed upgrade from the previous 3G connectivity. Downloading Audible content requires a WiFi connection as before.

Unfortunately I'm finding that global connectivity with the new 4G hardware is inferior to the previous-gen's 3G radio. For example, my year-old 3G Paperwhite connected without issue in Saigon, but the new one won't.

The user interface for turning Airplane Mode on and off could be improved. As it is, engaging Airplane Mode cuts all connectivity including Bluetooth. So if you're in the middle of listening to a book when the time comes to put your gizmos in Airplane Mode, it will cut your connection. Better to do what the latest iPhones do, and have the device learn if your usage prefers that Bluetooth remain active.

Browser
It's high time for Amazon to replace the minimally-functional "Experimental Browser" with something more useful. I get it that Kindles are all about battery life and browsers can be major energy hogs, but c'mon, it's 2019, and this browser feels like a relic from 1996. Probably is.

I've been watching a bunch of electronics repair videos lately and thinking back at my past purchases and the electronics I threw away, I wondered how many devices I could have rescued. Determined not to let electronics repair scare me off from tacking them, I decided to start collecting the tools that I need to do my own repairs.

I started with an affordable, but well-reviewed soldering iron: the Pinecil. A good silicone mat (same one as StezStix Fix), and now a microscope.

The LLIMINK Digital Microscope 7'' LCD, Coin Microscope is a great product. In the box, you'll find all of the accessories you'll need to get started, including any cables that you might need. What I wasn't expecting of this device is that it is actually battery powered and that the battery is removeable (see my pictures) -- very much in line with the Right-To-Repair philosophy. The remote control was a nice addition as well (taking a picture seems to be only controllable from the remote so make sure you don't lose track of it).

The base of the microscope is aluminum with two built-in LED lamps that are separately powered from the microscope itself. They provide additional lighting from other directions if you need it. The microscope itself has bright leds that shine directly downward on the board.

If the microscope mounted LEDs are causing too much glare, there is a collar that can be fitted to the scope. It will block the LEDs and instead, reflect them so that the light is indirect. Kinda like the lamps the dentists use. You're not blinded by the bulb when you're looking up at those lights.

Moving on to the screen, it is a 7" screen with passable quality. The viewable angle isn't great but it gets the job done. Any issues with the screen quality is solved by connecting the included micro-hdmi cable to your monitor. I've included pictures of both the 7" screen and the ouptut from my monitor.

I've already done a couple of simple projects with the help of this device. I built a garage door opener and gate opener using microcontrollers that are connected to my home automation system. I'm building my confidence with electronics and soldering. Hopefully, I can keep more devices out of landfills by repairing them myself.

These are around the same price as all the junky Chinese wireless earbud brands on Amazon but sound much better, are much more reliable, and are made by a company with good customer service that stands behind their products.

Ankers has several wireless earbuds with the cords that go behind the neck but only these, the spirit, the spirit pro, and the spirit x are worth considering for purchase. Their other earbuds are older models that cost just as much but have less features and weaker specs.

The bass on these is weak but I use these mostly for working out and for that it is fine.

I already have a pair of Apple EarPods but I wanted another wireless pair of headphones as well so I could switch back and forth while the other pair was charging.

These do not work with Apples w1 chip Bluetooth protocol, only apple and beats headphones work with that standard right now so those wireless headphones brands will sound better than anything other wireless headphones will with Apple products.

They also do not have aptx, which is the best sounding Bluetooth standard for anything other than Apple.

Ankers spirit pro headphones do support the aptx standard and supposedly have better bass than these so those are that models advantages.

However the spirit pro cost twice as much as these and only supports Bluetooth protocol 4.1 while these headphones support Bluetooth protocol 5.0.

Why is that important? Because the 5.0 protocol is the new “low energy” Bluetooth standard. Meaning that if you have both a device and headphones that support it you will get much more play time out of the same size battery.

Ankers other most recent model of earbuds, the spirit x headphones, have the same specs as these headphones in terms of the protocols they support but have a different form factor, obviously, and have 10mm drivers while these have 6mm. They also have a little more battery life.

I think I might buy the spirit x headphones as well in order to have a backup and to compare their sound.

As an Apple user the spirit pro headphones are just not worth the extra cost for me since I will never use the aptx protocol and they do not even support the Bluetooth 5.0 protocol.
If they were Bluetooth 5.0 compatible I might consider spending the extra 25 bucks in order to get that extra bass.

While these don’t sound spectacular they will get great battery life when I use them with devices that support 5.0 Bluetooth and they are very affordable.

It really sucks because good products, like these anker headphones, are barely visible in amazon search results because reputable brands don’t pay click farms to manipulate amazon search results.

It’s the consumers that lose in the end when their headphones, or other cheap Chinese products, break a few weeks after use or maybe never even work to begin with.

This is like getting nearly everything you'd get with Enterprise Cisco switches, but without all the awful proprietary nonsense: no licensing or forced accounts or anything like that - and it even comes with a power cord. AND that power cord - and the attachment point on the device - is industry standard IEC type and withOUT the Cisco notch! That's good, because I am using this with an IEC style PDU.

I believe you can configure this with standard Cicso command line, but it has a GUI very similar to other business and consumer products, so you can configure everything at your leisure and with just a search engine to figure out some of the protocols you may not be familiar with. Importantly, though, is that it just works when you hook it up - just like an unmanaged switch - and you can take your time with everything else (you should sign in and it will more or less force you to change the password right off the bat). There are a few "wizards" to help you through some common functions as well.

I'm using this in a small server cabinet, which is outside of my telecomm closet. I have three sets of 2x1Gbps port trunks for the servers, which all have two network ports, and then I'm using ports 8-10 as a 3Gbps link to my Cisco 250 series switch in the closet, which connects to all the end user devices. This is all new functionality for me, but something I've been looking for for a long time.

Here's some random stuff I figured out along the way:

-I knew this, but you should know that you can't use both the two extra RJ45 ports and the SFPs - It's a 10 port switch, not 12, but if you're just using <100m links, this will save you money on SFPs.

-I am using 10Gbps copper DACs between the two devices. They do negotiate down to 1Gbps, they are cheaper than buying multiple SFPs, and I can use them later when I get 10Gbps ports (so the only reason you'd use fiber is if you needed a >100m link.

-Port trunking works between DAC and regular Cat6 (apparently it won't work with fiber SFPs mixed with Cat6.

-Not sure what I was doing wrong before port trunking on another switch, but I couldn't get anything better than high-error best effort to work as far as speed. On these 250/350 Cisco devices I'm using, all four of my trunks are working perfectly and clearly working at full speed without uncorrected errors (if any at all).

-There are "green features" included, but off by default. The one looks at link length and lowers power on those links if less than 50m. You can only use this if you turn off the Energy Efficient Ethernet standardized protocol, which you might do if the device you are using doesn't work, but I haven't found a case where it correctly reads my link length (and my testers do figure out the correct length, so I don't get this). The other green feature is Energy Detect, which I've turned on across the board, but it's hard to tell if that really saves energy or not, because it just is "on" when the link is down.

-I noticed on my other switch - the 24Port 250 series (I'm telling you this because it would probably apply to 24+ port 350 switches) - the ports are counted funny. Port 1 is the top left. Port 2 is bottom left. Port 3 is top second from left, etc. This caused me some brief confusion. The great thing is that you can name all your ports in the GUI so that can make things a lot more clear for you, especially if you keep all ports in your building hot or if you at least keep most of the devices static.

I know you can probably blast through all these settings pretty quickly if you know what you are doing and can use the command line efficiently. I will say that even though the GUI is intuitive, it can be pretty cumbersome if you want to use it to go through and turn on a feature on every single port individually. Part of the problem is that you have to save each port individually and then use the drop-down to do the next port. BUT, at least on this switch, it is quick and responsive. The other switch - a 28 port Cisco 250 series - is a bit slower and gets pretty frustrating. I'm not sure if that one is slow because it has less resources being a "lower class" switch or if because it has more to deal with being a 28-port switch vice this 10 port switch. Oh, and you have to do the "save to running config" thing like you do with the Enterprise stuff. Seems strange, but I guess it more or less makes sense why. But at least in this case you can just click apply...and then go up and click the blinking disk to save (to running config).

All that said, for a guy like me with just two switches, it's not a big deal at all - it's not like I have to go back in there unless I want to make some real changes (and that is a privilege).

But there is just a ton of features here - nothing missing that I've ever heard of, and plenty of stuff I had to look up to even know what it is. Do I need all this stuff for my home network? Well, I guess not really, but I certainly am happy to have a lot of it!

Oh...worth noting is that the 350 series apparently allows many more trunk groups than the 250 series, which only allows 4, so I would not necessarily want a 250 series for my 24 port switch if I didn't have my servers separate on this switch (yet, ironically, it seems unlikely you'd need more than 4 trunk groups on this 10 port switch).

Other real-world applications for a home network would be setting restrictions for kids or renters or whoever from getting to all areas of your network. There is all kinds of port security features here, protected ports, and VLAN features, so you should be able to do just about anything you want to do with these switches. Also QoS, traffic limiting, etc.

If you're deciding between the 250 and 350 series, I suggest you do some serious homework to figure out if you actually need the 350 series. Here are just a few of the things I noticed the 350 series has that the 250 does not (not a comprehensive list):

On the 350, you can set link speeds lower on LAGS, use protected LAGS, more LAGS, UDLD, Ethernet tagging, VLAN mapping/private VLAN, lots of VLAN grouping options and more VLAN settings in general, and ISCSI status for QoS.

Oh, one last thing - unfortunately something I don't like. On some rack mounted equipment, you have one set of "wings/ears", but multiple positions/mounting options. These mounting brackets at least are included, but seem like they'd only work with this switch AND you can only put them on in one position, which means the switch will protrude about an inch forward in your cabinet, and that is really annoying for my small cabinet, so I had to get a recessed mounting kit. ALSO, I know it's pretty normal for a small switch like this to have an external power supply, but since I rack mounted it, I would have really loved to have the power supply be internal, especially because the whole thing would be small anyway.

Despite those two nitpicks, there's really nothing about this switch I don't love. Well, okay, I'd like some 10Gb SFPs, (which are available in this line). But having some real Cisco equipment is actually all it's cracked up to be!

Bottom line: While there are design differences between these two brands that affect how they are used, the performance of both is excellent. There is no “winner,” with the best one being the one that offers the design that works for your specific baking needs.

Full review: I’ve been a Chicago Metallic fan for many, many years. I have yet to have one of their pans or sheets fail on me even after 20+ years of use for some. So, I was very interested to see if the Island Ware sheet would stack up.

The build quality of the Island Ware (IW) is very good. It feels sturdy with zero racking/twisting of the pan when cold no matter how much force is applied. The finish looks attractive. There are some machining marks here and there, especially on the edges, but nothing objectionable. I’d rate the build quality the same as Chicago Metallic (CM) sheets. While I can't speak to the longevity of the IW as of yet, based on the way it looks and feels, I'd hazard a guess that it will last just as long as a CM sheet.

The IW pan is lighter. It weighs 1 pound 15 ounces versus 2 pounds 7 ounces for the CM. Despite the lighter weight, the IW feels just as sturdy. (Note: I weighed both on the same scale. While the actual weight listed may not be 100% accurate, the variation between the two is accurate.)

The corners and edges are where the IW takes a different approach than CM. The CM has the traditional rolled edge, has fairly perpendicular walls, and has rounded inside corners. The IW has no rolled edges, eased walls, and more of a squared off inside corner. There are pluses and minuses to both designs. The IW fits square silicon sheets or parchment paper better, and there is zero risk of having gunk get caught inside the rolled edge. On the other hand, the rolled edge is more comfortable to hold and grab without it cutting into your hand, and the perpendicular walls work better when baking a pan cookie or dough where you use the full sheet.

Baking performance for both was very similar. The IW seemed to heat a little faster, but the difference with the CM was minimal. Both heated evenly and didn’t have any hot spots. The IW did rack a small amount when hot but nothing that was objectionable or problematic.

So, there really is no winner – both are great pans and are 5-star performers. The choice is mainly on what you plan to do with the pans. If you mainly bake cookies, I’d go with the IW. The eased rim and square corners make it easier to line with square silicon sheets or parchment paper, and make it easier to lift cookies out using a spatula. But, if you’re looking to bake pan cookies, flat breads, pizza, etc. where you press the dough throughout the full pan, the rounded corners and more vertical walls of the CM will work a little better.

Again, these differences are not deal-breakers – you could certainly bake a pan cookie in the IW and have it come out just as good as the CM. You’ll want to take a look at pricing and see which one is the better deal in terms of cost. Neither will disappoint when it comes to performance.

Why is the cable size and breaker on this thing so undersized when it is presumably (due to the fact that it is Stanley Max) for running power tools? 16AWG and 13A is actually a bottleneck compared to a standard 15A 14AWG household circuit. Worse is that it is a huge bottleneck compared to the 12AWG 20A circuits I put in work and kitchen areas to accommodate the many tools (e.g., miter saws, medium sized air compressors, etc.) and appliances (e.g., microwaves) that push the envelope on the 15A circuits.

Point is, right off the bat, I can't run large tools on this thing (and that includes some plug-in-lawn equipment), and I can't run most medium sized tools two at a time on this thing (good drills, planers, grinders, etc. often draw around 9A), so what's the point of the multiple outlets except, granted, that you don't have to unplug one to plug the other in over and over again if working with two tools alternately.

On the flip side, this lighter gauge cable does allow this power hub to be lighter and easier to deal with. It does roll up nicely and I like that the cord can be attached on the side so it doesn't unravel itself.

But I think the outlets should be spaced a little further a part, given that the size could accommodate that. That would allow larger plugs, and maybe even some AC adapters to fit. I also think 20 ft. is way too short, especially for the reel setup (it's not that hard to untangle 20ft.) and the fact that this thing is probably large enough to hold more.

You could use it for Christmas lights or something like that - except it is not a true weatherproof cord - or some low power hobby in the house. This has no quality issues, and there are plenty of uses for it, but the name has me thinking it is trying to be in the tool market. To be really effective in that market, it should be 12AWG, accept 20A plugs, be minimum 50' long, and have the outlets spaced slightly further apart.

I got this hard shell case in the Clear style mainly to see if the grippers on the bottom of the case would keep my MacBook Pro Retina 15" from sliding off my [[ASIN:B00IV3AEZY lap desk]] when I'm climbing in and out of my recliner, which is where I work. The package comes with two pieces constituting the hard shell case, a screen protector that I may or may not use, and a protective keyboard skin that I know I won't use.

The case is GREAT. It is a perfect fit for my Mac, and I don't even realize it's on it except for the fact that it works MUCH better than the rubberized grips on the bottom of my Mac to hold it firmly on my lap desk—it stays put even when the board is slanted at a 45-degree angle! I wish I had gotten this when I first got my Mac, because I do have a few scratches on it now that this case would have prevented. The fit is so tight, the only thing I don't like about it is that I do have a [[ASIN:B00D6A2Z2C palm rest protector]] on my Mac, and on one side it won't quite fit underneath the case's tab. I'll probably wind up taking a hair off the protector so I don't notice it so much, but I wouldn't have to because it looks like it will stay stuck.

I don't really know how the keyboard skin compares to others on the market, because I hate the things and won't use one. I can say that it does fit the keyboard well and provides cover from spills. I think you can see from my photos how it fits; also how the case fits. The one with my chiweenie Bingo in the picture was taken when I had my lap desk at a precipitous incline, and there was no sliding!

The screen protector has a top and bottom. I thought at first it was not going to fit right, but it's because I had it upside down. It has a protective film over it that you remove once you place it on the screen. I don't know yet if I'm going to use it, because we've got a lot of dog hair floating around and I'm not confident I could get it on without dog hair under it. That happened when I first put the hard shell case on, and I had to remove it and put it back on again.

One thing to note about this case: there are no installation instructions, and there is a definite right way and wrong way to put on both pieces. The lip on the bottom part goes in the front, and the open part is in the back where all your ports are. The top of the case has three tabs on one of the long sides and two tabs on the other. The three-tab side goes at the top of the screen. I don't think you can see these details in my photos. You really can't see that there is a case on it at all unless you look closely.

I'm still just knocked out at how well the grippers on the case grip my lap desk. I broke my last Mac by dumping it off into the floor—actually, Bingo did it. This case is great insurance, and the price is definitely right, even if you wind up only using the case. But with all three protective items, this set is a real bargain. I got this item free in exchange for my honest review, but had I known how great it was, I definitely would have bought it a long time ago.

TLDR: Dropped my GPU temps from 75c to 50c under full load. Reduced fan noise considerably since I went from 5 case fans at 100% to 3 at 30-50% most of the time. LED's are ok. If you want to run cooler temps and less noise, get this!
UPDATE: after a month of use everything was still great. I did make a bad mistake that ended my card. I didn't want to take the cooler off to properly attach the back plate so I was just sitting on top of the card. All was well until I stupidly tried to move a fan from one side on my CPU cooling tower to the other, while my comp was on..... I KNOW, I KNOW, I"m an idiot. I dropped the fan which bounced around my mobo and slammed into the top of my card. Shorting everything out. GPU is toast, rest of system is questionable. Be smarter than me, DONT TAKE SHORT CUTS. TURN OFF YOUR PC WHEN WORKING ON IT AND PROPERLY ATTACH EVERYTHING! Still hyped on the this cooler. Aiming to still use it on my new card IF I can ever get one without taking a second mortgage.

I used this on a XFX RX 580 GTS 8GB Black edition. In a M-atx case, the stock cooler fans would run full RPM just to keep it at 75-80C under load. Add in 5 case fans (@full RPM) to keep the air flow fresh and I had an annoyingly loud heater just a few feet from my chair. Stumbled upon this in a random search and after reading a few other reviews I decided to order it and see how it goes.

Install was straight forward enough. If you can reapply thermal paste, you can install this cooler. Placing the heat sinks on the VRAM and VRM is time consuming but unlike others I found the supplied thermal sticky pads to be fine after applying moderate force for about 10 secs. Only issue I had was clearance on one of the VRAMs as it sat close to the plate and could only be half covered by a heatsink. Getting the placement on that one took slightly longer but by using a few dry test fits I was able to get it placed perfectly.

The MOSs are on the left on this GPU so I was hesitant but after a week of using it I haven't seen any issues with VRM not properly cooling. Board doesn't support junction temp measuring so I have no hard data on if they are hotter or not, but I do feel airflow around them and performance is still great.

The rad and fan were easy enough to install. In a M-atx case it is tight. It was a squeeze and took a few tries to properly get everything where I wanted but once in I have no complaints. I did hear "coil whine" from the pump once, but quickly sorted out that some pressure was being applied to one of the tubes right near the pump, once I shifted it a little, the whine stopped and never returned.

The LEDS are ok. The controller is adequate. The LED along the side of the GPU mount is a nice touch, really adds a higher end feel to the finished product. Obviously this isn't a high end ARGB controller but its got more than enough setting to make it fit into your overall lighting needs. Personally I just wanted some plain old solid white. I do find the white to be slightly bluish in the fans but I chalk that up to ARGB vs the RGB LED case fans I have installed.

Wiring was tedious but it included everything I needed. Other than taking my time to cable manage and tuck it all away out of sight, it was straight forward enough to wire up. Just double check they all get plugged in! I missed the pump power and on my first start up saw the temps just go up and up and got worried I installed it wrong. Luckily I thought to check the cables right before taking it apart and found the problem.

I did add/change a few things,
-Firstly I used Thermal Grizzlys kryonaut paste instead of the supplied paste.
-I also bought a 4-Pin PWM splitter adapter that allowed me to use the GPUs native fan plug to power the rad and VRAM fans. I can't recommend this enough! Using Afterburner to control the fan speeds really is awesome and allows for easy fine tuning for noise and temps needs.
-I did have to cut some of the metal shroud for the front of the GPU back plate. I didnt want to run no plate on top of the board and obviously it wasn't designed to have water tubes go through it. It was simple and easy to cut but is a permeant mod to make it look better. You can see in the attached pics, some are with the plate on and some with it off.

Speaking of which temps are mind blowing! It idles at 28c (ambient is about 22c) with fans set to 3%. in other words, silent! Under my normal full gaming load it chills at 50c with fans at 50%. Slightly louder but still much quieter than the stock blower! If I turn the fans to 100% it will chill at like 35-37c while full 1080p gaming. I've even pushed the OC a bit, went from 1425 Core clock to 1500, and Mem clock from 2000 to 2250. No way the stock coolers would have let that happen smoothly.

I waited a week or so to write this review just to make sure I was still happy. And I am! I'll update this review with any long term issues or problems so if there is no update, expect that its still just plugging along being super chill.

My guess is that this product is aimed at households with at least 2 TVs. However, the price is so cheap that you're basically getting an extra remote for almost nothing. It's wasteful but hard to turn down because of the price.

The packaging and the instructions are confusing. RCA claims that one remote controls 3 devices while the other one controls 6. However, the 3-device one actually controls MORE than 3 - it just uses one button to control the DVD/VCR (it treats 2 devices as 1), one button for the TV, and another for the combination Satellite/Cable/digital TV converter. Having one VCR, one DVD, one TV, one cable box and an audio deck with a set of speakers, I used the "6 device" remote. My audio deck with attached speakers, which are circa 1988, would not work with the codes. However, switching from DVD to VCR went smoothly, as did from TV to cable.

In conclusion, the universal remote functioned well overall and cleared up the clutter of remotes beneath my coffee table. I liked the battery saver function - if you by chance lost your remote between your sofa cushions, the battery turns off after awhile.

Now if I could only find a way to use my 3-device remote...

I've been a Magellan user for several years - have owned four of their GPS systems, and always appreciate how they have improved their products. This unit is my 5th, and replaces a Magellan 4040. After using it for a while I've confident in saying this is the best one yet!

The most visible change is the actual size of the unit. The screen size has been increased, but the unit is thinner and lighter. Very sleek appearance, and the screen is a real joy -- sharp, clear graphics even in the sun, and bigger on-screen buttons for easy use. The mounting system has also been streamlined, and looks and works well. It mounts very easily on a NavMat holder (basically a bean-bag system that I got on Amazon. I'm a huge Navmat fan - makes it a snap to hide the GPS with narry a trace. Best accessory by far for any GPS).

The power connector was not well thought out, however. You have to connect it to the GPS unit AFTER you mount it in the holder. They should have moved the connector it a wee bit to the side to avoid that.

The only button is a slide-type power button on the top. Boot-up time is OK -- not speedy, but not a huge delay either. It does not have a "sleep" mode, so you have to do a cold boot every time. Not a problem in real world use - by the time you get situated in your car, the unit is ready to go.

Voice is clear and easy to understand. Not as natural sounding as a TomTom, but understandable.

Pretty much any recent GPS unit will get you where you want to go. I've found the routing on the Magellans to be very similar to Garmins - could be because they both use the same mapping set (Navteq). The Magellan shines, however, in features that I find helpful. The direction of the next turn is always visible regardless of how far away the next turn will be. Up until recently, Garmin did not offer this (they do now on some of their units). Sounds like a small issue, but I find it very helpful. The Magellan also allows you to very easily exclude a route (or portion). That's a fairly standard feature nowadays, but Magellan allows you to do it in a snap.

In terms of routing, Magellan offers four options (fastest, shortest, most use of freeways and least use). You can see all four options on the map (as a summary) at the same time so you can pick the best one for your needs. Perfect!!

Love the AAA Guidebook, which is a unique Magellan feature. Lets you get details about restaurants and other points of interest just like the paper version from AAA. I used it a lot in my 4040, especially when traveling out of town.

Other unique Magellan features I appreciate is the "ding dong" sound right before a turn (incredibly accurate!) and the fact that the software reminds you to "stay on the current road" when you encounter major exits. Some find that to be nagging, but it has saved me from inadvertently exiting on more than one occasion.

A new feature for Magellan is the lane guidance. Very nicely done. I've used this feature on Navigon units, and found it rather unhelpful. Magellan's implementation is far more useful, with better, clearer graphics. However, lane guidance is not available for every road.

The software is also nicely done - very logical to use. If you're a past Magellan user you can pick this up and use it in a second. If not, there's a short printed user's guide in the box (plus a CD-ROM with more in-depth info) that gets you up to speed quickly. The box also includes the mount, power connector for the car, and a USB cable. It does not include an AC adapter.

OK, now for the bad news. When it comes to customer service, Magellan has been horrid. We're talking so bad it's almost funny. I'm hoping this situation will change - the company was bought by Mitac late last year, and perhaps this will signal a change for the better in terms of customer support. Lord knows, they couldn't get any worse.

The leader, in my opinion, for customer support is Garmin. They are nice to deal with on the phone, answer emails promptly, and offer regular firmware updates. Whenever I buy a GPS as a gift I always buy Garmin since I don't want to saddle the recipient with the miserable service that Magellan offers. It's a shame, since Magellan offers some real benefits over Garmin, and more value for the money. Tom Tom is also decent when it comes to support, but they use TeleAtlas maps which are less complete than NavTeq (sp?).

Bottom line -- if you're looking for a straightforward GPS at a good price, this should be on your short list. It lacks features such as Bluetooth and an MP3 player, but for me, I want a GPS to offer guidance and not entertainment. This has a very robust feature set, great screen, and well-designed software. It also has traffic capabilities -- did not test that feature out, so I can't comment on it.

The "safe" bet continues to be Garmin. You'll pay a bit more, and get less features, but you can be assured of solid support. Whether Magellan's new owners will put them back on the right track (if you'll excuse the horrid, but unavoidable pun) in terms of customer service is not yet clear. I hope so -- they make a great product!

UPDATE: 5/21/09 There's a firmware update on the Magellan site. No new functionality (in terms of new features) but, according to the release notes it improves overall performance. Easy to install - just follow the included step-by-step instructions. It seems like it makes the unit a bit faster, but that could just be my imagination.

The build quality is excellent. It feels solid and well-made. It also comes very attractively packaged in a clear, thick plastic box. While I would normally scold a company for what could appear to be wasteful packaging, in this case the packaging is useful: one of my primary uses for this speaker is as a take-along for my laptop, and the plastic case makes for excellent protection against the bangs and dings suffered by my laptop bag. So, in addition to making it look upscale, the packaging has an actual use down the road.

Setup is simple - plug and go. It has three outputs - 3.5mm cord for something such as a tablet, a USB port for a computer, and a 3.5mm cord for headphones. Covers all the bases as to potential uses.

I used it mainly for listening to podcasts and webinars (some of them actually work related!) and the sound quality was miles beyond what I was getting from my laptop speaker, and significantly better than the lower-end portable speakers I was using.

Now, the Cube doesn't sound as good as the Bose Companion 20. That didn't come as a surprise since the entire speaker is about the same size as just the power converter for the Bose. The size of the Bose make them non-transportable; the Cube is a very easy device to take along with a laptop.

It does not have a volume control. I don't miss it when using it with my PC since it's easier to fiddle with the sound level from the PC rather than have to use the speaker. I can see that as a negative, however, for other uses. On the other hand, a volume control device, be it a knob, wheel or button, would detract from the clean, simple design lines of the Cube. So, an equitable trade-off in my opinion.

This is one of those products that I really can't come up with a single negative other than the fact that it is pricy. But, if you value good quality sound but have to keep the speaker as small as possible, it is worth the cost. This is about the same size as the small take-along speakers that run in the $20 range, but provides sound quality that is miles beyond what they offer. Highly recommend.

I received a review sample from the manufacturer and was pleasantly surprised when I opened the box. I was expecting an 'erector set' of many pieces that I would need to put together. Instead I received a complete solution that literally unfolded and snapped into place in minutes.

Set up entails the unfolding and snapping step, plus connecting the antenna to a powered booster box with coaxial cable in from the antenna and out to your TV. Once connected you need to go into your TV's settings, select antenna as the input, then do a scan for available channels.

Since I live close to a major metropolitan area - Orlando, Florida - I decided to test this at a friend's home in Ormond Beach, which is about sixty miles from Orlando and roughly the same distance from Jacksonville. This location tested the claimed forty mile radius for the device.

The true power was when I did a quick test by temporarily setting it up, plugging it in and seeing what channels were available. With the device sitting on the floor the first scan found seven digital channels. Bear in mind that this was laying on the floor for the initial test, which is hardly optimum.

Test number two entailed raising the antenna towards the ceiling (but not permanently mounting it) and moving it around to various spots in a 15x10 foot room. That increased the total channels received to twenty-two, including Orlando and Jacksonville channels that were twenty miles beyond the claimed range, as well as a few channels in Cocoa Beach (right at the edge of the range).

Note that in both tests the Central Florida terrain is relatively flat. In other geographic locations the results may have been vastly different.

Installation does require access to 110/120 AC power for the signal booster module. The mounting hardware that ships with this antenna is heavy-duty and complete. You can use one of the clamps to mount it to practically any pole of beam, but there is a pipe assembly that provides you with even more mounting options. The kit also includes fifty feel of high quality coaxial cable, with a removable double male connector in one end in case you need to run it even farther. You will need to purchase a second coaxial cable to connect the booster box's out port to your TV.

For outdoor mounting (or in a ceiling that is not close to a 110/120 AC outlet) I recommend running the longer cable from the antenna to the powered booster, which can be placed close to the TV. If you decide to place the booster closer to the antenna's coaxial connection make sure you can do with without using an extension cord, which could be a safety issue.

The bottom line is this antenna works beautifully. Since it picked up signals fifty percent farther than the claimed range it greatly exceeded my expectations. For the record, although I received the antenna as a review sample I donated it to a worthy cause after I completed my testing and had enough information to write this review. I do recommend it as a wonderful solution and an alternative to cable if local programming meets your news and entertainment needs.

Reviewed by my husband, a photography enthusiast.

Over the last 20 years, my husband has purchased several LowePro camera bags/backpacks (i.e., Mini Trekker & Micro-Trekker 100). He has found that they have been some of the best he has ever owned. He prefers backpacks because they are easy to carry and keep up with, especially if you are on the go. Backpacks also allow for easy storage and are super convenient. They give you freedom of movement and your hands are free to capture those special moments that you may not otherwise get if you were holding a bag in your hand. The Viewpoint (LowePro) BP 250 is the perfect addition to his bag collection especially since it is specially designed for small video equipment.

Here’s what he liked:

• This bag is attractive. The design is smart, functional and full of surprises. The Viewpoint BP250 is well-made with plenty of room for your Go Pro and accompanying equipment. There is a ton of storage (inside and out). There are several compartments where you can store your accessories, cords, lenses and other equipment. On the outside of the main bag, there is a zipper pocket (which allows for small items like a memory stick/card or thumbdrive). There is a pocket on the other side of the bag which will fit a small tripod or other item (like an umbrella). The entire bag can be zippered so you won’t lose any of your accessories.

• It is ideal for those who use (small) video and other digital equipment. There is a space dedicated to a small computer. While this backpack will not allow you to carry one of the larger sized laptops (our 17” didn’t fit), it has adequate space for the smaller ones (about 15”), a SurfacePro, iPad or other small notebook or tablet. He finds that the option of carrying a computer is great because it will allow you to quickly upload and edit your videos wherever you are. There is no reason to wait….just review, edit (if needed), and upload!

• The straps are unlike the traditional ones that come straight down the shoulders. The BP250 LowePro’s straps are curved which he found to be less stress on his shoulders. After some adjustments (he’s 6’1, average sized with average shoulders), it was a good fit. The straps are slightly padded and comfortable. There are small snaps that lock the straps in place to ensure that they don’t fall down when walking or hiking.

• There is a small (lunch box sized bag) that can be removed and can hold your GoPro camera and equipment. Once closed, it fits directly into your main LowePro Bag. It is padded and once inside, will protect your camera and smaller lenses. Or if you want, this smaller bag can be used instead of taking the large one.

• This bag comes with a rain cover. Not sure how much you will use this feature, but if you are ever caught in a drizzle or rain storm, there is a plastic cover that can be removed (unzipped) from the bottom and cover your bag. This is perfect for keeping your bag and equipment dry.

• The price. While this bag may seem a little pricey (about $130) it’s worth it. The craftsmanship and functionality will prove invaluable for the amateur or professional photographer. It’s a small investment with some heavy returns. You’ve got protection and functionality.

Overall, my husband gives this bag 5 stars. He finds that it is not only good to use for a GoPro, but other small video and photography equipment. Backpacks are useful for photographers because they allow your hands to be free to capture those moments or events as they unfold. In the past he has purchased Lowepro equipment and found them to be sturdy and durable, and the Viewpoint BP250 is not different. It looks good and he won’t leave home without it.

I received these phones as a review sample and wanted to test the claim that they are studio quality. In point of fact they are very close. What I mean by studio quality is they are neutral sounding - there is no bias towards any particular frequency band. These are fairly even on the highs, mids and lows.

Of course, if you are listening to modern music that emphasizes low frequency response with a lot of bass you may want to check out other phones that do a better job. I will say that while the frequencies are naturally divided, the separation is excellent so I am certain these phones have a crossover.

Since there are ample specs in the product description (and two video reviews at the time of this one) I will spare you a recitation of that information. I tested these using a few key albums, and also plugged the 1/4 inch connector directly into my Roland RD-300NX keyboard to hear that instrument's natural responses. Both tests confirmed that these are studio quality. However, audiophiles who want unbiased sound will also love them. I played some of my favorite test albums like Miles Davis' Kind of Blue, Ahmad Jamal's Live at the Pershing and some 20-bit mastered CDs. In all cases the frequency response in each band was perfect and the ability to hear nuances (including the natural reverb on Kind of Blue) was a treat. More importantly I heard the albums the way the engineers wanted me to hear them.

To be sure I do have other phones that are at this level of quality, but most are in a much higher price range. For the record: I hate this trend in mobile phones to push us away from a standard 3.5mm jack. I tried to hold onto a phone that had one for as long as I could, but when my Galaxy S10 had to go, I needed an adapter. I love using my high end studio IEMs for music instead of bluetooth or cheap USB-C headphones, and sometimes if my bluetooth earpiece isn't charged, I want to grab my laptop headphones with their in-line mic to do handsfree calls.
Well, I'm happy to say at least I can use this for music with my IEMs and other wired headphones. But I think the jack might be TRS and not TRRS. That means it is missing the extra pin to support the microphone if your headphones have one.
In a nutshell, this will turn a pair of regular stereo (no mic) headphones into a USBC compatible one, but it still isn't as good as a native 3.5mm jack. The real ones used to detect if there was a mic pin attached and give you the ability to use your headphone mic, or use the phone's mic if there wasn't the extra pin. This just defaults to no pin.

The TOMTOM GO2535 TM WTE is quite attractive with a large screen and smooth appearance but because of its size, this is a heavier GPS than many others. A magnetic plug attaches the power supplies either to a computer with its USB plug or to a car with its accessory power plug. As with most GPS devices, no "home" DC power supply is included. I have found the car mount to be great, easy to attach and remove from the windshield with a simple turn. My only complaint with the mount is that it takes some work to direct the device to a visible position and I fear that it will not last as long as the GPS. The magnetic plug slips into a cutout in the mount, allowing it to remain in position so the GPS can quickly be inserted or removed for safekeeping.
As for the functionality of the GPS, it has some problems, thereby preventing me from giving this a 5 star review. I'll simply list the Pros and Cons.
Pros:
Start up time is quick and option to start from last destination can save time if the satellite connection is delayed.
Menu options are easily learned even if at first they seem to include extra steps.
Responds quickly to need for alternate route when a turn is missed.
Ease in moving through functions on screen.
POIs are expansive and easy to discover
Map identifies a location I frequent which is not identified by any other GPS I've used.
Identifies traffic light cameras adequately. Have yet to receive speed camera warning.
Voice commands are intuitive and a little printed card is included if you're in need of prompting.
Connectivity to my Mac is easy and the option to automatically check for updates can save time.

Cons:
Speed is not always accurate. Often has my car going at 10 mph less than actual speed.
When setting a new destination, I've been unable to change the state unless I do it using the voice command. This may be possible, but I haven't had the time to investigate. Since I'm in a metropolitan area and may venture through 2 states and the District of Columbia in less than an hour, it's important for me to access the individual states.
When using phone through the GPS, although I can hear the conversation with no problem, the person on the other end of my call can't hear me clearly. Every time I've used it with a phone, the call has been dropped. I've never had a call dropped otherwise with my phone or other Bluetooth capable device.
Does not recognize voice commands at times.
Voice prompts are very frequent and I'd love to be able to reduce them but not turn it off.
Seldom comes up with the routes I usually take, even with a second try after selecting the Change Route option.

These are a good way for me to extend my wifi to areas in my house that needed a signal boost.
Setup required a bit more effort due to vagueness or incomplete instructions. I had to reset these several times and start setup once I figured out what the units were doing. One key is to decide if you want to use these as a WIFI extender or a wired router system and setup the units with this understanding.

Once setup on the main router was complete adding the satellite units was as simple as pushing two buttons, and now you have a new MESH wifi network where your devices automatically transfer connectivity to the unit with the most powerful signal.

For speed the primary unit is pretty good. if my main router wifi speed is around 450mbs, the primary wifi is around 300mbs which is pretty good. Now the satellite units speeds drop down to around 45mbs which is good for an extender setup, and is somewhat dependent on how far from the primary unit they are, but the speed is never above 50 mbs. That gets us to range. if this was a wide open building with no interior walls I could see where two units would cover 2000 sq feet, but in reality 2 units are good for a around 1400 sq ft. This still isn't bad considering the install footprint.

What I do like these for is the network is always up no matter the main WIFI router condition. In other words if my main cable modem WIFI goes down, but I have my PC and Printer on this mesh system I can still print while the primary cable modem is down. Also devices connected to the mesh WIFI stay connected to the mesh WIFI, so those WIFI cameras outside are still able to record to my NAS drive even though my cable modem is offline.

The Fire HD 10 tablet is pretty much an unbeatable deal for a tablet these days. You get a really good display and decent processor and memory for a great price---especially when it's on sale. And the Fire OS (a rebranded and modified version of Android) works smoothly.

A trade-off is a not-so-good camera resolution.

And there are some limitations on what you can do. If you already own some Android apps, you might not find them in the Amazon app store, and those you do will not credited as paid for. You'll have to buy them again (if you choose to buy).

One option is to follow online instructions for installing the Google Play Store on your Fire. But that's kind of iffy. You don't know when the next Fire OS update might break that installation. And Play Store might download updates to some of the core Fire OS apps that might conflict with proprietary Fire OS modifications.

Another consideration is that this device serves as an advertising and sales platform for Amazon. It's tailored for that. Something to keep in mind.

The thing to consider is if you can be happy with what Amazon gives you. If you're going to be trying to root and work around the OS and app store limitations soon after you get it, maybe it's worth just getting an Android tablet and foregoing the Fire.

If you can be happy with all that, overall it's a great deal for a capable tablet.

Original review:
I received the Amcrest ProHD 1080p IP PT "WiFi" camera yesterday, 10/30/15.

I downloaded the Amcrest Lite iPhone app. Followed instructions. It would not connect via Wi-Fi using my router's password. Tried again and again. I have a TP-Link C9 dual band wireless router with both 5gHz and 2.4gHz transmission. The Amcrest website says in an obscure forum post that the camera operates only in the 2.4gHz band. I changed my iPhone6 (iOS 9.0.2) from 5G to 2.4G. Still could connect via Wi-Fi.

So I plugged the camera directly into the router via ethernet, completely defeating the purpose for the initial purchase. It finally connected. I saw the picture for about 30 seconds, trying to get the camera to full screen, I clicked around on the mysterious icons. Nothing seemed to work. I clicked on the "X" box. The camera disappeared. I tried to reconnect. It came back with "USER LOCKED." I went to their website to search for an answer. They said (at least for their DVR line -- virtually nothing was about this camera) "users are locked out after two failed logon attempts and that I must wait 30 minutes for the reset." I waited. Still USER LOCKED. No camera. I don't even recall trying to log in. I was in the app, trying to reconnect the camera.

I created my Amcrest user account and received their confirming email. I created a user and password for Amcrest.com. The account is actually for something called amcrest.Zendesk and Accumed.zendesk and Foscamhelp.zendesk. I then tried to log in at Amcrest.com. It won't take my log-on credentials. "Invalid Logon or Password." How many user names and passwords does it take to plug in a camera?

Trying to start over, I deleted the app and rebooted the camera. Still USER LOCKED.

Finally, I found that if you push and hold in the little LED network-activity-indicator button on the back of the camera for 10 seconds, the camera will reset to factory. Deleted the app again, set my phone to operate in the 2.4gHz band. Still won't connect via WiFi. Plugged in via ethernet, then used my router's password and it connected. Per the prompt, I then created a new secure password, replacing the default "admin/admin". Finally, I can see and control the camera. So, I have a WiFi camera that won't WiFi. The camera needs to connect to the router at 2.4gHz band (and in my case, via an ethernet cable) but after getting it set, the phone can go back to the 5G if desired.

They claim their products are "Simple, Reliable, Secure." Not quite. They fail to hook to Wi-Fi and then lock me out. Their website won't let me log on even with a user and password.

I downloaded the camera's big PDF user manual to find what the icons mean. The document looks nothing like the camera's icons. They went into great detail...about a previous firmware version, then changed the firmware to look very differently.

The camera works, eventually, and only via ethernet in some cases, but getting there is a real test of patience.

I am an EE who does communications projects as a profession. I don't do wireless often, but I am more or less up to date on its features. Frankly, I was pretty stunned by the amount of menu options you can set on this thing. I wasn't expecting such an overwhelming mass of things to update myself on and tweak, especially considering this is marketed more like a small business brand than an enterprise level brand. Impressive. You can check the data sheet for a full list of features.

To counter that point, it's not a super easy device to navigate. Not that it needs to be if you have full time IT guys working on it, but I often consider what hardware a small business might use (when I'm picking parts for my house) if the owner or another employee would be taking care of the network on the side. It can be done with this, but it will take some time to figure everything out if you want to utilize all the advanced features. A perfect example is, it comes working out of the box needing no authentication to associate with the AP. Fine, but I'm looking for that setting for what seems like forever, feeling like I've lost my mind. It's under the Virtual AP heading. I'd normally expect it on the same page as you enable each radio, right up front and center. But at least it's there...

And there are pull down boxes to change from one radio to the other, and you cannot see the settings of both at the same time in most cases. This also causes you to forget to save changes, stuff like that. These are just some examples. Nothing major. The more important take away from this is that there is a lot of substance there, but it doesn't have that super easy to use GUI that Linksys home products often have (However, there is a fine line when a little GUI becomes too much).

The speeds are really here, though! I'd swear I sense a difference with my meager 30Mbps Internet connection getting to me faster. It's only slightly perceptible, but I suppose if AC really cuts out some overhead and always sends on a broader channel, it could be true (I think it is, but I'm being careful not to "imagine" things).

Note that this is true AC, but it is not the end-all highest level of AC available. It uses the minimum required 80MHz band for the 5GHz radio, but the standard allows for up to 160MHz. You can get a lot higher throughput as well, although only with more antennas using the broader spectrum. I believe the 5 GHz band on this can deliver only 1300Mbps to another single device or multiple devices maximum; the other 450Mbps is from the 2.4GHz radio.

Still impressive. Really amazing to think you can get true greater-than-wired speeds this way (I'm assuming small businesses and homes are still using 1Gb ethernet connections) considering I've always touted wired as better in every way. However, you need channel bonding equipment on both ends to do it (If I'm running a small business, I may be using an unmanaged Gb switch without that feature). Keep that in mind. Otherwise, you'll get loops and other problems. Bummer. I am unclear if this feature works with other brands' products because there are a few proprietary channel bonding methods out there.

It can be mounted so that it looks good to a wall or a false ceiling with the included hardware. A little lame is that it does NOT mount to any type of electrical box and they just tell you to drill a hole for the cables to come through. That's not very professional to me, because pulling cables through a random hole distorts that hole over time, making upgrading or maintenance difficult. It may also damage cables depending on the wall material. Not a huge issue, but lowers the professional vibe of the product. It looks pretty decent, though, but it's bigger than I expected.

Even if you have the newer, higher amperage version of PoE that this requires, they still advise you to use the AC adapter as a fail-over. Better would be both ports provide power via PoE at the new standard, share the lower power of the old standard, and if one fails, the single port keeps it alive fully with the new standard or at reduced capacity with the old standard. Then I could make some use out of PoE injectors I have laying around and it would be more backward compatible with older Telecom room equipment.

Overall, I think it's a pretty great product at a very reasonable price point at this point in time. I think it could definitely accommodate medium or even large businesses if implemented properly.

I selected this specific micro to usb type-c adapter because it is gold plated. Gold is highly conductive and whenever adapters are introduced into a circuit, there is a negative impact on performance (in this case charging rate). In order to reduce a main cause of this problem, gold can be used to reduce the impact.

Using an android battery charge monitoring app, I was able to prove that using this adapter caused little to no difference in the rate of charge. I was still able to reach and maintain charging rates as if this adapter was not connected at all.

Also, all 5 of my adapters work and still work till this day (8 months later) including the wear and tear of putting on a micro cable and pulling it off, especially when I was testing for bad cables. This thing held up the whole time (over 50 cables tested)!

I wanted an adapter because I have so many USB micro cables collected over the years. I literally could not bring myself to buy USB type-C cables just because I bought my first USB type-C charging phone. I am glad to say after all this time, I have still not a single USB type-C cable as I use these adapters instead.

Honestly, I wish I had a tried a Wifi6 mesh system sooner. This is NIGHT AND DAY difference over my previous D-link router + extender. I thought that since both my router and extender were D-link and had the ability to "communicate" with each other, it would work pretty well, but honestly even when it "worked" it was pretty laggy, and outside on the porch it would drop to single digit speed tests, if anything at all (forget about streaming for backyard movie nights!).
This system, however, is incredible. I'm now getting nearly 200mbps outside where I used to have nothing, and in most of my house I'm hitting my maximum 250mbps that I'm paying for with my internet service. Everything responds quickly and smoothly, and I love the control that the TP link system gives over what devices are connected (it alerts me when a new device connects!) and being able to set restrictions and time limits as well!
The one downside, however, is the physical ports. For starters, there are only 3 of them per unit. If you use ethernet backbone to connect them, that leaves only one on the primary node (one for the internet connection to the modem, and the other going to the second node- only one available for anything else). In my case, I have an ethernet cable going to my desktop for work (the most reliable connection), and another going into a telephony system. The 3 port limitation would have been difficult if I hardwired the satellite, but thankfully I didn't have to. The wireless mesh over 6Ghz actually works quite well so far so I managed with only the 3 ports on the primary one.
That being said, at first I had a major issue with the speed on my hardwired connection. The desktop claimed to only connect at 100mbps. Meanwhile, if I turned on wifi I was pulling 250mbps. That can't be! Many chats to customer support and we couldn't figure it out until I switched ports on the Deco and now I'm getting the full 250 over ethernet. I don't know if it was the port having trouble or just reseating the wire that did it, but I never had that on my previous D-link router, and it had more ports too in case I needed them.

In a nutshell, I got it working, and for what it is supposed to do, I'm VERY very impressed at the performance. But the hardwire hiccup and limitation in number of ports available makes this a 4 instead of 5 star review.

I made absolutely sure everything was closed before putting it into water, not that one could have much faith in the mechanisms keeping it closed, as they are easy to accidentally open. I put it in the water gently, and only a foot or so, to film some stingrays and fish; this recording went fine. Later that day, I wanted to photograph a tiny little crab. I took one picture from above the water, and one from below. I noticed this time, when I put the camera underwater, that bubbles started to come out the top. I immediately took it out and noticed the screen starting to fog up with condensation and moisture, the first very bad sign. I double checked everything was still closed, and it was. No part of it had been opened. I put it back in, hoping for the best. After coming back to the sand (never having done more than a few feet underwater), I tried to turn it on to get some video. It would not turn on. I checked again, and nothing appeared to be open. I then dried the exterior and opened it, only to discover there was water on the inside. I immediately removed the SD card, in hopes of salvaging it, but the camera was (is) completely dead.

Two days later, there is corrosion forming on the inside from the water, but at least I salvaged the content on the SD card. The results? Video quality is fine above and below water. Photo quality is a mess. Absolutely the worst pics imaginable.
I am so glad I didn't have to pay for this product; I would have been furious it didn't even last a day in the ocean.
