Without repeating what everyone has said here, I will speak for Roku's support of the Plex media streaming software which is a free Roku channel. If you have never heard of it, it is a fantastic solution that allows you to use Roku (as well as all your portable devices and remote computers, including ones on the internet-at-large) to stream all of the movies on your computer, regardless of the format. On Roku, you can browse the movie collection on your computer using a slick interface and watch it in full resolution. (This is only if you have a fast connection like a home wireless network, and you need to configure it to do this- an easy settings change.) If your computer can play it, so can your Roku. The key to this is because all the transcoding of the video file happens on your computer so all Roku has to do is play the video stream. The result is that you can easily fast-forward and rewind, as well and have the jump-back feature like the TiVo has. This was the primary reason that I bought the Roku as it is a lot easier to use than trying to connect your computer directly to your TV and muddling about with computer controls to watch movies. The Plex interface on Roku is easy to use and very slick. It does nice things like look up movie data so you have the cover art, theme music, and movie info for you to peruse as you are browsing your library. Finally, there is the "Plex it!" feature which you can use with your computer's browser, so that when you find a video on the internet on your computer, you want to queue it up for later to watch on your TV, and it will appear in your movie queue in Plex on Roku, regardless of the video format! This also gets around the one annoying thing about Roku and that it doesn't have a native YouTube channel for some reason.

Overall I'm very pleased with these ear buds. They are my first pair of bluetooth buds and it has been wonderful to not have to deal with cords, especially when working out. I can't tell you how many times I've hit an earbud cord while exercising and ripped the ear bud from my ear. A real pain in the neck (and ear!).

>>>Pros:

Comfort - These fit very well in my ear. There are different tip sizes to create a good fit and, after trying them all out, I went with the medium size. Very comfortable to wear even for long periods of time.

Stay put - I've yet to have them fall out even when doing aerobic exercises or while on the treadmill.

Sound - they sound pretty good. The sound is not as good as my favorite (and inexpensive) corded buds ([[ASIN:B0053R0WWG RHA MA-350 Aluminium Noise Isolating In-Ear Earphones]]) but they are a solid B+ performer with regard to bass response and overall clarity. Keep in mind that good bass response is affected by how the buds fit in your ear, so it's important to try out different tip sizes to see how they affect sound quality. They do get harsh at loud volumes, but for normal listening they are more than fine for my non-audiophile ears. They do reasonably well at blocking out ambient noise.

Setup - I found it straightforward even though I've never had any experience with setting up bluetooth earbuds.

Size - nice and compact so you don't get the "radar dish" look that larger units can have.

Durability - they have a "sweat proof" guarantee which is nice (although I imagine, like most guarantees, there are some loopholes). Overall build quality is good, with a very solid feel to all components.

>>>Cons:

Battery life - The manufacturer claims a battery life of 4.5 hours but I've yet to get more than 3 hours off a single charge. Plus there's no warning about battery life (until you're almost fully discharged) or a visual indicator of how much charge there is left.

Usability - the buttons on the buds are too small, making it difficult for me to push the right one. A lot of fumbling and mis-presses, making it often easier to deal with volume changes on the device, which kills some of the value of having wireless buds. I guess I lack the nimble fingers of the primary target market.

But overall, I'm pleased. The pros outweigh the cons, and I think this is a solid 4-star device.

As befits its price tag, the Sony has the look of a budget receiver with its old-school silver chassis. Build quality is decent enough: the fascia has a mixture of polished buttons and knobs including an input selector and volume control. The unit's remote control will be familiar to some - it features styling similar to the remotes that come with Sony's W Series of LCD TVs.

Before we get stuck into how the SRT-DG820 sounds, it's worth noting that Sony went back to the drawing board for its whole 2008 receiver range. And the Japanese giant has introduced various new features that, it claims, help improve performance.

For starters, the chassis of the STR-DG820 has been strengthened and embossed in certain places to help control any nuisance vibrations and minimize their effect on the key video/audio components found at the rear of the receiver.

High-definition audio decoding

Sony has even used custom-made brackets to secure the front panel and chassis and improve rigidity. The key video circuitry has been positioned as close as possible to the receiver's HDMI inputs for a shorter signal path and minimal interference.

The STR-DG820 offers 7.1 channels of surround sound (100w per channel) and can decode all major high-definition audio formats, including Dolby Digital TrueHD and DTS-HD Master Audio.

An inquisitive look around the rear of the receiver reveals a good selection of sockets. These include four HDMI inputs, (including a dedicated Blu-ray input), one HDMI output and three sets of component video inputs. The receiver also includes one coaxial and three optical digital inputs.

However, there is one notable omission: multichannel analogue inputs. So, your player has to be able to stream the HD data through HDMI for everything to work properly. In addition - not that you'd really expect them at this price - there are no pre-outs.

At this point it's also worth pointing out that the STR-DG820 can't upscale (Sony's step-up 'ES' range can upscale to 1080p), nor can it upconvert (again, the 'ES' range can). These features aren't vital, but upconversion would have been a welcome addition.

Sky HD usability issues

It also has to be noted that early versions of this receiver have had compatibility issues with Sky HD, which does not carry surround sound via its HDMI connection.

When you hook the Sky HD box's HDMI feed into the Sony and the Sky HD surround sound in via an optical input, the receiver over-rides the optical so you only hear the stereo feed supplied via HDMI.

Sony is working on a fix that will be applied to all existing and future STR-DG820 models. In the meantime, you can get round the issue by connecting your Sky HD via HDMI directly to your TV or projector, and via optical through the receiver - in this way you'll get both HD pictures and full surround sound.

Silky sound, dynamic dialogue

But back to the receiver in action. Set-up is done through Sony's Digital Cinema Auto Calibration system. It's ridiculously quick, easy to use and accurate - the receiver takes just a few seconds to set up.

And, hooked up to a Blu-ray player such as the Panasonic DMP-BD30, the Sony sounds sensational. Fed the Dolby TrueHD soundtrack from Batman Begins, the STR-DG820 impresses with its solid, controlled sound.

When Batman's Tumbler causes havoc on the streets of Gotham City, the Sony delivers explosions with a fine sense of immediacy and impact. Bass notes don't wallow or linger. In fact, you soon forget you're listening to a `budget' receiver.

The Sony is a dab hand at dialogue, too. Voices sound full-bodied and boast exceptional clarity, even during the most boisterous action scenes. There's no trace of brashness or harshness in the sound that could prove tiresome over prolonged listening.

Sure, more expensive receivers can give you a greater spread of sound and greater scale but, for this sort of money, the STR-DG820 is an absolute star.

It's equally adept at music

Dare we say it, the Sony also sounds adept when it comes to CD playback. Press the Analog Direct button to turn off all unnecessary internal processing and the receiver's clear, composed sound once again comes to the fore.

It exhibits a fine sense of rhythm for an AV receiver and dishes out decent bass weight during Eminem's Without Me.

I received this as a free review sample. The reason why I docked it a star is the active tablet window needs improvement (and that could have been one of the stand-out features if properly designed.) Here is the problem: it's the perfect size for an iPad Air 2, but could not accommodate my Tab 2 10.1 inch tablet. It did hold my Samsung Tab Pro 8.4 (even in an Otterbox Defender case). The vinyl window wrinkles and also reduces sensitivity when you interact with your tablet.

If the active tablet window is unimportant to you, then the rest of this backpack is a winner. Pairing my phone to the bluetooth speakers was as simple as flipping a switch and scanning for it on my phone's settings. And the speakers are loud with better than expected sound quality. I was pleased with that - some thought went into the speakers.

The padding is more than ample for protecting electronics, and there are sufficient pockets for the geekiest geek. What I like, though, is the storage areas are not overly complex. I own a Booq bag that is a storage dream come true, but almost requires a photographic memory to remember were all of the pockets are. This one is designed much simpler, but still efficient and effective.

Construction (except for the active tablet window) is first rate. The tablet window is marred by a difficult zipper, whereas all of the other zippers on this bag are sturdier and smooth. The outer fabric seems tough (I have not had it long enough to make any claims beyond that), and all of the seams are reinforced, straight and tight.

It's very comfortable and can be adjusted to evenly distribute the weight of a fully loaded pack. Considering that the bag itself is somewhat heavy this is a major plus for me.

I do want to note one thing about the backup battery: it is rated at (and stores) the full 4000mAh. However, like all batteries using this one's technology it's only 70% efficient, so expect about 2800mAh of usable capacity. That is not a flaw in this bag, but a reality that I wanted to point out so your expectations are properly set.

Overall, this is a well made bag with some innovative features (battery back-up and bluetooth speakers). If the active tablet window is not an important feature it's definitely worth considering. This one will be replacing my Booq because the storage is there without the complexity.

I love the look and feel of this VERSO "DARWIN" CROCCO standing cover for the Kindle Fire HD 8.9" tablet. Red is my favorite color, and the faux crocodile texture is really fun.

This cover holds the tablet firmly with silicone-enhanced elastic corner bands (patent pending). The bands have a rubbery material on the underside of the elastic that grips the surface beneath it, so the tablet does not slide around inside the cover or want to fall out. (I have screen protector film on my tablet, which seems like a good idea when a tablet is held in place by elastic bands rather than a hard plastic shell. This [[ASIN:B009NHU556 3-Pack Ultra-Clear Screen Protector)]] is easy to apply, and you get three chances to get it on right.)

The cover's built-in stands are quite intriguing. There are two of them attached to the inside of the front cover. One stand supports the tablet at a low angle for typing; the other supports it more or less upright for watching movies. Both provide comfortable viewing angles. The stands themselves are flat, microfiber-covered pieces that match the rest of the cover's interior. You pick the stand angle you want, and open out the appropriate stand. The stand is connected to the cover on top and also with a ribbon underneath, so that the stand converts into a triangular support for your tablet. This design is very clever, and I would consider it perfect if I hadn't already tried the [[ASIN:B009X0167Y Marware Vibe Standing Case]], which is a little easier to set up and offers more viewing angles.

This Verso "Darwin" Crocco cover has an elastic band that holds it tightly closed inside a book or tote bag, as well as an automatic magnetic wake/sleep feature. For the wake/sleep feature to work, you must insert your tablet with the camera at the left and the charging port at the right. This I don't like, because the charging port ends up at the tablet's bottom edge when you use the stands. This means you are limited to using the low-angle stand whenever your tablet is plugged in, because the plug contacts the table top. (With the Marware Vibe cover, the charging port ends up at the tablet's top edge, so you can use the tablet at any angle when it's plugged in.)

According to the accompanying retail literature, this Verso "Darwin" Crocco cover is "compatible" with the Kindle Fire HD 8.9", the Nook HD+, "and more". Because the cover holds the tablet with elastic bands, it should fit any tablet near in size to the large Fire or the large Nook. However, it is definitely too small for an iPad 2.

For me, it's difficult to choose between the Marware Vibe cover and the Verso "Darwin" cover. But in the end, as usually happens, good looks win out. My 8.9" Kindle Fire HD tablet is going to stay in the red faux-crocodile-skin cover, which is eye-catching, looks and feels luxurious, and is extremely well made.

This mini tripod is a pretty good basic design, but to work in practice I had to cut a couple of inches off the center post and swap out the head for a decent ball head. The plastic pan head is simply not strong enough to hold anything but a point and shoot. Certainly not a D800. The head's main problem is the plastic hinge that allows the camera to be rotated into vertical. It's supposed to be an additional feature but makes the head so "floppy" that at best you can only shoot static shots: forget panning or tilting during a video take. It's also very difficult to level the horizon. That hinge again. It simply can't be tightened enough to hold the camera level.

The suction cup on the center post is supposed to attach to a flat surface, but the surface has to be perfect to work. Not likely. The cup deteriorated after a couple of years, too, becoming superfluous. Worse, with the legs retracted to their shortest (and most stable) position the center post has to be extended upwards. Now the camera is really top heavy and, again, the whole thing is unstable.

I speak from trying to shoot video clips in Washington DC, where you aren't allowed to use a full-sized tripod. So I carried this little guy, setting it on domed trash receptacles or benches. Those domes together with That excessively long center post made it almost impossible to use. It wasn't up to the job. I came home and shortened the center post, removed the pan head and replaced it with a sturdy ball head. Still can't really pan, but can at least level the horizon.

I'd recommend a different setup. After I got done cutting the center post and adding a [[ASIN:B000OODPTK Giottos MH1302-655 Professional Calibrated Ball Head with MH 655 Quick Release]] I should have gotten the [[ASIN:B00009UT1V SUNPAK MINI-PROPLUS/B Mini Tripod with Compact Ballhead]].

I've been shooting with my DSLR for a while now, and I never really had a use for film cameras until I got intrigued by the toy camera phenomenon that's been sweeping the nation. I thought about getting the Holga 120, but after doing extensive research on the cost of developing 120 film in my area (about $12 per roll, which has 12-16 exposures), I decided to go with the 35mm camera, where if I'm using Snapfish, i can get the whole roll developed for $3-5 for 36 exposures.

I must say, the Holga 135BC is a fun little camera! I took it on a trip to the mountains and got some great shots of the fall foliage. The vignetting (black corners) came out on about half the pictures; some of them came out without much vignetting at all, which was surprising. There haven't been any light leaks, which may disappoint some users, but I know there are some mods out there (involving drilling holes into the side of the body) to create that effect if you wish. Double exposures are quite easy to do. I recommend using ISO400 speed film for best effects, especially when you're just beginning. The aperture is pretty much set at something like f8 and the shutter speed is around 1/100 (though this can vary), so most indoor pictures and even outdoor pictures in overcast lighting came out dark and dismal. I kind of wish I had bought the one that comes with a flash unit (holga 15b) but I'm gonna purchase that separately. The ones I took in sunlight are great though, so i recommend taking your Holga outside on a pretty day for your first roll. As for loading and unloading the film, it's quite easy to do. Just remember to press the film release button on the bottom of the camera before you rewind your film to avoid stretching or ripping apart your exposed film.

Overall, i think that the Holga 135BC is a wonderful little camera, great for those of us trying out a plastic camera for the first time, and a great attention-getter in public. I would definitely recommend it!

When I first set up a home network, I selected a Cisco "Linkys" G router (EA1300) because I recognized the brand name. Later I upgraded to a Cisco dual-band N router ([[ASIN:B007IL7AKM Linksys EA4500]]), which was--and still is--a superb router. My latest upgrade, to this LINKSYS AC1900 (EA6900) DUAL BAND SMART WI-FI ROUTER, represents another leap forward in the performance of my home network.

The wireless signal is stronger in every corner of my two-story condo. All of my devices (some 25 computers, tablets, music players, Kindles, cellphones, Roku, etc.) connect very quickly. Best of all, I'm getting Comcast's promised high-speed Internet speeds of more than 50 Mbps with the Comcast-supplied new telephony modem. (An online speed test site just now clocked the download speed at 57 Mbps). In fact, my present home network is capable of even faster speeds--the home network is limited by the speed of the slower external Comcast network.

This router is extremely easy to set up. You just connect it, and follow the prompts from the built-in software. Whenever you access the router to adjust the settings, and click on some part of the Menu, you find excellent "contextual" help screens that fully explain the meaning of each of the settings. The Menu is set up differently from the menus for the EA4500 and EA1300, but the basic methodology for the settings is the same--the settings are just presented in a way that's easier for a non-techie user to understand.

I read a newspaper review that recommended NOT buying this excellent EA6900 router, because of testers' problems with the second band and with nonfunctioning USB ports. I think that the testers probably received a defective router--and should have requested a replacement. Even a reliable brand like Cisco may sometimes ship an occasional bad electronics device.

Because I only need a single-band router, I haven't tested the second band on my EA6900 router. (The second band did work fine on my EA4500 router, but using the second band didn't improve the signal strength, so I didn't continue using it.) However, I did test the USB ports on the EA6900, and both work really well. In fact, the router recognized and easily accessed a couple of external wireless storage drives--connected with a 100-foot (!) USB cable--when my PC was flakey about recognizing those same drives when they were connected directly to the PC with the long cable.

I absolutely love this EA6900 router, which I've been using for more than a month now. Because of my home wiring, the router is located a long way from any of my wireless devices, and I have a lot of nearby neighbors with competing wireless Internet connections. But with the EA6900, there have been virtually no dropped connections, and the strong signal is something that I've long been wishing for!

I ordered the 'Soundcore Wakey Bluetooth Speaker Powered by Anker with Alarm Clock, Stereo Sound, FM Radio, White Noise, QI Wireless Charger with 7.5W Charging for iPhone and 10W for Samsung' for review and would like to share some of my thoughts after a few weeks.

First off, this thing is actually pretty amazing. The build quality is nice and aesthetically it looks clean. The sound quality is nice but not phenomenal. However for how small it is, it does produce decent sound and for a bedside alarm clock it does quite well. The wireless charging works great for my Galaxy Note 8 (and does in fact Fast-Charge) however there have been a couple nights to where my phone was not charged the next morning. The fast charger also works with my wireless earbuds which I attached an image showing the charge light on the Wakey, and the wireless earbuds case indicating charging. However for the wireless earbud charging, it does take some precise positioning to get them to charge. I noticed in other review that others weren't happy with the bright display light with no way to adjust it any dimmer than the lowest setting, however they must have updated that with a firmware update (which was super easy to do) as I had no issues with the display being too bright at night. I use the auto adjust setting which seems to work quite well as far as I can tell. Also I love the sleep mode sounds that you can adjust several (or just one) sound volumes to create your own personalized preference. I do wish that there were more sound options but the ones they provide are acceptable. I also wish that you could download and install more alarm sounds. Bluetooth connectivity is super quick and have never once had an issue with pairing it up to my phone. Really the ONLY issue I have with the Wakey is that to get the sleep mode sounds going, you need to connect with the app, and via Bluetooth connect to the device. No big deal right? Well my concern is that you will need to keep it connected for this feature to work. This means you will be connected to the Wakey ALL night and this kind of bugs me. It's just kind of creepy that the Wakey is connected to your phone all night while you sleep. I wish there was a way to just play your favorite white noise sleep sound by pressing a button on the Wakey device without having to always connect and stay connected to the app and your phone. The other gripe is that the plug design is huge and makes it so that I have had to move my nightstand further way from the wall to use it. Other than those two gripes, and the only reason for docking one star, the Soundcore Wakey is a very good product and a really great value.
*On a side note - I just tested the Wakey while watching some Youtube videos and the latency is not so good. There is quite a bit of delay and the voices do not sync up at all so I wouldn't recommend using the Wakey for listening to videos.

Overall, this is a pretty decent gaming mouse (although it also works well as a “regular” mouse). It’s corded, which I prefer since cordless mice are usually troublesome with regard to maintaining a connection and having to recharge the battery. This is a traditional USB corded design that works very well.

The cord is braided, which is a great feature since it helps ensure the cord doesn't get hung up or pinched in use. Very well done.

The mouse itself is comfortable, with well-sculpted sides for comfort. The two buttons on the right are easy to find with your thumb, have a nice click to them, and have raised dots to help keep your finger from slipping off. The scroll wheel is similarly well-made, with a smooth feel and slight indents when used for fine-tuned movements. The DPI selection switch is right behind the scroll wheel for easy access. DPI selection is 800/1200/1600/2400.

Note that this is for right-handed use only (sorry lefties!).

Zero problems with installation (plug and play) on a Win 7 machine.

Misses are mainly on two issues: build quality and the casing. The build quality is pretty lightweight. While it’s working fine at the moment, the build quality doesn't give me the feeling that this would survive much punishment, such as being dropped on the ground. It has a more cheap feel than my Logitech mouse.

The casing is a plus and a minus. A plus in that it is a rubberized-type coating that offers good non-slip benefits. But it’s a dust and dirt magnet, and the rubberized coating makes it hard to clean. I would have rather seen a smooth surface with isolated grip points that are rubberized, rather than the full mouse.

The misses knock it down to 4.5 stars, but I’ll round up given the overall attractive look and excellent performance. Well worth considering if you’re looking for a corded mouse.

I wanted to find a cheaper alternative to my wife's wireless Bose headset, something with decent noise cancelling for flights and work. So far I've used Bose, the MPOW H5, Treblab, and Woltix with ANC.

Nothing will compare to Bose noise cancellation - but these Woltix are actually really nice for the money. The MPOW H5 don't have as good audio clarity as the Treblab, but at the end of the day I got noise cancelling headphones for the noise canceling. I ended up returning the Treblab and the MPOW H5 and I kept the Woltix because they are more comfortable than the MPOW and had the best low-price ANC. The MPOW also had some sound interference issues randomly when the ANC was on, and the Treblab had a slight hiss to them when ANC was on.

I ended up keeping the Woltix brand. They just work, they're very light, and they are not too tight on the ears. The Active Noise Cancellation isn't as good as Bose, but they actually work pretty well for a $65 set of wireless ANC headphones. For the price, I'm very happy.

The ONLY thing I don't like about these is that there is no battery meter display on my iPhone when these are connected via bluetooth. With the other brands there is a small battery meter. I have no idea when these are low, so I just charge them like once a week.

So, quick breakdown of my experience with these wireless ANC headsets:

Bose: Best noise cancellation, good audio, comfortable, but definitely expensive!
Treblab: Best audio, worst noise cancellation (you can hear a slight hiss when turned on), comfortable, but large and they don't fold down too small.
MPOW: Good audio, good noise cancellation, but was getting some weird sound interference with the ANC on sometimes. Tight on ears.
Woltix: Good audio, good noise cancellation, most comfortable (way lighter and less tight on the ears than the MPOW), and fold down the smallest. No battery meter displayed on phone.

Summary:
I bought this kit because I needed to recover the data on an 80GB Hitachi 1.8" Drive from a dead Vaio notebook. No setup was required after I finished installing the drive in the enclosure, and it was recognized and read on my XP machine without a fuss. The enclosure is a thin aluminum extrusion with channels on the inside. The end caps appear to be pot metal castings. One end cap contains the interface board with LED activity light and the USB connector. A USB cable is provided. The kit is cheaply made but did what I needed.

Installation:
Installation consisted of mating a flex cable and connector, sliding the drive and active end cap into the enclosure, and screwing in the end cap(s).

It takes a bit of care and patience to insert the flex cable into the connector on the drive, but I was able to get it done in a few minutes.
The cable needs to be made to assume an S-bend after attaching it to the drive so that the entire assembly will fit into the box. That is best accomplished by gently pushing the end cap and HDD together and guiding the cable into an S. I suggest you place the assembly next to the enclosure first so you can see how much length the bend will need to take up. It's not much. Then, slide the drive into the enclosure followed by the cable and end cap, gently guiding the cable bend as needed. Make sure the end cap fits properly in place before and while you install the screws.

Here's the part I deducted a star for: The screws go into unthreaded channels in the enclosure and their alignment is less than perfect. It took quite a while and a better screwdriver than is provided to get the screws fully seated. YMMV.

If the drive rattles around more than you like front to back, you may wish to install one or two of the stick-on rubber bumpers that are provided onto the far end of the HDD or the inside of the blank end cap. Be aware you'll have to deal with two more screws if you put them inside the end cap.

This is my first experience with Ultrabooks. Up to this point I have worked with laptops that are designed to be desktop replacement systems or family entertainment systems, so the journey into the land of Ultrabooks is a new one for me. So far, I have mixed feelings about this system, mostly due to HP's recovery media creation tool, but my overall impression is a good one so far.

In terms of size, this is a very thin and dainty notebook computer, roughly the size of a fat magazine. This gives it a very small footprint and it is relatively lightweight, making it good for stuffing in a briefcase or carry-on bag (though there are better cases for this kind of thing). I set it up on the kitchen table and as soon as my wife saw it she exclaimed "It's so cute!" Indeed, it's an attractive machine.

One of the things that caught my attention when reading the specifications on this machine is that there was no mention at all of a DVD drive. The packing materials even state "no optical drive". Sure enough, there is none so loading up software will require a USB DVD drive or a properly loaded thumb drive. This is not a huge deal but it is something that must be kept in mind - not everyone will appreciate having to get an additional drive just to load up software. I am not sure if HP offers a DVD R/W drive as an accessory kit.

There are exactly two USB ports on this notebook - one USB 2.0 port and one USB 3.0 port. For the traveler working on a plane or a student taking notes in a class, this does not matter. However, when working at a desk and getting synchronized with the office computer having only two USB ports may be problematic. This can be overcome by using a hub, but again this requires extra hardware. It all depends on the usage - two ports may be plenty. In my case and for my purposes, two is usually sufficient.

There is also an HDMI port, an Ethernet jack and an audio output jack. As is typical with most laptops, this one has an SD card reader. What this notebook does not have, though, is a VGA or DVI output. This is not necessarily a problem as this is a notebook made for someone on the go, but it does mean that connecting to a projector requires using another method.
This notebook is Bluetooth capable. This is a good thing for a lot of people. For me, though, it is less important as I have no Bluetooth accessories. I do appreciate the availability though so that I can connect accessories to it in the future.

Screen type is important to many people - glossy, matte, anti-glare... This particular system has a very bright and clear glossy screen which is fine for me but may disagree with others who dislike the reflections that occur and the glare from lights. Keep this in mind.

Pleasantly, there is not a huge amount of "bloatware" on this system. Looking through the list of installed software, HP has not overly cluttered the drive with extra stuff that you won't need (though there is some stuff that I know I will never, ever use). MS Office is preloaded as is Norton Internet Security - these are simple to uninstall if there is no need for them. That said, HP and Symantec have arranged a two-year license on Norton Internet Security which is outstanding for a new system right out of the box - every system I have seen up to this point came with only 60-90 days of updates for the bundled internet security suite.

My first order of business when I brought the system up was to launch the recovery media creation tool. I plugged in my DVD drive, kicked off the process, and burned 9 DVDs on the way to making a set of 5 recovery DVDs. The process errored out repeatedly, complaining of errors though the DVD media I have has been reliable. I am not sure if there is a weakness in the creation tool, the DVD drive or the platters, but the process took a lot longer than it should have taken. Regardless, there is something else about the process that is even more troublesome - HP allows you to make ONE and only one copy of the recovery media. If one of the five DVDs goes bad, then it's all over. This is specific to HP - Sony and Asus both allow you to make multiple copies, and my other HP laptop enforced the same limit of one copy.

I dug into the performance measurement tool and the system reports a Windows Experience number of 5.6, driven by the graphics chipset (and it was the desktop graphics, not the gaming graphics, that was low). The highest number was actually the SS hard drive at 8.1, even outscoring the CPU and memory! This is a snappy little system and while it's not built for heavy gaming it has enough horsepower to handle many games.

Relating to performance - because of the solid-state drive, power-on to operational time is less than 10 seconds. I absolutely love how fast this machine boots up!

I am no fan of touchpads and to be honest I find the touchpad on this notebook worse than average. It is raised which makes it too easy to inadvertently tap it while typing, and because of the way it is raised it's too easy to get stuff in the crevices around it.

As far as traveling with this notebook, it should be said that there are smaller, more portable machines out there. This one has a 13.3" screen but I have seen much smaller systems. Then again, these smaller systems usually have less power and are less capable. It comes down to whether you prefer more compactness at the expense of power or more power at the expense of compactness.

This system comes preloaded with Windows 8. In a nutshell I find it to resemble a cross between Windows 7 and MS Zune. I am not going to go into a full review of Windows 8 but I will very briefly summarize - though it's best suited for tablets, it actually works nicely on this notebook and though there is a learning curve it's not bad.

Finally, I should mention the speaker system. My very first HP laptop came with Altec Lansing speakers built in to the unit. This system comes with Beats audio, and I have found them to be roughly equivalent. Sound quality is very good, especially coming from such a small machine.

HP has put together a very nice system in this Ultrabook. It is small, fast and powerful. I do not like the way it builds recovery media (and restricts you to a single copy), and I am a little bit concerned by not having more than 2 USB ports, but when considering that this machine is built for the traveler or student, this is a very nice system that's worth a look.

The ports are well-anchored, with no movement even when I over-stressed an attached cable. The power input is on one end; the USB input on the other. But the case issues aside, this is a good performing hub that offers 7 USB 3.0 ports. Good choice if you’re short on desktop space.

I recently purchased a new zoom lens for my camera after I broke the old one when I took a tumble. I had filters like these for my old lens but the thread size was different so my old filters were no longer useful. I selected this filter for my new lens, somewhat apprehensively because of the relatively low asking price. It has proven to be a decent filter but it is not useful in all situations.

The idea behind this filter is light diffusion which will give an image a very slight haze or softness, depending on the lighting and subject. This is an effect that can be emulated in software during post-processing but in doing this type of enhancement I have found it is sometimes unnatural. It certainly is less fun than making it happen while shooting, which is why these types of filters are available.

In use it works, though I have had mixed results. When using it with certain light sources, the filter seems to have no real effect at all, while with others it creates a subtle, soft glow around the subject. I am still working out the situations where it is most effective. I have had similar issues with filters like these with other lenses, and as such I assume the problem is in my lack of practice with them. It will take some time and practice to make my results more consistent, and for now I lay the fault on myself.

The build quality seems to be good. I have received filters in the past where the glass rattles in the frame which is unsettling. This one is tight and there is no play between the glass and the frame. It screws on to the lens securely and is easy to clean.

The asking price is quite reasonable. I have seen these filters priced much higher, and I have also seen much cheaper ones that do not work well. The pricing seems in line with the product, if not slightly low.

I have no complaints with this filter. The issues I have with it are probably my inexperience, and I will keep working with it to improve my results. I will return here and update my review if my impression changes. For now, though, I am satisfied.

This review is for the TP-LInk Mesh WiFi M5 system.
—————
Amended April 28, 2020
Now that I’ve been using this for a couple weeks, I am returning to add these units HAVE NOT cured the dead spots that needed more signal strength. Yes, the WiFi signal is present in those areas of my home. However, the signal strength has not improved over what my centrally located router produced on its own. Essentially for my roughly $125, I got a couple stylish WiFi access points. What I DID NOT GET is the improved coverage promoted in the description.
—————
This IS NOT a plug it in and it works system. You need to know at minimum:
—Your current router’s IP address, the user ID for it, and the password. If you haven’t changed them from the default, you have no business installing a network anything, because you put EVERYTHING on your system at high risk for hacking. Why? The problem is that the default user ID and password are the SAME FOR ALL routers of the same brand (every brand router has a published default user id and password).
—You need to know which of several comm protocols your ISP uses.
—You need to know that IF YOU SWAP OUT YOUR ROUTER for one of the units, the others WILL NOT WORK to extend your WiFi network. For that you need to set these up as extenders, with the first being connected to your existing router.
—To set up a network of WiFi extenders, you need to know how to turn your existing router’s WiFi transmission off. Only then can you use these as extenders, satellites, or whatever you know them as.
—You are highly likely to have to update the firmware on each M5 device.
—You should set aside about two to three hours to set up a network of multiple devices.
—If you set these up as extenders, some of the default security features are switched off. You need to be sure these security features are enabled on your router instead.

I am so very pleased with these headphones. I was expecting them to sound pretty good given the Sennheiser lineage, but they really set me back on my heels with the sound quality, comfort, and overall design.

Let's start with the easy one - how they look. To my eye, they are very nicely styled. Classic-looking rather than flashy. I especially like how the headband is not excessively padded -- it does not stick out when you wear them. Very elegant overall. Everything looks and feels high quality.

They also hit the mark regarding comfort. I usually have a 1 hour limit when it comes to over-the-ear headphones, in that after an hour of wearing them I've reached my limit of tolerance. These, however, felt wonderful. They are light enough that I hardly noticed the weight. More importantly, the ear cups fit me just right. Cushy enough to seal out ambient noise but not at the expense of having my ears feel like they were trapped in a vice. They felt just as good well into hour 2 as they did in the first 15 minutes. I found the headband also very comfortable for long stretches without getting "sweaty head" as I get with other headphones.

But it's the sound that counts. To my ear, these `phones deliver in spades. I started off with some Stanley Clarke. Wonderful -- ample bass but not at the expense of hearing every string being plucked. I listened to School Days a couple of times in a row, just amazed at how good it sounded. The same for Florence and the Machine -- solid, deep bass but not overwhelming.

Next up was Metric to see how vocals come through. Again, superb. I was finally able to figure out some of the lyrics on Synthetica that never came through clear enough on my ear buds. Regina Spektor was also an absolute pleasure to listen to and have all facets of her unique vocal styling come through so clearly.

I also tried them for movie watching on my Fire, and again was very pleased. Dialog was clean and pronounced; explosions were, well, explosive.

The noise isolation is quite good. These are not noise cancelling headphones, so some ambient noise will leak in, but it keeps out everything other than the most significant ambient sounds.

I really can't fault these on any criterion. They look great, feel great, and sound great. Granted, the price is not so great, but good quality costs. If you're a demanding headphone user, these are worth the money charged. Highly recommend.

I bought this camera for my wife last summer when she was in China. She was looking for something with less shutter lag than our last generation of Nikon and Canon digital point-and-shoots, and something cute and portable. The Panasonic DMC-FX30 is both of these things.

Out of the box it overexposed and undercolored things, but this was easily fixable after fiddling with the settings menu. Even set up right, photos using the flash still look too shiny whit, and photos taken at high ISOs are pretty noisy. The lack of a real viewfinder also makes capturing action clunky, but this is obviously in part an artifact of my preferences. This camera takes fine outdoor pictures, and the wide angle zoom allows for some cool shots and works well in confined (well-lit) spaces.

The camera is a small, precision-made jewel of a camera, with controls and buttons designed for smaller hands than mine; they fit my wife fine. We both missed the lack of a real viewfinder; pocket cameras seem to making an unfortunate departure from this useful standard (bright sunlight washes the display out, and it's easier to take a picture from your eye, as that's what you're composing with in the first place). The camera performed fine in its role as a city camera in Beijing, and for snapping quick shots back home when lugging the SLR around was inconvenient.

Now, however, we are in rural China for a year doing field work, and I was using the Panasonic as a backup to my Nikon DSLR. It was nice having a wide-angle lens in a pouch in my pocket when I had my normal or telephoto primes on the SLR. The Panasonic worked great in this role for 3-weeks, and then the automatic lens cap froze shut and wouldn't open, despite my coaxing, cleaning, etc. I finally just pried it off so I can still use the camera (I keep a business card over the lens in the soft pocket pouch), but let's say that I am not impressed with the camera's durability, compared to any other camera I've had, film or digital. It never got wet, dusty, dropped, or sat on; it looks brand new, but the lens cap won't work, and failed in a way that renders the camera useless to someone unwilling to take pliers to a Leica lens (failing and staying open would be preferable).

Anyway, if you're looking for a field or reliable travel camera, pass this one up.

Tired of cramped cases? Pain in the butt to get nice cable run cases? Having to remove a hard-drive to get a graphics card out? Having to remove a graphics card to take out a HD? Tired of black cases?

I love this case. But it's bigger than it looks in the picture and it's wider than it looks here. Which was not a problem because I checked the size before ordering.

So whats to love about this case. I'm going to try to skip what is obviuos unless it's something I really like about the case.

It's not black
It's quiet even with the stock fans. It wouldn't take much work to make this REALLY quiet.
The audio and USB panels are on the top.
All the 'guts' are on the bottom of the case and laid out in a way that makes it very easy to cable everything together compared to mid/mini tower cases
The rear panel (for all the ports) sits flush on the back of the computer and the computer back is flat. It makes it much easier to see the ports when you bend over the top of the case. Each port has a colored ring around it the same color of the colors of the plug making it very easy to see where what plugs in.
The HDD fit great without a screw in sight and mount in a what that makes connecting them really easy. They are also rubber mounted to help quiet the HDD.
All the screws are in little baggies with a sticker saying what they are for.
The CD/DVD drive mount has to two sets of holes for mounting. One set of hoses is in set positions, and for me they put my drive just about right with the front of the case. But there are also longer slots for the mounting screws so you can slide the drive back and forth to get it to sit exactly where you want your CD/DVD drive fit in the front of the case.
There is room for cabling to run next to the motherboard sides keeping cables away from the top of the motherboard. There is a lot of room under the top of the case (if you don't use extra fans there) to coil up extra wire/cables. If you wanted you could do a very clean cable installation.
It's VERY easy to plug in the ATX power connector and more important easy to take off (which was a real frustration on my old case)
There is a lot of room in general to work in this case for a micro ATX case. You can take the top off and both sides to work inside the case.
The thumb screws holding the sides on are nice and large and both sides come of easily.
This is the first case I have had that has dedicated brackets for 2.5" SSDs. The brackets have rubber grommets you attach to the sides of the SSD. That then slide into grooves holding the drive loosely by the rubber grommets. Seems overkill for a SSD drive that has no moving parts but it works.

A few random thoughts

The top can be a little finicky to get off. But on the good side it fits well when it's in place. Sits nice and flat etc.
The plastic slide that latches the top in place is a very simple plastic latch and can pop out pretty easily. ( I don't know where/when I accidentally popped off but when I went to pickup the top the latch was on the floor) But it does what it is supposed to do and has not come off in normal use.

The bracket to hold the expansion cards in place is a clever design (no screws) but takes two hands to close and you have to wiggle the cards/brackets around a bit to get to get the holding mechanism closed again.

A solid 5 stars from me

Edit at the nearly 4 year point: I'm a single person who doesn't actually watch a lot of television - at less than the four year point, the picture is going bad on this. I get large purple spots on bright/white parts of scenes on several spots on the screen (about half the screen at this time). Makes it very annoying to watch some shows - especially cartoons, which often have vibrant/bright colors. It also show up on the menus, as they have rather bright backgrounds. Not sure I'd trust an LG tv again. There was a time when an expensive tv would easily last for 20+ years. Four years at this price is ridiculous.

First the good. For the most part, this tv has a nice picture with almost uniform blacks (my lower left is always bright). The DNLA server is nice if you have a home NAS or other media server. However, almost every other aspect of the smart TV features are not useful. The software is slow, the browser does not support modern flash or quicktime (Yes, sites that work on my iPad don't even work on this tv). The youtube software can not let you log in, so you have to do manual searches for everything, and it automatically plays sometimes inappropriate videos as soon as the software loads. IT IS NOT KID FRIENDLY! (Edit: The youtube software was ultimately updated and fixed, but this took quite a while for LG to do)

Now the foolish: One of my 4 VESA bolt sockets was mis-threaded, and no M8 or other bolt would fit in the hole. Clearly, cheap foreign parts with poor spec control. The speakers vibrate - a lot - even at low volumes. This is very annoying, forcing you to use a separate sound system to watch any television show (unless you like constant vibration from your speakers).

I would not recommend this tv to others - especially if you want to hang it on a wall or use the built in speakers.

EDIT: After a couple of months, it has stopped working with my Yamaha receiver. If I turn on the receiver, the signal drops to zero. I can watch this happen on the signal checking page. Also, if I plug my computer (and I would assume any device) into an HDMI in, the signal drops to zero (if the computer is on - if I turn off the receiver or computer, the signal comes back immediately). If you plan to use this tv to control your receiver or use a receiver to broadcast the sound, it will not work with television signals (works fine with DNLA). This sucks, as the speakers vibrate even on low volume.

Let me start off by saying I've owned Kindles and other e-readers so I can say I'm already somewhat familiar with the concept. I really like what I'm seeing here for the price of this product! This is a small / affordable e-ink device that makes it ideal for all kinds of things.
Personally, I'm a big fan of Overdrive to take books out of our local libraries for free on readers. My biggest complaint on Kindle readers is that this was always a hassle - I needed to do it ON A DIFFERENT DEVICE. A laptop or phone with a browser was necessary because you could not access Overdrive to explore content directly. On the Kobo, like other non-Amazon devices, you are free to browse directly on the reader, find a title you like and click borrow, all for FREE and 100% legal! This is a huge selling point to me. My kids can browse the YA and children's' section and find all kinds of content right on the device using an account they made with their local library card.
The screen is great for little hands as well as big hands, it even looks great displaying some graphic novel pages (albeit in greyscale obviously). I found that I had zero problems connecting to my Wifi, and downloading books is fast and easy. Battery life is excellent as well! The only caveat is that when you DO need to charge it, it's the slightly-older micro-USB charging plug. I wish it would have been a USB-C as most of our micro USB cables are being replaced with the new standard, and in 2021 its a little weird to still have a new product use an old standard... but this is a minor issue at best.

Some really cool mentions:
1) There IS an experimental web browser function. It's very limited, mostly due to the limitations of using E-ink instead of a display that can be updated faster like LCD/OLED, but super cool for browsing websites for text articles!
2) You can manually load a document to use as a screensaver!! This was a very cool find for me. There's a folder on the device when you plug it into your computer called .screensaver , and if you place a document in there (jpg, pdf, whatever) it will display it when the device is powered off / sleep. I actually put our weekend calendar information on there so we can refer to times / reminders, and stuck some magnetic strips to the back of the reader. Now it sits on our fridge when no one is reading, displaying our calendar and saving us at least one sheet of paper to print per month! Then whenever someone wants to read, my kids (or me!) can take it off the fridge, read a few pages, then put it back there for the next person. Because the Nia is a small and light tablet, it stays on really easily! My old Kindle was too large and fragile for that.

Way to go, Kobo!

I have been using Wacom Intuos and Bamboo tablets for years, not really for graphic arts but more for digital handwriting and for use as an alternative to traditional mice and trackballs. My present solution is an Intuos 5 medium which seems to be about the right fit for my hands and my work space. The one drawback has been that it’s a wired solution. This new Intuos is a Bluetooth solution and it is definitely a step forward. For me the challenge is downgrading to the small from the medium, but it’s a good fit for me when traveling and when working in cluttered spaces.

To approximate the size, it is roughly equivalent to 7” tablet in size. It’s small enough to tuck away in a corner of a desk when not in use, and when it is being used it does not take up large amounts of real estate. The design itself makes it suitable for use just about anywhere it can be set down and kept stable - one of the reasons I like drawing tablets more than traditional mice.

The Bluetooth connectivity is new to me, and I was pleasantly surprised to find that this unit can connect via USB as well. So, if your system is like one of mine and the Bluetooth doesn’t work, this drawing tablet still will work.

I have it connected to my Windows 10 system. I have not yet made the effort to get it working with my Linux system, though I expect there will be some labor involved to make that work. I’ll revisit that later.

In operation, this is a straightforward drawing tablet though it is an improvement over my Intuos 5 in some ways. Of course the Bluetooth is a step up, but I was surprised by the increased number of pressure levels which is effectively doubled over my old tablet - 4096 vs 2048. For someone like me, this is not a huge difference and I don’t take advantage, but for someone who is very serious about fine digital artwork this can be a huge benefit. For use in handwriting, it is not especially important as even 512 pressure levels (like my original Bamboo small) is more than sufficient.

When you register, you get a choice between three Corel titles, of which you can select two (for the medium you get all three). Some may find the choice difficult - Painter Essentials 6, AfterShot 6 and Clip Studio Paint Pro (2 years) - but for me, having AfterShot is more than enough.

There is a downside to this little tablet, though - the pen is mediocre. There is no comfort grip, changing the nib is a pain, and there’s a very limited number of replacement nibs for it. It’s the one weak spot in an otherwise nice product, and even then it’s not all that bad.

The hardest part for me with this specific tablet is the move from a medium to a small, but this this counterbalanced by the Bluetooth connectivity and the inclusion of the Corel titles, specifically AfterShot. This is a very nice drawing solution and is it priced nicely. I’d recommend the small for anyone either just getting started or experimenting; the medium is a better fit for those more experienced or needing more real estate. I would choose a different pen if available, though.

When I saw this I thought it would be a great addition to my camera gear. The description says it's good for DSLRs and up to six pounds. After opening and inspecting this monopod system I reluctantly tried my ultra-compact Sony WX9 camera on this mounting system. My conclusion is I can't and won't trust this rig with my WX9 let alone my much heavier mirrorless Fuji gear.

The padded extendable main monopod shaft consists of three sections that are secured with a twist. It's easy to not torque the sections hard enough for them to unexpectedly collapse while you're trying to take a picture.

The ball-head mounts, this system comes with two, are fairly smooth metal on metal construction. Alarmingly these have no secure locking system. You simply use your thumb to engage a friction locking system. All it takes is a tap to cause the ball-head to be completely free moving. I would never trust a camera I liked on these mounts.

There are two feet that come with this set. A rubber edged magnetic mount and a suction cup -
The magnet is too small for a secure mount. With the monopod vertical and not extended it was reasonably stable. Horizontally it felt unsafe set up in any configuration. Extending the monopod drastically increases the ease with which this tips over. The magnet is just not wide enough to be stable.
The suction cup mount was surprisingly strong but like every other securing point in this rig the slide to release the mount does not lock in place. It's just too easy to hit the release while trying to set things up. I had thought I could mount this low on the car to get some interesting video but after trying this out I'd be worried road vibration would cause this to release and drop the camera.

In conclusion: While the materials are of decent quality this system lacks security. I won't risk my cameras on it.

This is the first mesh system I've used. I had a Linksys router and an Asus router before this, both installed with third-party firmware. After the Asus upgrade, I used the Linksys router as a repeater. The signal was okay; considering I had Xfinity 250Mbps, the Asus worked fantastically, while the Linksys trailed behind. We live in an old apartment building with thick, plaster walls, so signal can be very spotty.

With this mesh system, I saw a huge upgrade the first week. Setup was very easy; quick instructions are provided. As soon as the setup was complete, I delved into the firmware. I recall being a little disappointed as I was used to the Asus custom firmware (Asuswrt-Merlin). The Asus firmware "just werqed." I run a small server, and setup was super easy with the Asus. With the Netgear, it was a lot more involved. Setting up outside ports was a pain; at the time, there was no simple way of forwarding ports. I recall a little workaround I was able to conduct with the server, but it took me days to figure out.

The firmware also lacks time restrictions for devices (at least of this writing). Asuswrt-Merlin allows me to set specific times to shut off internet for devices, which comes in handy with a large family.

As for the actual mesh system, so far so good. I can't tell when I'm using the main router or the satellite. The devices connect automatically without hiccup. I've since ditched Xfinity in favor of RCN 1Gbps; this mesh system works very well with the service. Once we have fiber, I can't wait to see the results.

I have come to understand the value of a good camera strap. It is more than just a designer item and more than just a simple strap to keep the camera hanging around your neck. It needs to be strong enough to keep the camera secure and it needs to be long enough to allow for grabbing the camera and taking a quick shot instead of having to struggle with getting the camera from around your neck and risk missing the shot by a second or two. The strap that came with my camera is functional but much too short and I expect it to rip eventually. This strap by Orota is a much better strap than that provided with my camera.

This is a well-made strap. One side is a heavy weave not unlike a car’s seat belt but not as smooth and shiny. It is also quite a bit thicker than a seat belt and will have no issue with supporting the camera. Sewn to it is a decorative layer that is also a heavy weave, similar to but not exactly like canvas. These are stitched together with heavy thread and I see little risk of them separating.

Each end is clamped with a leather reinforcement that is held in place with four metal rivets. The leather ends each hold a metal buckle with the thinner nylon straps that actually connect to the camera. Looking closely at each component I found no loose threads, no uneven seams, no flaws in fabric or materials. There is nothing about this strap that suggests it will fail under daily use.

This is a much longer strap than what came with my camera, measuring a little less than 3' long. I like the fact that with this trap attached to my camera I can lift my camera and quickly get the shot I want and I don’t have to take it from my neck in order to focus on it. I can hold it far enough from my face to actually focus on the camera. This is a very big improvement over my old strap which was short enough that I could not get the camera in front of my face at a comfortable distance.

This is a very well-made strap and I am very pleased with it. It is stylish, well constructed and it is long enough to make it much more useful to me than my old strap.

The WD_Black 1TB D50 Game Dock has quality written all over it. Metal construction for heat dissipation, thunderbolt support, nice RGB lighting, and a fast NVMe drive. It is quite obviously geared toward the PC Gaming crowd, but which segment?

The build of this product screams high-quality gaming accessory. Its outer design is reminiscent of a cargo container and its collection of ports are impressive. Each USB port is well labeled with its speed (4x 10Gb/s Type-A and 2x 10Gb/s Type-C), two thunderbolt ports, one of which outputs 87 watts of power, one displayport, one network port (gigabit), and one 3.5mm headphone jack. Add to this, the 1TB high-performance NVMe drive. All in one sleek-looking, compact container (pun intended).

It is obvious that this dock is geared toward the Gaming Laptop crowd, whether its for gaming or for video/graphics production work, but I find that it really doesn't make sense for me. In my tests, this product does not work without the power adapter (it really should be able to power itself through the thunderbolt port). This means an additional outlet that's drawing power at all times. This would make sense if gaming laptops can actually be powered and charged from the 87w thunderbolt port but I have not seen a gaming pc with discreet graphics that actually accepts anything in that range.

So what other advantage would this product provide? External storage through a fast Thunderbolt connection. At $450, this product provides 1TB of additional storage. Which 2TB NVMe drives available for much less, I would opt to upgrade my internal storage to 2TB instead.

Then that leave the docking station. The ports are all of the high quality and your monitor, network, keyboard, mouse, headset, and speakers can be connected via a single thunderbolt connection. This is convenient, but I don't think this justifies the price as there are many docks out there that work just as well, albeit through a USB 3.1 connection instead.

WD has really done well to package a lot into this dock but is charging a premium for it. Personally, I think that there are just better ways of achieving equal or better results when it comes to upgrading a gaming laptop.

**update**
Coming back to think about it some more, I realized exactly what niche WD was going for: Macbooks. Some Macbooks have only two thunderbolt ports and all of them are not easily upgradeable so this product does indeed provide a value to those consumers. But then does it make sense to spend an additional 35% of the price of the laptop (Macbook Pro 13" is $1299) to address problems that Apple introduced into their laptops? I guess if you're already in their ecosystem, it's par for the course. That's not to say Apple is the only one. Microsoft has made their products impossible to upgrade as well, but none of these are actually gaming laptops.

This unit is made in Malaysia, unlike my previous lower end Yamaha receiver, which was made in China. Malaysia has been churning out high quality electronics for some time now. One example of that is the "Boston Acoustics Recepter" (not the inferior HD version). I purchased my Malaysian Recepter new in the '90s and it still works as new. While I think some of it is trial and error for getting the right fit, I think I happened upon a really good fit and feel with my first try. I really have nothing to compare it to, but so far I am really quite pleased.

--I dont have small hands, but they aren't exactly big either. Size can be in length and width. I have quite small fingers, but wide palms (3.75"). So typically a size "large" in gloves, but the ends of the fingers always dangle quite a bit. Hope that gives impression going forward with my review:

--My hand easily grasps the width of this mouse. Feels very comfortable. My pointer finger just reaches the scroll wheel. I dont need to reach for it; my finger pad sits directly on top of apex of the wheel.

--Press of left or right side is easy and comfortable. Plenty of length to accommodate even the smallest of fingers. Yet plenty of spare room for fingers longer than mine.

-- Not a loud click, but I can feel the click. I personally find that satisfying. Gentle yet makes me feel my action.

--Scrolling is smooth.
--No stuttering or jerkiness
--Instant connect when I first got this, and no problems since

--Impressed with how natural it feels. Didnt realize how much the wrist and forearm twist to use a standard mouse. With this, the mouse and arm are in a natural alignment

Take a little getting used to, yet at same time feels really natural. Good grip, good responsiveness, all around good experience in the short time I have had it. Your experience may vary in terms of fit, but I think the quality is evident. I will update if I have anything else worth sharing :)

I've been using a Keurig machine for several years -- I currently own 2 of them. But I've always had an ethical issue with all the little plastic cups that get tossed into the environment. To that end, I've tried and used several different varieties of reusable K-cups, and had finally settled on the Ekobrew cups.

I was offered an opportunity to try this set, and decided to do a side-by-side comparison. The results were interesting. These Brewooze cups perform just as good as the more expensive Ekobrew cups.

I tried several different coffees and several different grinds. As with all reusable cups, you have to be careful how fine/coarse the grind is. Too coarse, and you get weaker coffee; too fine, and you get either overflow and/or sludge. I found that a medium-fine grind worked best for both cup brands. This way, I get the right strength and almost no powdery sludge in the bottom of the cup. One advantage of the Brewooze over the Ekobrew: I was able to use LESS coffee in the cup to get the right brew strength. With the Ekobrew, I needed to fill the cup; with the Brewooze, I filled it about 2/3 full to get the same flavor/strength.

As with all reusable K-cups, you need to take care when you seal them prior to use. These are no trouble to seal correctly -- you can easily see if there are gaps and do an extra "squeeze." Inserting them into the machine takes a bit of attention, too -- otherwise, you can pierce the cup. There are arrows on the lid that show which direction, so that shouldn't be a problem.

This set comes with 20 paper filters plus a replacement charcoal filter for the Keurig filter wand. I didn't see much advantage to the paper filters except possibly ease of cleaning. The coffee was weaker, and using a finer grind didn't seem to help. And it still resulted in some grinds getting "around" the paper filter and onto the mesh, so I still had to clean the cup. It's not a big deal, really -- the cups are easy to rinse clean after use. So I won't be using the paper filters, but you may find them useful.

I'm a little surprised at how nicely these performed, given the price. You get 3 cups (brown, medium tan, and light tan color -- the photo makes them look orange, but they're more of a tan/brown), so if you want to assign a color to different family members, there you go. Since I usually brew 2 cups into a large mug, I just fill 2 of them with the same coffee and run them one after the other in the morning.

kI have to say I was impressed. I didn't expect these to perform as well as they did. Definitely comparable to the Ek​​​​obrew so far -- the only question I have is durability, and only time will tell. I've been using these for about 4 days, and after the initial side-by-side test (when I brewed about 12 cups total), I've been brewing 2-3 cups every morning, rotating them, cleaning after each use, and so far, no signs of any wear problems. If I notice a serious issue, I'll update this review.

I bought this router in December, 2010 to replace my Linksys WRT54GS wireless router. I was a bit surprised to find that there are no external antennae and no place to install one on the E3000, but I haven't encountered any problems with signal. This router hasn't bottlenecked once, whereas my WRT54GS would bottleneck if the wind blew wrong. The only time I have unplugged this router was because I had to reconfigure it from scratch when I discovered I couldn't configure any of the settings using the built-in software once I'd changed the router configuration in the browser config pages. I read some work-arounds in the Amazon.com reviews and had to reset to factory defaults. I had to fully uninstall and reinstall the Cisco Connect software as well. As long as you go through that software first and THEN make adjustments in your advanced configuration settings via your web browser, you can still access things like parental control and guest wifi security. If you change your router's address, however, from 192.168.1.1 to anything different, expect to never be able to get into Cisco Connect again. The only reason I can envision needing the Cisco Connect software is to access the guest wifi and the parental controls, so if you don't need those things, don't worry about making changes you normally would via the browser interface.

The wifi button on the router is handy for setting up wireless devices such as cell phones and internet tablets, it hooks right up to your wireless network and you don't have to rely on the guest access to connect. You will also have the ability to set up a physical key using a USB thumb drive (you must provide your own) for setting up other computers on your wifi network, which works like a charm. It is especially compatible with the Cisco-Linksys WUSB600N Dual-Band Wireless-N USB Network Adapter, which I also highly recommend. I haven't tried the networked storage option yet due to the location of my router in relation to my external drives, but it is definitely an option that I will look into setting up some day.

I would say this router is worth the $150 I paid for it (locally), with the biggest reason being that so far I haven't been able to bottleneck it, even with my 60MB cable service, wireless-connected computers, Wii, and other various wireless devices. Cisco/Linksys really did a good thing with this model and I'm quite pleased with it; it is definitely worth the price.

The UPRIGHT SMART WEARABLE POSTURE TRAINER is an "anti-slouch" posture trainer that really works! I discarded my [[ASIN:B00N9P8GMW Lumo Lift]] after a week or so, because my sitting posture is pretty good, and I rarely slouched badly enough to trigger the Lumo Lift. In contrast, the Upright buzzes me whenever I start to relax my posture even partway to a full slouch.

The Upright needs to be pasted to your back with gentle adhesive pads (60 included), rather than pinned to your clothing (like the Lumo Lift), but the greater sensitivity makes the extra effort worthwhile. Packets of one-time-use adhesive pads are available from the Upright web site for about $15.

You can wear the Upright between your shoulder blades if you're going to be standing, walking, and sitting; or at the small of your back if you're an Upright novice or generally sitting. As long as it's turned on, the Upright works even without the accompanying app (Android or iOS) that tracks your training progress. The Upright app uses Bluetooth to connect with the wearable Upright.

The app walks you through the simple setup, which mostly involves (1) finding the proper spot for placement on your back, and (2) calibrating the device so that it can detect a slouch. Once it's calibrated, the device will gently buzz you whenever you sink into a slouch--which inevitably happens as your muscles tire from holding a single position--so that you can straighten up. (There is no sound. The product page video that demonstrates the buzz is kind of amusing.)

When you create an account (free), the app collects information about your height, weight, and age, and then generates a daily posture training program that is personalized for you. The training program begins with your wearing the device for a few minutes, and then for longer and longer sessions. At the end of a session, the app gives you a score, based on how long you held your upright posture. (Mine was only 86%, because I intentionally slouched to test the buzz.)

The Upright arrives fully charged. The app tells you how much charge is remaining in your Upright. When you're charging the device in the supplied charging dock, a solid red light tells you that it's properly connected and charging.

I had been eying up the [[ASIN:B00B981XQC Ion Audio Job Rocker Bluetooth Portable Jobsite Sound System]] for a while. I was interested in a highly rated Bluetooth speaker because I had been using my [[ASIN:B00MPMK3GW Goal Zero 94014 Rock Out 2 Green Solar Rechargeable Speaker]] with my Google Nexus 7 since last year but was disappointed with it because that was the only device that the speaker would work with. I could not use it successfully with my HP OMEN Gaming Notebook or my boyfriend's iPhone 5 or iPad 3.

I almost purchased the old Job Rocker but did not like that it did not have a USB port. Therefore, when I saw that this recently released Block Rocker IPA76C was on sale at Costco for $119.99 plus tax, I purchased one immediately and I am thrilled that I did.

FEATURES

- This Bluetooth speaker pairs beautifully with my Nexus 7, my boyfriend's iPad 3 & iPhone 5, my BLU Life One 4G LTE SmartPhone that I use only as a portable tablet, and my HP OMEN. All I had to do was press the Bluetooth button on the speaker after I activated Bluetooth on the devices.

- There's an auxiliary cable with stereo 3.5mm (1/8") input that can be used to connect a CD or MP3 player and such to the unit.

- A microphone is supplied with volume control. At first I had trouble getting the MIC to work but once I turned off Bluetooth, it worked okay. It's not a great microphone but good enough.

- There's AM/FM radio with 6 presets and a "rubber" covered antenna.

- This Block Rocker can be paired / linked with another one for even more amplified power.

- There's an On/Off power switch in the back.

- It has wheels, side carrying grips, and a luggage handle making it portable enough to roll it around like luggage.

- There are two 5V 1A USB ports for charging devices. I charged my phone with this port.

- When not connected to a wall outlet via the supplied power plug, the internal battery is rated at 75 plus or minus hours of battery life depending on conditions associated with temperature, age of battery, and volume usage of the speaker.

- The manual also says that it can be left plugged in indefinitely and it will not damage the battery (for those like me, who are not planning on taking this to a job site or garden party).

I'm truly impressed with the sound and functionality of this speaker; so impressed that I am tempted to buy another one. In addition to home use as a theatre producing surround sound experience, this would also be great for outdoor parties and construction sites and such where there is limited or no electricity.

My daughter and I do a lot of photography of jewelry. We have had a variety of tripods and camera aids. This kit seemed like a good one for us. I got it.

WHAT IS THIS KIT LIKE?
CASE
This has a hard case that zips around the edge. It has a pocket in it to hold things in place and a cupped side to allow for the tripod storage.

LENS BAGS
There are bags in here which fit small medium or large lenses. I don't have any lenses yet, but I do have a small light that fits in one.

CLEANING CLOTH
These come in a zip topped plastic bag. This is pretty nice and works well as is expected with microfiber cloth for cleaning glass.

QUICK RELEASE CAMERA STRAP
This comes in a nice package with good instructions in it. The idea is that this helps stabilize the camera when you are taking a lot of photos. You can not have to grip the camera so hard so your hand does not get tired too. If you accidentally slip your grip, it does not crash to the ground.

This had a learning curve to it, but I finally figured out how to use it for me where it was helpful.

LENS PAPER
This paper allows you to clean the lens off gently wet or dry. The wet means that you use the Altura cleaning solution for greasy heavier prints.

PUFFER CLEANER
This is a rubberized ball that when you squeeze it, there will be a blast of air that will blow things off of the lenses. This works quite well when I get a particle on the lens so I don't have to touch it.

BRUSH
This is when the dust won't blow off the lens or other glass you can gently brush it and then blow it away with the puffer cleaner.

EMPTY BOTTLE
This is for alcohol or lens cleaner.

TRIPOD
This is why I wanted this kit the most. It has an ingenious design to it. It folds up flat and quite small, yet when you take it apart and tilt it, you can stand it up for close photos, or use it in your hand. It has rubber on the bottom to keep it put, and it also has a rubberized grip if you want to hold it. The camera platform tilts, but it locks into place which I love. This is working great for us taking close up photos of some of the small jewelry we are photographing. It has come in really handy.

What I love is that we can pick it up and use it by hand if we need another angle than the table top one.

THE BOTTOM LINE
This kit is a nice kit. I got it mostly for the tripod, but the cleaning accessories and the wrist strap make it really nice. The puffer ball is one of those things that you don't realize you need until you have it.- at least for me. The case is protective and easy to travel with.

MY RATING
FIVE STARS. I am happy with this kit. It has worked better for us than I expected. We will be using this a lot in the future too.
