This past weekend I got to use both the SN600N and the Yongnuo YN568EX with the YN622 triggers. Basically both function completely with the YN622 triggers in both manual and iTTL modes. The only thing that I noticed with the SN600N was that manual power 1/1, 1/2, 1/4 all seem to be about the same output using the YN622 triggers - you have to lower it to 1/8 or less to start seeing lower outputs. Not a huge deal, but I'd like more output options. More on this below:

Here are a few details that a pretty important about these two alternatives to the Nikon SB series:

a) The 568 light is much higher quality - and I really mean the LIGHT quality. It is even, consistent, and clear. On the other hand, the SN600N is very scattered - what I mean by this is there are lines of brightness and darkness from the flash burst. This must be an internal flash "lens" issue - whatever the light is bouncing around and through within the flash is creating texture and light inconsistencies. This is not the case with the 568.

b) Yes, the SN600N is a more powerful flash, but in my opinion, it needs to have more levels of output on the lower end (1/256) because it's TOO bright for some situations. I use grids and modifiers during wedding receptions, and I like balancing the natural light with the flash output. 1/128 with the SN600N is equal to about 1/64 on the 568. I use the 568 at 1/128 quite a bit for details - so this was kinda a bummer to me.

c) The AF beam on the SN600N is better and more centered than the 568 - but they both need to improve designs. The ONLY reason I'm holding onto my Nikon SB900 at this point is the AF beam - which makes accurate AF possible in pitch black - no joke. The AF beam on the Yongnuo is a joke - they need to fix it on the 622 triggers too - it's basically worthless and too bright/annoying to the subject.

d) In my experience using the 568EX, the batteries get warm and stay warm, whether you're using the flash or not. If the flash is on, the batteries will get warm. It also EATS through batteries. I used to be able to photograph 2 weddings without recharging my Nikon SB setup (using SB600 previously) - now I have to recharge between weddings. I've upgraded to 2800mah EBL AA rechargeable (previously using Amazon 2000mah) and it has helped quite a bit.

So this is my current setup: SB900 on camera, 2x 568EX off camera group A+B for reception lighting, and then SN600N as group C for periodic fill. Rather than commit to a single brand, I'm using them all as tools for different situations, because they all work differently. I also am really enjoying the SN600N as on-camera if I don't need the AF beam - the quality of light is bright, crisp and rich - and the SN600N "brain" (basically how it works using iTTL mode) just works really well with Nikon - it's a very consistent flash, sometimes even better than my SB900. I like that it can zoom all the way to 200mm, too. If the SN600N had a better AF beam and better quality of light, I would ditch my SB900 and use it all the time. But I switch between the SB900 and the SN600N for different effects. I actually like the previously mentioned internal lens flash inconsistencies at times - it creates a grittiness that I like.

My laptop came with a Dell PA1900-02D (9T215) which I still have and works fine. I wanted a second charger for another location. The EasyStyle SK90B195462looks like the original but is much lighter, probably due to being a switching power supply. My laptop had been discharged down to 5% prior to plugging the replacement charger in. The connector fit fine, but the laptop did not recognize the charger and warned that it may not work. I figured that's just Dell telling me it's not a Dell accessory. I permanently shut off the warning (an option) and continued to use the EasyStyle charger. Charging appeared normal and battery status was indicated as charging. However, after a short while it seemed stuck at 11% charge. I came back a few hours later and it was still indicating at 11%. I plugged in the Dell charger and 100% full charge was indicated immediately. I unplugged the Dell charger and the computer still indicated nearly full charge. I plugged in the new EasyStyle charger and the indication was charging and still near full charge.
My conclusion is that the charger works, but may cause the computer to give incorrect charge status under some conditions and it will be best to unplug the charger to get an accurate battery status.

A couple weeks ago I put a protector on a phone and they had a really great trick for positioning - which I used on this big thing, too. I don't think I could have gotten it exactly right had I not used this method: Before peeling any film, lay it where it needs to be and use scotch or masking tape (easily removable kind) to tape the long edge nearest the 'tab' to be pulled. (2 pieces positioned a couple inches from the ends should do it.) Then lift the film and start pulling the tab to remove the plastic a little bit at a time - with it up in the air a bit, adjust so it's straight (the tape keeps it aligned) and let the uncovered tabbed corner adhere to the screen. Slowly work your way diagonally pulling, adhering, and (I used a credit card) smoothing out. It just takes a bit of patience. I have zero air bubbles and just one tiny speck of dust I'd missed.

I picked up these bone conduction headphones on a Woot sale to try them to see if there would be any difference. I like that you can wear these with hearing aids.

I really wasn't sure what to expect, but I have to say that the clarity of the sound makes it possible for me to understand speech on TV without having to read lips. I can keep the volume relatively low and still understand what I'm watching. DP can talk to me when he needs to without having to wave his arms at me to get my attention, and I know that I can watch TV now without disturbing him.

I was able to pair these pretty quickly with my Amazon Fire TV and a bluetooth transmitter that I use when watching cable. The latter took several tries, but it did finally pair. I'll have to get used to how to switch between the two devices, because you can't connect to two bluetooth devices at once. I love that this surge protector and plug strip has two USB ports for charging my Kindle and cell phone, but the placement of the USB ports, which is a major selling point for this unit, is hindered by the position of the cord wrap feature as well as the areas to plug in your larger electronics that have the big boxy plug. The USB ports are tucked right in between the cord wrap spot and the place to plug in larger plugs, so if one isn't blocking your USB ports, the other is.

In addition, I kind of wish that the majority of the plugs were spaced farther apart. I have a few electronics that have very small boxy plugs, and those don't fit right next to one another on the main area of the plug strip. The only thing that will fit on those plugs without overlapping are the traditional small plugs that are on lamps and other uncomplicated items. I don't have too many of those, and I'm guessing that most people buy plug strips because they have a bunch of electronics, almost all of which would have those bigger boxy plugs.

That said, the surge protector feature is absolutely effective, and I know this because we had PG&E replacing some poles in our neighborhood recently and we had many incidences of brownouts, surges, and spotty power, and this unit kept any harm from coming to any of my electronics that were plugged into it.

And while it is easy to make design suggestions, I have to say that I haven't found the perfect plug strip yet. Almost all of them seem to have some design characteristics that make them not quite ideal. While this unit is not perfectly designed with regards to the placement of the USB ports and the spacing of the regular plugs, it is certainly a high-quality, very functional unit that does what it says it does, and I trust the Belkin brand that it's going to function for some time. This plug strip is also nice in that it has a space so that you can mount it on the wall or on the back of your desk if you so desire.

I'll admit, I'm a fan of Sony. I've owned all sorts of things from the brand, from the aftermarket stereo in my car to my professional camera equipment I use at work. They just make reliably good products. However I've mostly owned Samsung television sets just because it's what I had access to on a more regular basis.
I was therefore excited to try out this TV and see how it compared. To be honest, I really REALLY like Sony's color science. It's part of why I prefer their camera equipment, and it shows on this display. The contrast ratio and dynamic range are everything I wanted it to be and more. The skin tones as well, however the average consumer probably wouldn't notice or care about these things. Where the big differences lie in major TV brands these days is going to be features. The latest crop of Smart TVs have so many bells and whistles, you practically don't need anything other than an internet connection anymore. Unlike Samsung's UI which has embraces Amazon's Fire Stick style UI, Sony has gone the Google TV route. There are pros and cons to both approaches, although I think perhaps arguably there isn't as much free included content as Samsung (Samsung actually includes free live TV channels via "Samsung TV", which Sony does not have). But for all the content I actually WANT to see, Netflix, Prime, Disney+ etc, it works perfectly!

So why only 4 stars? This isn't the fault of Sony's TV, but I really wish they'd make it easier to spot and turn off... I really REALLY hate the default motion smoothing (aka "soap opera effect") that all the big brands use these days. As a content creator, I shoot videos in a particular frame rate on purpose. The motion blur or lack thereof helps tell the story in some kinds of scenes. But most TVs want to show off their high refresh rate and therefore use realtime smoothing algorithms to create fake overly-dramatic effects to pump out extra in between frames. The motion looks too smooth to the point it seems CGI (because it sort of is). It just looks off once you notice it, and Sony is no exception. You have to dig around and figure out what they call it on every TV just to make it look normal again, on this set it is called Motionflow and it can be confusing to turn it off. I wish manufacturers would make it a simple and easy to understand toggle switch... maybe even present it as an option to the viewer upon setting it up so they can understand what they are enabling and decide if they want it or not (I strongly recommend not!).
But again, that's true of all modern Television sets, on its own right this is a solid TV and I would recommend it.

I received this mat as a review sample and own a number of brands to which I compared it. First, there are only nominal differences between and among most of the silicone baking mats on the market, so the main factors are price and construction. For former is highly variable, but if you comparison shop what you are looking for are size and overall construction.

These are about 3/10ths of an inch thick so are well constructed in my opinion. They are designed to fit an 18 x 13 baking sheet, and have a slight textured surface that makes them ideal for not only baking, but for rolling out dough.

Another factor is this one will withstand heat up to 450F, whereas some brands will only go as high as 425F (and others will go higher at 480F). Consider those factors too when selecting a baking mat. If you have never used one of these from any brand they are infinitely better than parchment paper, and you do not have to use any kind of grease or shortening because they are naturally non-stick. Do note that you cannot use them in direct contact with flame or heat source. I mention that because I gave a similar mat to a friend who tried using it on a stove eye. Don't!

If you opt to use these without a baking sheet know that your times will need to be slightly adjusted. That is because the heat transfer is a little too efficient, but also these will cool a lot quicker as well, so when you first use them keep a close eye on baking times by visually checking on what you are baking a little earlier than usual and making sure that this mat is not causing the process to over bake.

Cleaning is a snap and these can actually be cleaned in a dishwasher. More importantly, they are perfect for rolling out dough (I sometimes use a pair of silicone mats - regardless of brand - with one on top and one on the bottom of the dough. When I roll out the dough by rolling over the top mat I can get a more ever, thinner dough.

Bottom line: this mat is well made, has a fairly wide operating range and a slightly textured surface for true non-stick.

It provides a significant upgrade on the pseudo-4k projector with an impressive 2600 lumens making it one of the brightest projectors out there easily surpassing the 1500 lumens you would get with the entry level Sony true 4K projector. Even with the reduced bandwidth that you get with the wireless setup, it is a great convenience to have the ability to stream from sources without having to run a wire from the source to the actual projector.

Another great aspect of the 5050 is the motorized lens which is a feature that other more expensive true-4k projectors do not offer. Of course with Epson you do get exceptional HDR quality as well as amazing black.

This is an impressive pseudo-4K projector that provides features that are not even found in some entry level true 4K projectors. If you are not absolutely dying to get true 4k, then this should be one of the projectors you should consider.

THE GOOD:
--------------
* High quality, sturdy build.
* 360 degree omnidirectional, allows you to place the antenna virtually anywhere.
* 2 inch magnetic base.
* Standard coaxial F-Type male connector.

THE BAD:
-----------
* Nothing bad at all, but just a FYI. I collect vintage tvs, and I broadcast my own analog signals for fun. When I see an antenna, I grab it for testing purposes. To broadcast a signal, you need a modulator, and an antenna attached to it to act as transmitter. I tested this antenna as a transmitter, and you can see in my photo, my vintage tv gets the signal crystal clear. My in-depth review of the new Garmin Vivoactive HR that debuted this week ($249/AMZN) and that I've been wearing since Saturday is as follows:
-- It buzzes and vibrates a lot. Not sure what it's doing because by the time I look the message has disappeared.
-- I ran with it and managed to stop it at 1.46 miles and don't know how I did that. Had to restart another run. I should be able to figure this out in about 3-4 months.
-- It is counting my steps for some reason and I really don't care how many steps I take. My goal is to take as few steps as possible to get where I need to go, especially if where I need to go is the bathroom
-- It's waterproof and can be used in the pool for lap swimming, yet I've still taken it off each time when I shower. I don't know why.
-- It has a green light under it that's tracking my HR at all times. When I was running it showed my HR was elevated. This was not suprising in any way, considering I usually look like I'm in the midst of an anuerism when I run, even if it's just to the bathroom.
-- It is "tracking" my sleep. I found the little screen that showed my HR while I was asleep and or/if I was "deep sleeping" or if I had any movement. Unless it can help me remember what I was dreaming about, or at least stop dreaming about being back in High School with no pants, I plan on taking the watch off when I sleep.
-- I was able to sync it to my phone and put the Garmin Connect App on my phone. Both are legitimate milestone events for me. Now whenever I get a text message on my phone my wrist buzzes and my phone beeps. The writing on the phone is small and I can't see it without my glasses, so I don't need this, especially since my phone has to be close by for the bluetooth to even work. This seems redundant and at some point I'll figure out how to stop this.
-- Other things it shows are the weather (again, it's on my phone which is 2 feet away), and "intensity minutes". I don't know what Intensity Minutes are, but I'm wondering if that would include me stressing out looking for my keys each morning or trying to convince my child that she needs a shower.
-- It's impossible to see the screen in the dark. I run in the dark. Now I need to bring a light to see how far I've run in the dark.
-- The app for my phone for Garmin has all sorts of things on it as well, mostly the same things we see on the watch, but with loads more information such as circles, graphs, and lines. It continuously tells me that it's not synching with my watch, but my watch has the little BT symbol showing, so I think it's purposely pi#‪#‎ing‬ me off to add on some Intensity Minutes.
Overall, it's black and tells the time. If I remember to wear it and start it when I run, it'll tell me how long it took to do my runs and how far I went, which was never really that important to me in the first place.

The performance of the drive is pretty great though, no complaints.

I understand that it's certainly non-tangable, but it comes with a longer cord that makes absolutely no sense. The longer cord isn't the major issue, though; it's the short cord that extends from the headphones: it's so short, it can't attach to *anything* without requiring the longer cord. Maybe if you were on your bed and the iPod/music device was on your chest it would work, but I imagine people aren't buying these cans for bed use. The longer cord is absolutely fundamental to using, so I don't know why they even bothered separating it from the cans themselves. They should've made the shorter cord longer and the longer cord slightly shorter.

While the design is superb, I'd look elsewhere if you want good sound quality.

I have a TomTom Start and I have disliked the EasyPort mount from the day I got it. I had been telling my wife for months that I was going to get a “proper” mount for my TomTom and that day finally came when I accidentally broke the EasyPort mount. After a little research I decided on this particular mount, and so far I have been very pleased with it.

I wanted a more “normal” windshield mount - a suction cup with a lever instead of a twist ring, and that led me to this particular mount. The design is simple - press the suction cup against the windshield and flip the lever to make the cup stick to the window. In operation this is an easy-to-use mount and it seems to hold the navigator in place without too much trouble. As expected it does not hold well when it the windshield is cold, which is an issue with every suction-based mount I have ever used - including the EasyPort.

The ring in which the TomTom attaches to the mount holds the TomTom in place well enough but I have observed that it does not hold the navigator tightly. That is, the TomTom has a tendency to turn a little in the ring. So far this has not been an issue and the TomTom has not fallen out of the ring so this really does not bother me.

The mount is adjustable and provides for a couple of places where the position can be tweaked for maximum visibility. There should be no issue with getting the position of the GPS just right so it can be seen but not in the way.

So far I am pleased with this mount and am happy to recommend it. It’s a lot easier to use than the EasyPort mount that comes with the TomTom and it’s adjustable enough to make visibility a non-issue, even while in motion. If you have a TomTom and you don’t like the EasyPort mount, this mounting system is a big improvement.

I got this internet radio and tried it for a few weeks. At first I was happy with it - the sound quality is quite good, it seemed pretty easy to set up, and I was able to find my favorite NPR station streams as well as connect to my Pandora stations. But after the first two weeks or so, I started having problems with connectivity.

- I'd come home from work and the thing would be on, not playing, with "error connecting to network" or some similar message flashing on the screen. The best way to solve this seemed to be to turn it off, then turn it back on, and then it would work (for a while).

- While listening, it frequently stops playing in the middle of a song. Then the display says either "Buffering" for a few minutes, or more frequently, will actually say "Connecting" for up to five minutes at a time! This happens, on average, every 4-6 minutes. The thing is, I have a wireless router upstairs on the same floor as the radio (Apple Time Capsule) and the wireless signal is quite strong. The other devices that connect to this router never have a problem with connectivity - devices that include a Roku box, a Chumby, my iPhone, my HP netbook, my Macbook, etc.

The problem with losing connectivity started infrequently but got worse and worse over the past two weeks or so, to the point where I can't really listen to music on it at all anymore. At the tender age of fourteen, Davie Adams's life is ripped apart. His mother's loose ways leads to a series of events that leave him homeless after his she dies in his arms. Grief-stricken, Davie makes the decision to leave Blackburn and go in search of his father.

Davie could have returned to his grandfather's house but he can't imagine remaining in Blackburn and having to endure the pitying looks and talk about his mother. After his mother's collapse, Davie runs for help and finds Tom Makepeace. They get his mother situated in the back of his wagon and are getting ready to head to the infirmary but she passes away moments later. Immediately afterward Davie jumps from the wagon and runs into the woods. Everyone assumes he'll return. Tom even yells into the woods for Davie to come to his home when he's ready that he's welcome there. Davie has other plans though.

He does go to the Makepeace's home but it's only to spend the night in their barn. He hadn't expected anyone to see him but Judy, Tom's daughter and Davie's longtime friend spots him from her window. She goes out to see him and reassures him that his mother's body is taken care of and his grandfather will be just fine. Judy realizes that Davie has to do what he feels is right for him but she also knows that her feelings for him have gone beyond friendship.

Davie leaves the following morning with nothing more than the desire to leave his memories behind him. Life on his own isn't everything he thought it would be and his search for his father proves fruitless. For years Davie travels and holds many different jobs but through it all Judy and his life in Blackburn remain firmly at the forefront of his mind.

THE LONER is sure to pull at readers' heartstring. Spanning over an eight year time period, you get a lot of insight into the characters' personalities and backgrounds. I love that Josephine Cox doesn't focus solely on Davie and Judy's story, there are many other characters who possess stories of their own which add a feeling of realism to this storyline. Davie's journey of self discovery is the main theme and it's a story you won't want to miss. Josephine Cox is a gifted storyteller who knows how to keep readers engrossed page after page so that the doldrums of winter just disappear.

I have waited a while to review this because I got it for my daughter who was very interested to have it, but after a while, she lost interest so it was back to me. Let's take a look.

WHAT IS THIS LIKE?
This comes in a box with a cord for recharging. It has a type C connector. There are also earbuds in the box. Insturctions? Well, not so much.

TOUCHSCREEN
That is kind of deceptive. This has a touch screen on bottom, but the top is not - where you see the photo of the album playing, the play button or other information.

MUSIC QUALITY
The music quality of this is fabulous. It is better using bluetooth headphones than the speaker or the cheap buds that come with this.

EAR BUD JACK
The problem with this player is that the jack is very touchy. If you move just right it will disconnect either ear and that is totally annoying when using this.

MUSIC SEQUENCE
That is another odd feature of this player. This will play in order when I have albums in it and so far they play in alphabetical order which is rather strange. I can not get it to play any other way than this way, so if you are using this and want to hear what YOU want to hear in a certain order, plan to play around with this a lot.

RECORDING BUTTON
This has some storage on it, so you can record with the little red recording button. That can come in handy if you need it, but I don't use it much. It works.

SPEAKER
This has its own little speaker on it which is handy for using the auto alarm function if you are camping or something and don't want to use your phone for that.

AUTO ALARM FUNCTION
This will wake you up if you want it to.

FM RADIO
This works pretty good, but again, the jack is toast, which is part of the antenna grounding the signal, so in my case, it is good but not WOW.

INSTRUCTIONS
This really is frustrating. This should have extensive instructions in it. This thing is really frustrating despite it being almost user friendly in some ways. In others it is downright frustrating.

BATTERY LIFE
The battery life on this is great. If not in use for a long period, it will keep the charge nicely, a feature I appreciate.

TOUCHY TOUCH SCREEN
This bottom half with the touch screen is very touchy. If I have it in my pocket and it hits my body just right, it will change to another song. Sometimes it will go to another direction if I put my hand in my pocket which is frustrating. That part is also difficult.

BLUETOOTH
This is a great feature. I had no problems hooking this up to my bluetooth headphones at all. It was easy and stayed connected, but I am at home when I use this and not around other wireless items, so I am not sure how well this would work when around other devices.

WHO MIGHT LIKE THIS?
If you are in need of some music and don't want your phone handy and feel like it does not matter what songs you hear in what order, then this might be a good mindless device for running, or working around cleaning, etc. It also might be nice for a young person who is not supposed to be using their phone and you want to give them something else to play music with.

THE BOTTOM LINE
For the price, the music quality is fantastic, the bluetooth connection is also very easy and one of the best I have used. As for other things like the music order, lack of instructions, and super touchy controls, this takes the fun out of using it.

MY RATING
I am between 3 and 4 stars for this. I am going with FOUR STARS. It is BARELY four stars though. The bluetooth and music quality are excellent. The screen is also decent too. The price is right. However, the other frustrations and lack of instructions frustrate me a bit. I am sure there are ways to put the music on there, but I just don't have the time to mess with it. Kids would probably have a lot of fun messing with this and making it do all sorts of amazing things.

For me, it is good when I need a quick set of music to drag along with me (I refuse to wear my phone out by overuse for music), so I put up with it.

This HP Pavilion desktop is a solid, but basic PC that, while it can be considered a gaming PC with its discreet Radeon RX 5500 card, that isn't going to raise too many eyebrows with its specs. What's out of the realm of this machine would be 4K gaming and VR, but it can run most modern games at medium settings at 1080p.

That's not why I needed this machine, though. As a Plex server, this serves well. It is quiet and can transcode videos using hardware transcoding. Unfortunately, it only has a single slot for an additional hdd. As a video editing machine, it can handle 1080p videos, but will struggle with 4K. As a photo editing machine, it can edit pretty much anything from the devices you have, but if you work in print, you'll find this machine lacking. For emulation, this machine will work quite well for all classic systems and even some more modern ones. Of course, for everyday web browsing and watching videos, this thing will be more than enough.

Overall, this is a fairly priced machine that is a step up from the basic computers that one may find and the discreet GPU will help to make this machine last longer than those with embedded graphics.

This is a nicely design USB hub. It has the two feature I look for first in a hub: a compact footprint, and the ability to plug into the wall without having to deal with a wall wart at the end of the plug. While this does have a transformer, it is an in-line version that doesn't interfere with the plug end.

Installation is the typical plug-and-play that is typical with a USB hub. It includes a USB 3.0 cable, and works very well as a USB 3.0 hub under Win 7. I also tried it on an older USB 2.0 machine running XP and had no problems at all (running, of course, at USB 2.0 speed).

The build quality feels very solid. No problems with ports wiggling around even when I stressed the USB cable far more than in normal use. I’ve used other Sabrent hubs and have yet to have a problem with them, even after dropping them.

The hub includes a base that keeps it well-planted in use.

In addition to using this as a USB hub, it also has 2 charging ports that provide 2A output each. Both worked fine when used to charge a phone and a tablet.

The only quibble I have is that it lacks an on/off switch. Not a big deal, but having a switch can come in handy at times.

Overall, it’s a well-designed and well-built hub with a number of good design features. Well worth considering if you’re looking for a compact 3.0 hub with a lot of ports.

I have a good tangle of cables in my home office for a variety of devices that require a micro-USB cable. Most of these cables are very nondescript and I have no idea who made them, though there are a couple of them that have manufacturer names printed on the plugs on the end. Most are plain black and are mostly indistinguishable from one another. These cables from Magic-T are absolutely the most easily identifiable cables on the desk and it has made it very easy to assign cables to every device on the desk. But, there is more to these cables than just pretty colors.

The most obvious advantage of this cable set is the colors. Each of these cables is a different color and none of them are black or gray - there’s blue, pink, orange and green. And, even more important than the color is the fact that they are insulated in nylon weave, not plastic coating, which in my experience holds up a bit better under stress and the result is a more reliable cable.

The plugs on both ends are metal shielding with a plastic base, sufficient to give these strength for the connections. The cables have been inserted in the bases and attached within, not attached to the plug base, but those connections are very tight and seem to be solid so I am not concerned about them pulling loose.

Each cable is about six and a half feet in length which is much more convenient for me than the regular 3' cables.

These cables are capable of high-speed charging so if you have a device and a charger that are both capable of high-speed charging then these cables will work well for you. I used one for my tablet and a high-speed USB charger and the tablet did charge faster than when using a lower-grade cable.

I want to mention the pricing. As I write this, the price on this set of four cables is about $9. That’s about $2.25 per cable, and the cables are of good quality. The price can change of course, but at the current price this is an absolute bargain.

There’s something else I need to mention. The manufacturer offers a 12-month warranty on these cables, and to me that’s just amazing. For a cable that costs less than $2.50 per individual cable the manufacturer thinks enough of their product to back it with a 12-month warranty. I doubt I would ever need to use the warranty for one of these, but it’s reassuring to know the manufacturer believes in their products.

It is hard to find fault with these cables. They are made well, they are easily identifiable and they are very inexpensive. This is a fine set at a great price.

I've had several Amazon Basics' items since the line was introduced. Most have been quite good. Unfortunately this tripod wasn't one of them.

The feel is cheap and plastic-y. I wasn't expecting bearings in the pan-head but the plastic on plastic mechanisms are terrible.

I tested this item with my Kodak Z990 digital camera. It weighs approx. 21 oz. with batteries.

The camera mount has a good rubber pad for your camera to sit on and the tightening screw has a butterfly head so no screwdriver or coins are needed to attach/detach the mount from the camera. The mount attaches to the tripod with a spring-loaded release arm. There is actually very little contact area on the tripod itself (only two corners) holding the mount in place, also the release arm does NOT have a safety catch.

Pan Functionality - Fully tightened down I can still, with not much effort, swing the head from left to right. Fully loosened the motion is heavy and awkward easily upsetting the tripod's position. Tightening this knob fully actually interferes with the...

Tilt Functionality - The action is not much better here. You can lock the tilt angle into place and it does stay there. There's just as much plastic on plastic drag when in motion. The arm is generously long and comfortable to grip. The side-tilt mechanism goes reasonably easily from flat to 90°. It does not lock in place well.

Leg Functionality - The legs extend and retract with mild effort. They lock into place firmly. With just the larger leg section extended the tripod is fairly sturdy. Extending the smaller leg sections dramatically increases wobble. There is a weight/gear hook for added stabilization but it is plastic and feels easily broken. The swiveling rubber feet are innovative but only held on by friction and can easily become detached. The center stabilizer locks and unlocks easily with only a quarter turn and holds in place well. There is a serviceable carry handle attached to the leg mount section.

The tripod has two bubble levels. The first, a small button level is at the top of one of the leg mounts. The second, a tube level, is just under and inch long and is under and partially obscured by the camera mount. With a camera attached it becomes useless.

The center section extends and lowers via a crank mechanisms and locks in place with a plastic collar. There is no positive safety lock. Loosen the collar and your camera comes down rapidly on its own. Extending your camera this way will only increase the instability of this tripod.

The included carry bag reflects the quality of it's tripod. Its material is unpadded and thin. It has no extra pockets and the half-inch nylon shoulder strap is also unpadded making it rather uncomfortable to carry.

In conclusion... I wouldn't recommend this tripod even as a starter for someone just getting into photography it will only add frustration to the experience. Spend a little more and get a far better tripod or spend a little less and get something of equal quality.

Update!!: my review below was originally written 07/2019. I wanted to add an update THREE years later, 07/2022. This little laptop is still kicking. I use it every single day from comfort of my couch to write reviews, do basic doomscrolling (lol), write emails, etc. Camera still works. Speakers still good. No major issues. I never did do any adjustments to it. Just sort of kept using it as is. I;m maxed out for memory, so it isnt something I would rely on for loading pictures onto, but as mentioned.. if you just need something to get online with and do some shopping or searching, then this is fine. Has been worth it. I happen to be sniffing around for another laptop so I can go more photo work with it, but I havent been in a rush. I came back to this review so I could refresh my mind on the specs. It was then that I realized 3 whole years has gone by! OK.. back to orginal review:

It's a basic laptop. The price is right. You aren't paying a lot for a little. You are getting quite a bit of what you need for a couple hundred dollars. Cheaper than most tablets. If you just want something to get you online, to browse the internet, watch some videos, listen to some music, write some messages, play some basic games, do some video chatting, then this might be for you.I think most people want that. It doesn't have a lot of memory or speed, or a slew of storage- but it will get you far if you don't expect a lot from it.

I'm a gamer, so I won't be playing any MMOs on this (nor on most prefabs that are out there). But I will use it to play a variety of offline and online games such as those found on FB or POGO (ie; puzzles, word games, board games, hidden object, casino style, etc).

I use youtube to listen to music, watch videos, listen to podcasts etc.. the speakers are fine. I can hear what I need to, clearly and loudly, if I wish. Some of the sounds that come through are more dynamic than I expected, so that is a plus.

I do a little bit of office stuff, so I will continue to make use of Google docs but there is an option to activate a free 1 year trial of Office 365 which includes 1TB of storage (One Drive); after that there is a fee. The Microsoft website breaks down the pricing options, which include pay for the year, or by the month, if that is of interest to you.

This Windows 10 is in S mode, which is a special mode that essentially limits Windows 10 in a variety of ways to make it run faster, provide longer battery life, and be more secure and easier to manage. YOU DO NOT HAVE TO KEEP IT THIS WAY! The idea is that there is less security with non proprietary items (apps, browsers, internet security), and greater chance of phishing, slower processes, decreased PC health, etc. So "S Mode" isn't a different version, it is simply a different mode, with the usual Windows 10 home, underneath. From what I understand, you can take it out of S Mode, and you will have Windows 10 Home (and then you can use browsers of choice, apps of choice, security software of choice, etc) BUT you CAN NOT switch back to S Mode. It is a once and done deal. S Mode default browser is Microsoft Edge, the default search engine is Bing.

I'm used to using a different browser, and having more freedom of choice, but I am curious how this S Mode will do, as I have noticed in my time of using it that it never bogs down. It is likened to Chrome on Chromebook- it seeks to streamline all the while being as secure as possible. If at any point I just don't like it, at least I know I have the option of just using Windows 10 Home. But again, it is a ONE WAY DECISION.

The laptop itself is super light weight. It comes in at just 3.24 lbs according to description. Full keyboard, touch pad, USB 2.0, USB 3.1, headphone/microphone port, media card reader, web cam, 3 prong charge plug with long cord. Attractive black textured design. I've got some fingerprints on the lid/cover, but doesn't look bad.

No dvd/cd player. I bought a cheap external for those times I want to use it for storage, watching a video, or listening to a CD. Hey, I like options.

Set up is quick and easy. When Cortana (Microsoft virtual assistant) came on, I let her guide me through the start up process. I could answer a lot of her questions with speech. It did well with recognizing my words.

I still have quite a bit of learning to do about this laptop. One thing that I find interesting is that it has an option to use a phone app- where it will link your laptop and phone to each other, so you can (according to Microsoft website)
-Link your phone and PC to unlock a variety of cross-device experiences for Android and iPhone.
-See recent photos from your phone on your PC for Android only.
-View and send text messages from your PC for Android only.

Again, the price is right. This does come into play for me in terms of rating. For a couple hundred dollars, I am able to scroll through FB endlessly, add some comments without tapping them out on my phone or tablet, can access full webpages, can take pics, or video call with web cam, can play some lightweight games, etc..

At this point in time, I give it a full rating. I mean, I wouldn't go below a 4 for this anyway, and a 5 might be pushing it, but it is a nifty little machine, and I am happy so far. Once I realized that I am not stuck with S Mode, that boosted my opinion of it (not all PCs or laptops are given this S Mode option).

If I learn anything more that I think you will find useful, I will come back to update. I hope what I have provided thus far has been helpful to you. Take care :)

Arlo is not perfect, but it is wicked close.

What's Great: You can put it anywhere within range of the link/router. The alerts are reliable, if a little slow on the uptake. The picture is good. Set up was simple and worked the first time. A reasonable amount of cloud storage is free, and it's easy to download whatever you want to save. The cameras are easy to move around to wherever you need them, and you don't have to set them up again.

What's Okay: A person who walks fast can get through a room almost faster than Arlo can start recording. Now, it's still much faster than an old Belkin Netcam HD, which sends pictures of where the motion WAS. Before the picture. And the D-Link 930L, which is a fine monitor cam, but has never been able to send a snap or a clip, no matter how many times it has been set up to do that. However, both of those cameras have audio and stream reasonably good images via their apps (the Belkin video resolution is way better than the Dlink). That makes them okay monitors next to smart security sensors - if the sensor alerts, you can look to see what tripped it and listen to see what's going on. Arlo will - most of the time - catch whatever set it off and let you know within seconds. And it's free, not an extra $$$ feature.

What Could Be Better: The link thing is enormous. It could be a little less expensive. And it would be WONDERFUL if it integrated with Z-Wave or Smart Things. The plan here is to station the Arlo cams near other devices that send push notifications - Nest Alarms, Smanos smart sensors, etc.

How It Compares: Beats the Canary I couldn't get to activate. Way better than the other netcams in the house. Love it. Just added another camera.

I have worked with a lot of active noise canceling (ANC) headphones by a lot of manufacturers, including an older pair of Philips headphones. I’ve seen a wide variance in ANC implementation and sound profiles, and to be honest few manufacturers get theirs right. With this set of headphones, Philips comes close.

These are over-ear phones which I prefer over on-ear phones. They fit snugly but not tight, and they actually do a good job of sound isolation. Even if you don’t like the ANC function (which would defeat the purpose of having these phones), these do a surprisingly good job of sound isolation. The pads are soft enough and comfortable enough that I can wear these for quite a while without discomfort. After a bit of time they do start to get a little warm but not to the point that I need to take them off.

These connect via Bluetooth and they connect very quickly. The connectivity of these phones is absolutely amazing: this is the very first pair of Bluetooth headphones I have used that maintains a steady connection up two flights of stairs with closed doors in between the phones and the source. The connectivity alone makes these very much worth checking out.

The ANC function is very good though it is not quite as aggressive as that of Bose or Sony. It is strong enough to mostly drown out a droning high-volume fan (my baseline for testing), such that music at a low volume while the ANC is turned on completely drowns out the fan. While Bose and Sony go to the extreme for noise cancellation, and other manufacturers often have ANC that’s barely there, Philips has implemented a system that is good enough for most. I am pleased with the ANC and will use these phones when I travel next.

The ANC function on these phones can be turned off if desired. There is also a special “awareness mode” that is an in-between mode that doesn’t completely turn off ANC but allows more environmental noise in, and this mode is really designed for permitting conversation without having to turn everything off completely. It works fairly well though the noise this mode produces via the external microphone is slightly harsh and shrill.

The default sound profile is not exactly perfect but it is better than many I have used and heard. These do boost the bass by default though not to an uncomfortable level. Bass boost is very common in headphones and it’s often too aggressive, but these actually give a modest boost. The midrange is a little soft though present. The highs sound bright and clear but not piercing. As a result, the sound profile is not quite perfectly balanced but it still good.

The sound profile can be tweaked via an app. I found the Philips Headphones app, installed it and started messing with it. The app works better than the reviews have suggested and it does a decent job of adjusting the headphones on the fly. The mode can be changed as well as the sound profile to adjust for different could quality based on music type, and there is a custom setting so that the equalizer can be adjusted to taste. The only complaint I have with the app is that there is about a 1s pause when changing modes between ANC. Awareness mode and Off, though this gap does not occur when changing the mode via the button on the headphones.

I like these ANC phones. They’re not perfect but they’re better than average with a good ANC function and decent sound. The have absolutely incredible connectivity, and they can be adjusted to taste via an app. This is a pair to keep on the short list if you need Bluethooth headphones that maintain a connection a long way from the source and provide ANC in the deal.

My main TV - and thus my comparison point - is a Sony Bravia Z series from 2009. Here are some things I think are outstanding about the Samsung. I'll try to only talk about things that aren't mentioned constantly:

1) I dislike the overly contemporary look of most high-end Samsung TVs, and therefore don't usually consider them for purchase. This, however, is a classic looking TV that won't look old next year and doesn't draw attention to itself at the expense of everything else.

2) Sony - and most other companies - no longer make a high end 32" model, which is stupid. My main TV is most likely to have a local computer nearby. It's the kitchen and the bedroom where I need the SMART features most. For that reason, this TV actually has very little competition.

3) USB ports. These are outstanding, especially if your network is too slow for streaming (or if you don't have a port nearby and your wireless is slow). Where my older Sony only plays some pictures off USB - and way too slow to actually want to use that feature, this newer Samsung can play almost all my media files locally or use a wireless mouse/keyboard. I have one USB port filled with a Logitech receiver, which allows me to use a mouse and keyboard I have stashed under the bed. Haven't actually bothered to use those yet (except for testing), but it's nice to know I could turn them up and use them without having to mess with any options. In the other USB port, I have a micro-SD card reader about the same size that always has 32GB of TV series that I can watch in a pinch, say if they put on some reality crap instead of a decent show that I was expecting over the air. Neither USB device can be seen except from the side. It reads the files on the micro-SD card directly from the source menu and as quickly as Windows Explorer.

4) DLNA. As much as I love that micro-SD card USB reader, you really don't even need it because the DLNA features are pretty mature. The fact that it reads .mkv files so easily, and you can control integrated subtitles and audio tracks so easily is amazing. My other TV requires transcoding for anything but MPEG, which really bogs down the processor on my laptop. I really recommend Wild Media Server because it works so well with both this and my Sony, and can easily spit 720p to both TVs (different shows) simultaneously. I couldn't get Serviio or Mezzmo to work as well. Samsung apparently has some freeware available that you might want to try as well.

All that said, despite the high contrast ratio, I don't feel like the picture is quite as good as my older Sony (which I believe only has a CR of 100,000:1), even after a lot of playing around. As you'd expect from its small size, it does play SD (and lower) very nicely on its screen without pixelization (Comment for 32" ONLY!). Even so, I love this TV for the bedroom, and felt the price was reasonable. It may get moved to replace the TV in the kitchen one day, and it will be great there, as well.

Also, I would prefer a browser with adjustable transparency over the TV, as the PIP version has the sound and picture cutting out sometimes. Even so, I would absolutely recommend this TV if you're looking for a 32"er.

Oh, but one more thing: I just had some apps "pushed" on me, like the cell phone companies do to your smart phone. If this continues, I'll be lowering my rating. I did not buy a TV to have a bunch of useless crap sold to me. A warning to you, Samsung.

[[VIDEOID:a23b5cd930e819bd2cae7872ede2dd37]] I decided to finally upgrade my Kindle from the first Paperwhite when I found out I could get a 25% discount and a $5 Amazon gift card for trading in my very old and unused Kindle Keyboard 1st gen, as well as other bonuses of 6 months free Kindle Unlimited (approx $60) plus a 30 day Audible trial.

I also am really happy to have buttons to turn the page again. It’s the ultimate laziness to be able to just keep your thumb in the button and depress it to turn the page instead of having to actually move your thumb a half inch to touch the screen, but hey, why move a half inch when your can push down 1/16th of an inch? All that extra movement add up over the years.
The real reason I like the buttons is this: I live in Alaska and we have very long, cold nights. But even in the winter, we turn down the heat at night. I read in bed every single night, tucked all cozy and warm under my down comforter... except for having to have my hand out in order to touch the screen on my Paperwhite to turn the page. My hand starts to get very cold. It’s uncomfortable. My half frozen hand takes away from my happy bedtime reading experience. I also like that you can select which button to the the page advance button and which is the page back button. The Oasis comes set up with the top button as the page advance and the bottom as the page back, but I switched them: the bottom is the advance, the top is the back. I hold my ereaders at the bottom sides, and had to stretch my thumb to advance the page when it was set for the top button. It’s just easier and more comfortable to use the bottom button. And this is cool: the bottom button stays as my page advance button even when I rotate the Oasis 180 to use left handed!! Smart!!

Others have covered the size and weight so I won’t go it I all that except to say it’s comfortable to hold. I do use the official Amazon Premium leather cover and it fits perfectly, and the magnetic closure/sleep/wake functions work perfectly also.

The books they are featuring for me are “romance” genre. I am sooo not a romance genre girl. I don’t believe I’ve ever purchased this genre in my life. I’m a hardcore sci-fi/dystopian. I have an adverse reaction when I see romance special offer.

Other than that, some of the complaints by others leaves me wondering.
I just don’t think it’s THAT big of deal that it has a micro usb. Really, it’s just not that hard to figure out the big end of the cable from the small end. As for charging speed, charge mine while I’m sleeping at night so it doesn’t matter if it takes 1 hour or 4. I suppose having to carry a micro usb cord and charger when other devices use a usb-c cord/charger may be annoying but I think I can find 2 square inches in my purse/pocket/bag/backpack for it.

Also remember that this is an e-reader. It’s not a tablet, computer or smartphone, nor does it make any claims to be. Expecting an ereader to function basically like a computer/tablet/smartphone is expecting too much. It does an outstanding job at doing it’s job as an ereader.

I have sent many different type of files to my Paperwhite using my kindle email address and it’s worked excellent with that old ereader, so I expect this new Oasis will do excellent with those as well.

My suggestion is to read the description fully and know what you are getting and what you aren’t.
If your reading experience will be destroyed because this doesn’t have (nor claim to have) a usb-c, then this isn’t the ereader for you.
If you want it to be like a tablet or smartphone or computer, this isn’t the ereader for you.

The printed manual is basic and you'll want to spend time reviewing the online documentation. Something I come back to again and again as I figure the FDRAX53/B out is the absolute wonder of it. The small size, the quality of images, the ease of operation -- I just can't get over it. Beyond sensational and well into the realm of magical. I've never seen anything like the FDRAX53/B before.

Having recently dug my music collection (odd how we go back into hobbies after years of stagnation), I took time to curate my setup (and by setup I mean my Note8 with a USB DAC) for optimal listening. Until recently, but "best" headphones were my Shure Aonic 4, which are excellent for the price range. The cable it comes with is okay, but preferably replaceable. It comes with an inline mic and makes a lot of feedback-noise when moved. I know cables are a mixed bag when it comes to audio equipment, so I shied away for years. But rather than place the emphasis on audio-quality improvement when looking at cables, I realized I'd rather get a cable if it looks and feels good. This one fit the ticket.

This is the only cable I have that's meant to be swapped with MMCX in-ear headphones. They pair well with the Aonic 4. First, I'll get the problems I have out of the way.

Since this cable is meant to connect with around-the-ear IEMs, there's a plastic wrap near each MMCX adapter. It makes wearing around the ears easier, but putting them on initially takes a few tries. They are easy to tangle, even if I use the "roadie wrap." Putting them on while on the go proved to be suboptimal; I have to be sitting or standing to put them on.

Sometimes I get some feedback noise, but rarely. Definitely not the same as the stock cable that comes with the Aonic 4.

The biggest problem I have is that the end connection disconnects nearly every time I use the cable. Having a modular cable is awesome, but the connection from the cable to the audio jack doesn't lock. I expected there to be a click, indicating it's on and snug, but no such thing. Since I use this cable while on the go, it's connected to my phone, which rests in my pocket. At least once the cable end will come loose. It's easy to press back in (just a little nudge will do), but it is rather annoying.

Now for the good.

The cable feels awesome. I get now why people prefer to upgrade certain cables. I care very little for how much the audio quality is "improved" (there's too much immeasurable subjectivity in that area), but having a cable that doesn't tangle easily and is very light makes enough of a difference to justify the upgrade. The cable is soft to the touch, though I don't doubt its ruggedness in the long term. The MMCX connectors snap satisfactorily into the Shure IEMs; at least those haven't come loose. The metal ends and Y-splitter are very nice and definitely attribute the cable with a premium look.

This cable has sold me on the reasons to upgrade headphone cables.

I travel quite a bit and many of the trips I take are short in duration- often only two or three nights. I don’t need a lot of luggage space for these short trips and I like taking backpacks because I can often avoid carry- on and baggage fees if my backpack can fit under my seat. This desire for economical travel led me to get the Case Logic BRYBPR116 Bryker Backpack Roller.

With this Case Logic Backpack, you get a two-in-one backpack and piece of luggage well suited for travel or business. The wheels make it perfect for traversing an airport and with the added straps, you can carry it on your back, like a traditional backpack. There is an outside pocket where you can tuck the straps so they are not hanging out, flopping around when you don’t need them. And the handle can be completely pushed inside the backpack and sealed off with a zipper so that no one sees it. I like these qualities because it means I can make this look like a backpack when I want it to and I can make it look more like a piece of luggage when I want it to.

Inside the backpack, there is a separate compartment for a laptop and I like that you can unsnap this if you like, making for a larger interior space that is just right for stuffing your two- day supply of clothing and personal items. Like I said, my primary usage with this backpack is for travel and I usually don’t take my laptop with me when I’m on a two- day trip, so I would rather have the open space, to make it more like a piece of luggage.

There is one thing to keep in mind if you take this backpack on a plane, and that is the size of pack makes it only barely able to fit under your seat. It will stick out some, so be prepared to have a snug space where your feet normally go. And unlike other backpacks, it’s too rigid- thanks to the handle- to make it collapsible and flexible. To save having to pay carry- on fees on certain airlines, I am willing to place it under the airline seat in front of me regardless, even if it does stick out some. If your flying on an airline that doesn’t charge extra for carry-ons, then this won’t be an issue since you can easily place the backpack in the overhead, which is what I recommend doing. For everyone else, just bear in mind that the length of the backpack makes it a challenge to fit under a seat.

I have a wide assortment of backpacks and luggage in my home to accommodate different needs. This Case Logic rolling backpack is a nice addition to my collection and I like that it performs a dual role. It has suited me well so far and it makes a good choice of luggage/backpack for business people and others who are constantly on the go for short spans of time.

I have worked with a lot of different headphones, mostly active noise canceling (ANC) phones but also more traditional phones. Over the years I have had several Sennheiser phones and they typically have balanced sound and good build quality. This set is a step down from many of the others with which I have worked, though they’re still decent.

My preference on headphones is over-the-ear phones which for me are more comfortable. These particular phones are on-ear, and these pinch a little after extended wear. They’re better than some of the other on-ear phones with which I have worked, but I still prefer over-the-ear phones. One preference I have is a headphone that clamps down fairly tightly when worn so they’re less likely to slip off when I tilt my head down; these are a lighter fit.

These are Bluetooth-only phones and as such cannot be used with non-BT devices. This is unfortunate but isn’t a deal-breaker. These connect easily and quickly.

These are not ANC phones, but they have excellent passive noise canceling which is quite surprising for on-ear phones. They reduce ambient noise in my office considerably, which us especially noticeable when running a large fan that I use to generate white noise. I am pleased with that aspect of these phones. These are still not as effective as a set of ANC phones.

The sound profile is fairly typical of Sennheiser phones, though the bass is mildly beefed up.. The trend with phones these days is overdriven bass, and these do increase the bass response a little bit but not to a headache-inducing level. The midrange is full and warm, and that’s a good thing as many times the increased bass comes at the expense of the midrange. The highs are bright and clear without being piercing. Overall, the sound is reasonably balanced, but certainly not audiophile quality.

Build-wise, these actually feel a bit on the cheaper side which is surprising. These aren’t exactly fragile, but they are definitely not of the same build quality as other Sennheisers I have used in the past.

These are probably best described as entry-level headphones. They’re not the highest quality, and they are not the most sturdy, but the sound quality is fine and the cost is right. The main thing I would change is the addition of an audio port so they could be used as wired phones.

I have a set of Bose QC-15 headphones and I damaged the pads some time ago. I was able to find replacements, though the original Bose pads are quite expensive. I have been looking for good replacement pads that are less expensive and I have tried some off-brand pads in an effort to save money. So far I have found none that are an exact match though I have seen some that are quite close. These are a reasonable match though they are definitely different than the original pads, but at a fraction of the cost.

In appearance these are close to the originals though they are smaller and they do not fit exactly the same. When I put on the headphones with these pads in place, I have to fiddle with the phones a little bit to get them to fit right, more so than when these had the original pads. It’s a noticeable difference but it is not a real problem unless you have to have an exact match.

The pads are soft, but not as subtle and buttery as the original pads. They will soften over time with use, but brand new they are slightly more stiff.

The main difference I have found with these pads is that they do not do as good a job with passive noise canceling as the original pads. I replaced one pad with one of these new pads and put them on my head. With a fan on in the background I listened closely. The new pad allowed more ambient noise to reach my ear than did the original pad. As it softens I think it will fit a little better and will help with the noise isolation, but even new the Bose original pads did more for sound isolation. They still do a good job, just not as good.

So, why would you consider these? There are two good reasons to buy these. First, these are a LOT less expensive than the Bose replacements. At under $10 these represent a very significant savings over the manufacturer’s own replacement pads. Second, although these are different than Bose replacements, they do a good job of making the phones look new and they do the job well enough for most people. The phones are plenty comfortable with the new pads on and unless you are looking for difference you probably would not notice.

These are good pads to consider if you need replacement pads for your headphones and you don’t mind the small differences. If you have to have 100% identical pads, these aren’t what you’re looking for. If you are content with approximately 85% the same, these are a very inexpensive alternative to Bose replacement pads.

System preferences>sound>output>slide that over to MacBook Pro speakers and take it off that Z1 crap. (That took me a while too.)

I received this as a free review sample. This is NOT a bluetooth device. These phones are strictly for 3.5mm stereo connections. That means that this will work with a wider variety of devices.

The sound quality to my ears is why I awarded it five stars. There is definitely a crossover built into these phones because I could hear the separation of low and high frequencies, with a prominent bass in one ear. Also, there does not seem to be any compression at the high end of the frequency spectrum, which gives these phones a more natural sound. I listen to mainly acoustic jazz (piano jazz trios, vocalists, and similar), so I appreciate the realistic sound these phones provide.

There are a few areas that I would love to see improved: the cable is long and would be nicer if it were flat, tangle-proof. Also, the controls are a little too high up on the cable in my opinion. I can easily reach them, but when testing them I could not see the buttons. Of course, those are not show stoppers - just my own preferences. And regarding the controls, I already am familiar with their placement from use and memory, so that is really a non issue.

The phones are comfortable. They ship with small, medium and large tips and I used the ones that were already installed. The fit was perfect. These also ship with an extra set of premium, noise blocking tips. I have not tried them since the regular tips are more than adequate for me.

Other nice features are the zippered, hard case, velcro cable wrap and shirt clip. To be sure, they are value-added items, but the real value is the sound quality and these phones have that without a doubt.

Bottom line: if you want hard wired phones that allow you to listen critically to music (or transcribe it), this is a surprisingly inexpensive solution. I have used everything from high end studio in-ear monitors and premium phones, and these come close at a much more affordable price. I am not saying that these are as good as the expensive phones, but am saying that bang for your buck these are hard to beat and will surprise most audiophiles.

It comes with a wide angle lens (that is oddly called "macro", but no- it's not for macro shots, its for going wider) which screws on to the front, as well as a handle mounting bracket, an LED light and a microphone. It even comes with a 64GB card, a spare battery, and not one but TWO useful carrying cases (a large one for everything, and a smaller one for just the camera solo). But that's about all the positives I can say about it. If you are outside with a lot of light, you can get decent shots, but this isn't a zoom lens, the zoom is digital only. You can go wide with the external lens or just stay at a fixed medium without it. So no closeup shots for soccer moms. The dynamic range when using it indoors was pretty bad, worse than your average mid-range cell phone. Forget about low light. But that's ok, because the ergonomics of a camera make it better than a cell phone, right?
Well, sorta. Holding it with the strap and the flip out screen is nice. But the UI is confusing, it's hard to go back and watch clips you took because everything is kind of sluggish and not intuitive- once we went past the first page of recorded clips, it was really difficult to move to the next page without accidentally clicking and opening a clip for playback. It just feels really laggy to navigate. Then there's the mic input... it's actually a proprietary plug that goes into the charging/USB plug, and gives you a pigtail for USB on one side and a mic input jack on the other. Odd, considering it COMES with a mic, you'd think it would have an input directly on the body. But no, just this weird mess of wires. Everything about this feels like jumping through a hoop to make it do what you want, and at the end of the day you have to wonder if you couldn't just be better off getting a mic adapter for the cellphone you already own and putting it in one of those holster cages.
Speaking of cell phones, this does have an app which supposedly lets you remotely control and perhaps even copy files from it, but I didn't get that far. I tried to install the app but then gave up when I decided I didn't want to grant this all the permissions it wanted from my personal phone. And I didn't think the video quality was worth it either.
Oddly enough, I kind of like the accessories it comes with. The LED light is pretty nice, the mic isn't terrible either. But for the money, I feel like I would have rather skipped those accessories and just gotten a better camera for a little bit more. It feels almost like they realized this camera was a hard sell so they beefed it up with lots of a accessories for the price.
In conclusion, you DO get a lot of accessories for the money. It's not the worst camera I've ever used, and you can't really get a set with everything you need for any less so I'd say it's worth at least 3 stars for being a functional kit. But I can't really imagine a scenario that I would recommend it.

MY HISTORY WITH THIS PRODUCT:
I've owned this headset for almost a full year. Technically, I've had two of them, since the boom mic snapped off the first one and had it replaced. I use these every day, for multiple hours and a variety of uses (VoIP calls, gaming, music, and movies).

PROS:
The audio quality, when it is working, is good. The bass in 7.1 mode is great, and the overall surround sound is pretty convincing. They are comfortable and rechargeable via USB.

CONS:
The biggest problem here is the wireless connection. Both headsets I owned suffered from this same problem - they would frequently just restart or lose the signal and reconnect. The process takes about 3-5 seconds each time, and sometimes you get multiple restarts in a row. It doesn't sound too bad until it happens when you're watching a movie and you have to quickly pause or rewind a bit because you suddenly couldn't hear anything they were saying (which also completely pulls you out of the movie), or when it drops out in the middle of a phone conversation, or drops out at the worst possible moment in a game... It happens probably two dozen times a day, if not more. At first, I didn't care too much about it, but the first time you have it drop out 3 times in a matter of a single minute, it's simply maddening. Imagine going randomly deaf for several seconds throughout every day of your life, and you'll get a sense of what it's like.

If I could simply plug the cable in and it would use the USB cable to transmit the audio instead of wireless, that would be perfect, but when it's plugged in, it simply charges the internal battery - you still get audio interruptions all the time. The interruptions will also reset the "mute" status on the mic, which can be troublesome if you're intentionally muted on a conference call and suddenly your mic is on and people hear you eating lunch.

Second problem is that the power button is a bit flaky. If the headset is plugged in via USB and powered off, sometimes it will not power on unless you unplug the headset and THEN power it on (and then you can plug it back in to continue charging). I thought it was a defect in my first headset until the same thing happened with the second one.

A minor third problem is that the boom mic is a little flimsy on the construction. I am careful with my toys, but it still cracked and finally snapped off one day when I was lowering the mic to use it, and that was only a few months into owning it.

OVERALL:
If they would fix the wireless, I would rate this 4 stars in a heartbeat. If they fixed the power button, it would go up to 5. That said, the G35 seems to be the G930 but wired, and cheaper. The number of times that I've wanted to really make good use of the wireless (go to another room and keep the audio going) is far less frequent than the dozens upon dozens of times that the audio cuts out, so it's just an unacceptable point for me, since that is what this headset is about.

This is a really nice looking mini speaker that is styled after a guitar amp. It allows you to connect any portable device that has a 3.5mm connection. I used it with a couple of different tablets (Fire, Nexus and iPad) with great results.

I love how easy the controls are to use! No fumbling around with mini buttons – nice big old- style knobs you turn. The settings are marked 1 to 10 (sorry, no going to 11).

The sound quality is pretty good. It’s somewhat tinny and gets harsh at loud volume, but for normal listening it puts out a more than acceptable sound. The bass and treble controls make a noticeable impact on the sound – more so than I expected given the price.

There’s a cutout on the top to hold a phone. This is not an active dock – all devices are attached using a 3.5mm cord. The cutout is just that – a simple cutout that holds the phone.

It can be powered by 4 AA batteries (not included), a wall adapter (included) or a USB cable (included). I use it mainly with the wall adapter, but it’s nice that it can be made fully portable with standard batteries.

Misses are mostly minor. The battery door is held on with screws, so you need to have a screwdriver if you want to swap out the AA batteries. Also, the flap covering the “dock” port on the top is on the flimsy side.

This is something that you get more for the look rather than the sound quality (although the sound quality is pretty good as well). It’s one of the more novel looking small speakers I’ve seen, and well worth a 5 star rating.

I've had these earbuds for a few months now and thought I'd revise my review.

My main gripe with these expensive but ultimately underwhelming earbuds is that they make a "thwomping" sound inside your ear drum whenever you jog or walk fast with them. I was at the gym recently and the sound of the earbuds jostling about in my ears was distracting. I don't recall ever having that problem with cheaper earbuds. This sound persisted even after I customized the buds to fit the shape of my ear.

On the positive side, the sound is decent though the bass and treble weren't that impressive. Its most effective feature was the noise-cancelling feature, which effectively blocked out any other noise. It worked so well that I would never use these buds while driving, crossing traffic or walking alone home late at night. With the spate of iPhone robberies, it's better to be able to hear a stranger's footsteps behind you. It's perfect, however, when you're on a subway or a bus and you want to block out that annoying person next to you who insists on complaining about her day.

The set includes a microphone for your iphone, which I don't use that much but works well enough - I heard my friend's voice on the other end of the line in very crisp, clear tones.

What's convenient is that the buds work with even the oldest ipods around. From the classic 2009 model to the most up to date Nano. Sony was smart to do this - that means a lot of people, not just techies with the most up-to-date devices, can use this. As an example, a friend of mine still has a working iPod mini (don't laugh, he's a Luddite!) and we tested the headset on that too. Surprisingly, it worked! - though the volume controls did not work with such an old, outdated model.

Another convenience is the location of the controls, which are located on a box located on the cord, which prevents you from having to reach all the way down to your iPod or iPhone to adjust the volume. My second favorite feature is the included clip, which allows me to wind up any slack on the cord and prevent it from getting tangled easily. In the past, I've killed so many earbuds because I pulled too hard on the cord by accident, so this is a welcome feature.

This deluxe model includes a pouch that offers an array of different sized earbuds - one set is noise-cancelling, while the other isn't. This is overkill, though. I tried out different sets of buds but none of them fit just right. And the "thwoping" sound I mentioned earlier still remained.

So I have mixed feelings about this product. The "thwomping" (sucking) sound is its biggest drawback for me, as the buds work best when you don't move around a lot.

This is a nice little set of radios, improved from my last three-pack of similarly priced Motorolas, but has some room for improvement.

Goods:

+ Good size - small enough, but big enough to fit in your hand comfortably like a radio should. Yes, it could be smaller, but at some point you don't really want smaller.

+ Some basic options to customize, mostly the noises the radios make. LCD screen shows you what you need to know.

+ Batteries can be charged while in the radios via standard Micro USB adapters - two are included. One charges one radio while the other charges two simultaneously.

+ Belt clip included. Head sets can be added.

Bad:

- While it's great that the battery packs can be charged via USB and the chargers are accepted worldwide (whereas my previous set for work had barrel connections to the charger and I burnt one out the first night I tried to charge due to being in Europe, the battery/charger setup is still imperfect for two reasons:

1) Battery packs are not three separate batteries that could be charged with other chargers and switched with other batteries (think Eneloop). My Garmin topo GPS came with actual rechargeable batteries that could be used elsewhere. This makes sense when you want to be able to carry standard alkaline batteries for emergencies/backup. These battery packs are great that they can be replaced with AA when necessary, but not as good as standard, replaceable rechargeable batteries (but you can use rechargeable batteries as your backup batteries).

2) N-MH doesn't make sense for this application because these are the type of batteries that develop a "memory". If you use these every day for work, then you want to recharge them every night. Actually, you would be inclined to recharge every time you want to use them, period, to be sure you get the most from the batteries. But because of the memory, you really want to discharge them fully. The appropriate type of battery would be Li-ion, because they would be chargeable every night AND would last longer. This is the biggest negative to this rig. If the battery packs were Li-ion, I would not care that they are packs versus separate batteries.

- Belt clip should be taken off to remove battery cover without beating the two up. This is apparently an obvious issue to the manufacturer because they have a protective piece of plastic between the two for shipment.

Neutral (strange):

Two standard USB chargers included, at 500mA output each (1A would be minimum standard and expected these days, but whatever; they may have done this to avoid overcharging overnight). Both have the same rated input, but the output is the same (samex2 on the 2 output charger). That actually doesn't make sense, unless the single charger is half as efficient (or they are just too lazy to change the nameplate). Not really sure what's up with that, but I sort of like the 2-output charger. I expect most people have so many USB chargers laying around that they'll use whatever is at hand anyway vice these.
